- Totirg. PROSPERITY3AND ADVERSITY. 'Fair smiling Fortune but we are strong When with free hand she doth bestow her favour! And in our hearts youth sings a valiant song, And to our taste life bath not lost its savour. Grief, anguish—these are sounds that have no,sense, 'While the world's toys and treasures wait to charm us; Such dolour may be, but with insolence Of strength untried we doubt its power to harm us; And God ?—Well, of a truth, in lives begirt By prosperous comfort nothing more is needed; Too oft we take the gift as our desert, And letthe gracious Giver go unheeded. Anon there comes athwart the sunny skies The,shadow of misfortune and grim sorrow; And laughter changes into weary sighs. And the dark day threatens a darker morrow; And Joy, who proffered once a cup of bliss, Hath only draughts whereat the soul will sicken; And Pleasure is a hag whose hollow kiss Can never more our jaded senses quicken. Then to our God right humbly do we kneel, L*Ev weak and waywaritchildren justfr chidden! ~ We Adice not, His smile, but quickly feel-. The blank which follews when His face is hidden. Wherefore, although prosperity be sweet, And every want seem answered, this possessing, If it but lead us to the mercy seat Adversity shall prove the greater blessing. —Sydney Grey in Sunday at Home. •

thoughts of God.. - 1 A good word is an easy obligation, and not, to speak ill -1 requires only our silence. He who strives after a long and pleasfmt form of life • must seek to attain continued equanimity. CUTIING.--;" You dear thing," she said gushingly— "how handsoine your bonnet does loc&I. I'm sure it looks as well as it did last spring !" Mrs. Mulvaney, the • laundress: " indade, ma'am, an' it's miserable I am. I'm just on me feet with the paia in my back, an' Jimmy he's as bad off; .he has a cough on i'm that sounds bike an empty bar'l. Cough- for the

lady, Jimmy !" Let no young man ever permit it to enter his mini I that economy is meanness, or that it is to be despised. It is he who saves who can afford to givet and nothing is mean which is honest; and which goes to establigh one's independence. The sweetest thing on earth is. to be forgotten'hydl with the exception of those who love us. All else brings more trouble than joy, and as soon as we have com- pleted our task here, and fulfilled our mission, the best thing for us to do is to disappear altogether. Gentility is neither in birth, wealth, manner,, nor fashion, but in mind. A high sense of honour, a deter- mination never to take a mean advantage of another,-sai adherence to truth, delicacy' and psliteness towards those with whom we have dealings, are the essential characteristics of a gentleman. A very loquacious lady, calling one day to consult:her ,1 physician, talked on and on with such volubility that the latter could not get in a word edgeways. Growing impatient he at length told her to put out her tongue, which she did. He then said: "Now rkeasekeepit there till you have heard what I have got to -say to you." Jeames knocks a cup off the mantel, shivering it into *thousand fragments. His mistress, .nearing the noise, rushes in, and stands for a moment stupefied byike result of her servant's awkwardness. .44 Oh," She cries, with tears in her eyes, "my beautiful old Sevres:" "Oh," exclaims Raines, in a joyous tone, a seraphic smile spreading all over his' face, "I was so frightened at first. ma'am I thought it was something new,

ma'am." Lord Brougham used to tell the story of the crossing- sweeper to whom be was accuotomed, when a little bay, to give a penny every Sunday nsorning on his road to church. One Sunday afternoon the beggar demanded a second penny, but the child replied that lie had already given him one before. " Aye; but that is gone. Now do give me another—there's a good boy." "Oh, but you mustn't expect me to be a good toy twice a day," was the reply of the future economist. Few persons are -so debased as to form-evil or low de- signs deliberately; on the contrary, most people Wish to do good and to further good objects. It-is in the pro- 1 cess. in the attempts to carry out these plans, when ob- stacles arise, and mingled motives present themselves, that their mental and moral defects appear. Only as the character is true and pure and faithful will the methods adopted be guileless and effective, and only by the best and truest methods can high aims and ncibla purposes be thoroughly fulfilled. "What is lifer someone asked Montford. His answer was one of the most charming things ever written "The present life is sleeping and waking; it is 'good- night' on going to bed, and good morning" -on getting up; it is to wonder what the day will bring forth;- it is rain on the window as one sits by the fire; it is to walk in the garden and see the flowers and hear the birds sing; it is to have news from the east, west, north, and south; it is to read old books and new books; it is to see pictures and hear music; it is to have Sundays; it is topray with family morning and evening; it is to sit little twilight and meditate; it is to have breakfast and dinner andtea ; it is to belong to a town and have neighbours and to be- come one in a circle of acquaintanoes; it is to have friends and love; it is to have sight of dear old faces, and with some men it is to be kissed with the same loving lips fifty years; and it is to knew themselves thought of many times a day, in many places, by.children and grand- children sad an friends. AMATEUR MEDICAL TREATMMIT.—CaStOr Oil is the foandation of amateur medical treatment in Italy. If anybody is angry, very angry—a dose of castor oil; if violently shocked and startled—a dose of castor oil; if in deep grief—a dose of castor oil—and this because any sudden, intense, and dispieasinn emotion "makes bad blood." The oil is not given iminediately, but very soon in six or seven hours, and a good large dose of it. The next day the dosed one must diet, a " senuniss'7, a peculiarly disagreeable, thin farina water gruel, slightly salted, a cup or two of very weak broth, and a small • quantity of thin dry toast, being all the nourishment al- lowed for twenty-four hours after the dose. -Sometimes the'dose:of oil is preceded by a hot foot bath, whin mustard and salt, buena always. The castor oil, gives as above stated, is looked upon as a supreme and universal panacea, and probably. the principleis a right one, so, at least, physicians say. They would zay the same un- doubtedly of the popular remedy for the sting of a scorpion, practised throughout the length and breadth of Italy, and invented by some man or woman whose name has long since been lost in the mists of the ages which have elapsed since first the remedy was applied. It is a distinct instance of similia similibus, and is pre- pared in the following manner. A living scorpion is dropped into a wide-necked glass bottle which contains a few drops of olive oil of the finest quality. More oil is poured oft instantly, until the bottle is filled and the scorpion dead. In its struggles to free itself it ejects all its poison into the oil, and this poisoned oil forms a sovereign remedy which homceopathists would approve of on very rational grounds. It is doubtful, however. whether they, or any other medical men, would approve of the "application of the comb," as practised in Lom- bardy and the Venetian provinces. This remedy is highly unique and reflects honour upon the'originality of the brain which first conceived it. It is applied forchronie dyspepsia, and acute internal inflammation of all kinds; the reader's imagination may fill the blank, and need hesitate at none of the evils common to man or woman. The sufferer is laid upon a bed, and firmlFheld by assistants—ten of -whom have sometimes been required in the case of a strong man—the comb is then prepared and applied. It must be a very old comb, and a very dirty one—the dirtier the better—and it is wrapped in tow which has been well:soaked in oil and alcohol. So prepared, it is -placed on:the bare stomach of the victim, is set alight, blazes for a moment, and is then coveredliby a bowl or soup-plate (slightly raised on one side), under which it is allowed to 'smoulder until the tow is reduced to ashes, ailorofosm. and ether:being either unknown to, or mortally dreaded by, the Italian peasants, the agony:ndured by the wretched beings to whom the" comb" is applied may "Letter be imagined than described. It is said that the screams of persons subjected to this torture are audible sometimes at a distance of two miles. But sound travels far on these vast, tranquil plains.—London Society. economise his strength. - A three-year-old disce-yered a neighbour's hens scratch- ing in the garden. In a most indignant tone she reported to her mother that the hens from next, door were " wiping their feet on our grass." "Mr. Smith," asked the professor of natural history, "which animal exhibits the greatest susceptibility for attaching itself to the human race?" Smith, after re- flecting, " Ah—er—l think the leech, professor." A drunken parishioner was admonished by his parson. ' "I can go into the village,' concluded the latter, "and I come home again without getting drunk." "Ah, reeenis- ter, but I'm sae popular." was the aPologetic repiy. I "You will lose yotir pocket-handkerchief," said one of his friends to George Coleman, whom he met walking up the Haymarket. "Not if you will pass on," replied Cole- man, as he stood still for a moment and waited-for his friend to go by. "That broth's no guid," said a grumbling yeungster at the dinner table in a Scotch farm. "Weal, weel;" says his mother, a quiet -sort/ of body, "if ye don't tak' yer broth you'll no get ‘ony beef, an' if ye tak' yer broth you'll no need ony." Method in everything is incalculably valuable. It pro- motes comfort. It caves a large expenditure of time. It avoids numberless inconveniences. It is of great mo- ment in relation to Mind and character; and it is essen- tial to the despatch of all business; for that which is well-arranged proceeds with ease anciregularity. All shams, all shallow and impeded work, one with- out earnestness or for gain and show, must .eeTentually be as destitute of reel beauty as they are of practical use. But, just as a true diamond gains in lustre by , polishing that would wear away a false stone,sc superior work honourably performed is capable of taking on it , more and more beauty with every fresh effort. 1 "This is my last 'birthday," said a handsome girl to her adorer on the twenty-ninth of August. " That do you mean ?" lie exclaimed, clutching at his heart. "You are not going to die, are you ?" "Well, I should hope not, I'm twenty-one to-&.s, and a woman never has e. birth- day after that you ktiow." He remembered then that they didn't. The Rev. Mr. Thom, a former minister of Govan, and a wag in his way, was once appointed by the Presbytery to assist at the induction of a young man, of whose talents lie did not entertain a very high opinion. On his ' return home, late in the evening, he met a friend, who I asked him " whaur he bad been ?" Mr. Thom told him. , "And. did you," said his friend, "ride your puir auld ' 1 mear a' that road and back again ?—you'ilkill the puir beast." "An' if it should, John," replied the .minister, "it'll be only killing ac-beast by settling anither." Will Gordon was the town officer of his day in May- hole. Being at a roup at Kilhensie, lie was offered some drink, Which he had not declined. Sir Adam Furgueson, -of Kilkerran, passing by, accosted him—" Ah, Gordon, 1 you should never think .so early in the day." "Deed, HSir Adam," said Gordon • "you can drink when you I like, but I maim drink wl:en I can get it:" One wintry day Gordon found himself very drouthy at Slateferd,and going into a public-house there, lie "drank his shoes." When stepping out again, he was . heard thus to soli- locinise--" Step forrit, bereft Gordon, if it's no' ease, tiVain ye!". There was a man in theenountain region of Tennessee who was a stereotyped candidate for localeiffices of all deceriptions, but who woUld never give a decided opinion on any question. On one oecasion, when he was a can- didate for the position of fiheriff, there was great excite- meat with respect to the enforcement of a. school-tax. He addressed rather a large gathering, but evaded the only.question the audience wanted to hear about; and, just as he was closing, a fellow shouted, "Tell us about the school-tax—are you for at or are you not ?" The crowd cheered; and the orator, thug pressed for a de- claration of opinion, said," Gentlemen, you have a right' to ask for an answer. I have no concealment to make. I am a frank man; and to you if say in all frankness, if it is a good thing, I am for it, and if it is a bed thing, I am aglif it." . . . LITTLH , SCOTCH GRANITE.—"LittIe Scotch/Granite!' What a curious name to give any one. Yes, but it was appropriate. The boy who got, it was firm and steadfast in the line of truth and duty, and his playmates, know- ing what a strong, solid thing granite is, gave him this , name, not in derision, but in a cempliment, as we shall , see :—Burt and Johnnie Lee were delighted when their Scotch cousin came to live with them. He was little, but very bright and full of fun. He could tell curious tliines ;bout his home in Scotland. Ile was as far ad- vanced in his studies as they were, and the first day he went to school they thought him remarkably good. He wasted no time in play when he should have been study- ing, and he advanced finely. At Right, before the clese of the school, the teacher called the roll, and the boys began to answer." Ten." When Willie understood that he was to say "Ten" if he had not whispered during the day, he replied—" I have whispered." "More than once ?" " Yes, sir;" answered Willie. "As many as ten times ?" " May be I have," faltered Willie. "Then I shall mark you zere," said the teacher sternly, "and that is a great disgrace." ." Why, I did not see you whisper ,once," said Johnnie that night after school. "Well, I did," said Willie; "I saw others doing it, and so I asked to borrow a book; then I lent a slate pencil and asked a boy for a knife, and did several other things. I sup- posed it was allowed:" "Oh, we all do it," said Burt, reddening. , '!` There ifP:f t, any sense in the old rule, and nobolay could keep it, nobody does." "I will, or else I will say I haven't," said Willie. "Do you suppose I will : tell ten lies in one heap?' "Oh, we don't called them lies," muttered Johnnie. ' " There wouldn't be a credit among us at nightif we were so strict." " What of that, if you told the truth?" laughed Willie, bravely. In a shorttime the boys all saw hoWit was with him. He studied hard, played with all his might in play time, but according to his account he lost more credits than any of the rest. After some weeks the boys answered" Nine" and "Eight" oftener than they used to. Yet the school- room seemed to have grown quieter. ' Sometimes, when Willie Grant's mark was even lower than usual the teacher would smile peculiarly, but said no more of ells- • grace. Willie never preached et them or told tales; but clean cloth by the half-soiled somehow it made the boys ashamed of themselves, just h ns tgu they ; 1.11 ey tine-eyed:boy must tell the truth. one, and they felt like cheats and story tellers. They talked the seeing einltgw that aSp this utti • him all over, and loved him, if they did nickname him ' "Scotch Granite," he was so firm about a preinise. Well, at the end of the term, " Willie's name was ,very low • down on the credit list. When it was read he had hard i work not to cry, for he was very sensitive, and he had tried hard to be perfect. But the very last thing that day was a speech by the teacher, who told of once cloak. He was passing seeing a man muffled up in a c that - - t the man was him without a look, when he was told .. signs of his rank General —,the great. hero. "The. e __ re just the same," said were hidden, the hero was the hat I mean I the teacher. "And now, boys, you will see what bo F when I give a little gold medal to the most faithful y —the one really the most conscientiously ' pe .rfect in his . 1 Ate deportment' among you. Who shall have it?' "L Scotch Granite !" shouted forty boys at once, for the child whose name was so low on the credit list, had made truth noble in their eves. HORSE SHOW' AT BISHOP AUCKLAND.—The second an- nual show of the South-Western Durham Cart Horse Club was held on Thursday at Bishop Auckland. There were eleven entries, and the whole of them made their appearance in the prize ring. After a long and careful examination, the judges selected Hertford, Border Buck, exhibited by Mr. Crawford, of Bridekirk Mains, Annan ; and Baron of Buck, shown. ,by Mr. Drummond, of Pit- carthie, Annan, thus passing over several prize-takers at other shows. Mr. Forshaw's Hertford, a bay Shire horse rising four years old, was awardedthe prise (50). During last month the winner was exhibited at the Agricultural Hall, Islington, and in a class of 88 he succeeded in se- curing the fourth place. The Club's prize horse of last year, Wyndham,'has received a premium of £lOO to travel in Aberdeenshire. , .DAIRY MANAGEMENT. Primrose .M'Connell, writing on Dairy Management, says :--" The feeding of a dairy cow is a subject of vast importance in the general management, and one on which a great deal—perhaps most—of the efficiency of the animal depends. In order to understand the subject sufficiently well, it is necessary to become acquainted with the analyses of the various foods and:the part each ingredient plays in the animal' economy, especially with reference to their influence on the production of milk. The substances found in a food are water, albumenoids or flesh-formers (nitrogenous), 'fats or hydrocarbons, starch, sugar; &c. (carbohydrates), fibre, and ash. Water is found in all foods to a greater or lesser extent, and acts simply as a vehicle or solvent for the others. The nitrogenous substances (albuininoids) are more directly utilised in the tissues to repair the waste and supply material for the growth of the flesh or, muscle, but can also go to the formation of fat. The fats and earbohy drates are primarily utilised for combustion in the lungs in the act of respiration, whereby the animal heat is kept up, any surplus being deposited as fat in the tissues. The fats thus act as savers of tile albuminoids ; and research goes to prove that the fats of the milk are not derived from the fats of the food, brit from the alburninoids. In practice we find that a large supply of starchy or sugary food, such as maize or rice, is not followed by any marked increase either in the butter or total solids, but that a very small quantity of albuminiod food, such as bean-meal or decorticated cotton-cake, is immediately followed by an increase of cream, total solids, and quantity. For food purposes one of fat is reckoned equivalent to 2.44 of starch, while the fibre, though having much the same chemical composition as starch, is more or less indiges- tible, and is only of tage to give bulk to the food. The ash is composed of the mineral matters, and is Drinci- phlly represented by phosphates; and as such goes to form the small quantity of these found in milk, and of use in the animal system for the building up of the bony frame. Common salt is a mineral substance of vast importance for the health of all animals, as about half of the Solids of the blood are composed of this, and cows require about 4 or. daily, which must be either given in their food, or by allowing them access to lumps of rock-salt about the pastures. It has been found in practic3 thatthe nitrogenous and the non-nitrogenous elements of food must bear a certain proportion to one another for healthy and economical feeding, and in the case of milk cows this ratio is one of albuminoids to five of nitrogenous matters for winter feed, but that grass has a ratio of one to three, the difference being due to the ,fact that a larger amount of heat producers is needed in the cold season -than in summer. This is further borne out in practice, when we find that the rations used and found to be suitable to workout to the figures of this proportion. Two pounds of albuininoids will keep a cow . living, such as we find in twenty-five pounds of hay; but for milking, some five or six pounds are necessary; and cake would require to be added on. The manurial value, and also the market value of purchase foods, must be taken into ac- count, as these may have a great influence on the general success or economy of the.eystem. In summer there is nothing which can beat good grass, and inferior pasture may be improved by giving a pound or two of cotton-cake daily to ,each animal. Meals and foods of that nature ought to be given in the shape of warm mashes, as there is nothing Which so helps to keep up the flow of milk as warm food in winter. Some cows respond more readily to good food than others, and those 'which do not increaseaccording,to the standard of feed- ing adopted ought to -be weeded out and sent to the butcher's. Washy feeds, such as brewers' grains, yield a very large flow of milk, but it will be low in solids, and the animals will very soon wear out. Even turnips or other roots are objectionable', their feeding value is not high, while there is great danger of their giving a bad flavour to the produce. Again,i roots are a very expen- sive crop to grow, and ft s to be hoped that ensilage will take their place, and that very soon. This latter promises to be one of the most valuable substances for winter food yet produced, as there is almost universal testimony in its favour, both .the quantity and quality of the milk being inapseved by its use when properly made. Though we can increase the total solids by good food, we cannot increase any one ingredient of the milk without .also increasing them all. The ratio of ingre- dients remains the same, any difference being due more to breed and individuality. Exercise develops the caseine, as on poor land, while rest (as whendthe animals are tied up) is conducive to formation of butter fats.'i

THE ENSILAGE COMMISSION. ' This Commission has resumed its sittings at.the Agri- cultural Department of the Privy Council, Lord Walsing- ham presiding. Professor fames Long, a member of the Committee appointed by the Royal Agricultural Society to visit the stacks and silos in the kingdom, was called. He -said he had considerable experience in regard to the maize crop both at home and abroad. He planted the Giant Caragna maize from French seed, which was recommended by Professor Leconteux. All other kinds have failed with him. He put it in about the sth or 6th of June, and cut it in the milky stage the first week in October, when it had ceased to grow. The crop weighed about 16 or 17 tons per acre. After his maize crop he put on 20 tons of fariuyard manure. Maize was not an exhaustive,crop, ,it cleaned the land better than turnips. For a silo he would most recommend a plain brick building cemented inside, round corners, with dry earth as a weighing ma- terial. Of course, if the earth were mixed with the con- tents of the silo it would rather spoil it; but in prac-- tice it does not become mixed. It does not take much time to shovel off the earth. Bran was an entire failure for that purpose. He had not found in practice that the earth got mixed with the silage. He had seen in a silo in France sawdust used, and when it was taken off and •the top-crust removed, he found it did not permeate in the slightest degree beyond half an inch. The Commit- tee were very favourably impressed with the stacks. The loss on the outside of those stacks was extremely small : 1 in successful instances. They estimated the loss upon the priz.e stack not to be more than 2 per cent. That , was owing to the system of compression by steel ropes. : He thought it was a very cheap system. Roughly, the cost of appliance for a rick of 100 tons was £l7 10s. He had seen some stacks in Holland. The system there was a very rough one. In stacks the use of salt had been generally abandoned. The worst stack they saw was , one which had been daubed with a concoction upon the outsides, principally of salt and fenugreek. The loss on the outsides of stacks was less than the loss in the average of good silos. Although it amounted in some cases to 15 or 20 per cent,, there was no necessity that there should be such a loss if proper precaution be taken. One of the great advantages of stacks was the possibility of erecting them on the field in which the stuff is grown, and that at a time of the year when labour was dear. Other advantagesXwere their efficiency, economy, and simplicity. 1 Sir John Lawes, recalled, said that since he had given evidence last year his opinion had not been changed.— Mr. Gathorne Hardy asked if he had found that a larger quantity of stock could be kept on the same ground with ensilage than with dried hay ?—Witness replied that he did not hold that opinion; his past ex- perience had caused him to form the opinion that a ripe crop of oats, being food cut up, straw and corn mixed, produced more meat than the silage. The chief value of silage consisted in its storing, thus producing food avail- able at all times. Stock could not be increased by en- silage.—ln reply to Mr. Mitchell Henry, who inquired if there was some overplus of rough grass and vegetable growth rejected by cattle which could be rendered edible by being passed through a silo, witness said he had riot succeeded in that in the preceding year. Ensilage-fed milk was richer to look at and to taste, but still they could not trace that the animal fed on ensilage had made so much butter as that fed on mangels. It was desirable in making silage to avoid chemical change in the silos as much as possible, because fermentation meant loss. In some of his oat silage, as far as they had cut it, the analysis showed a loss of nearly 30 per 'cent.--Asked whether, after his experience, he would now go to the expense of building a silo, if he had not got one, witness said he was rather doubtful about it. It was very use- ful, no doubt, but he was not quite sure he would go to. the expense. He could not do without roots. Dr. Voelcker said he believed that a number of sub- stances could be new utilised by the process of ensilage,

Fro' that day I began a-Join' my own. We lived wi' owd Johnny o' Semmes a month or two, till we'd scraped a two-thri bite o' timber t'gether, an' teen we shifted into a cote we could ha' to eaursels. It didno' tak' us lung for t' flit, I con tell yo'. Two journeys wi' a wheelbarrow, after we'd set up th' looms, cleared o cant. Slogger wur he:pin' ; so he put a little colour upo' th' last looad, an' th' childer i'th' fowt sheauted like heigh-go-mad, an' owd Thuston's jackass leafed till it's blinkers blew off. But we geet o settled, 'an' as niony corners o'th' heause filled as we could shap eaut o' what we had to do it with; an' then we warmed th' hearthstone wi' a potato pie, ut wurno' badly keseent (christened i, for th' gravy hadeo' a star for t' leet it up vii', an' th' beef wur so skase ut Slogger said rootin' for it war summat like fishin' i' owd Thustou's pit— plenty o' layin' in, but no pooin' cant. I shall nevet forget lookin' reawnd me when o wur straightened up. Eaur Sal had made th' floor fair glisten agen, an' rubbed th' cheears till they looked fit to be etten off. I'd driven a mop-nail up for t' hang my hat on, an' as everythin' ut could be made int' an orniment must be, hoed blackleaded it, an' made it shoine bike th' oon-dur (oven door). Fender we had noane, so hoo'd made a white mark, th' shape of a rainbow, reawnd th' hearthstone, for t' let th' cinders see heaw far they must row), before they'rn coed canto' limits. Th' chimbly-piece orniments wur two church- warden pipes crossed i'th' middle—a pepperbox at one eend, an' a tae-caddy at th' tother. Ther two paecock fithers at th' yead o'ih' heeuse, ut did fur picture • a reannd lookin'- glass abeaut th' size of a spoon hung i'th' window, an' as th' wife had notions o' bein' grander than some of her neigh- bours, boo made her weddin' shawl do duty for a table-cloth of a Sunday ; an' when her bonnet-box wur put o'th' top o' that, an' an owd Bible fort' creawn o', I felt as preend o' my start as if I'd bin in a paiace, an' as fain as if I'd wed a queen, for I could see ney cord rib wur determined t' mak th' best o' everythin'. Things went on swimmin' for a while, an' I thowt Pre lookin' up nil' wall. Then ther a backenin'. Ther begin aabein' moors music i'th' heauee than what eaur Sal an' me i made, an' an entry spoon had to be bowt, an' a name fund I ut turned cant to be " Ab," for ther a son an' heir (come , tbAt's grand), suckin' his thurnbe, an' crowin' i'th' kayther. 1 This younester wanted a bit o' extry scrattin' for; but after th' fust week or two we could hardly feel difference, an' didno' care if they coome as thick as midges i' spring. We kept gettin' an odd thing or two fixed i'th' heause, moore than what we had at Or lust, ut made it look thronger an' nicer, till in about two year we'd as pretty a neest as here and theere one, an' another chelloper i'th' kayther, wearin' eaur Abs socks. For o this time not a single relation coome a-mein' us nobbut my Uncle Jammie, an' I ceuld wed l understond what browt him. Nob'dy wanted owl off me, an' nob'dy 1 1 coome a-offerin' me owl, so at th' dur-step war kept as 1 cletan as if it had bin a mahogany table. Ther wur neaw 1 an' then a Scotchtnan peeped through th' window; but 1 when they could see nowt nobbut a table, an' cheeare, an' 1 th' two peacock's fithers i'th' heause, they darted off as I sharply as if someb'dy had helped 'em with thur foot. When th' heause geet a bit thronger an' prettier-Whin' thay warn° satisfied yid' a peep through th' window, but oppent th' fur (whoa ever thinks o' knockin' at a poor \on's dur ?), an' banged packs deawn, an' said they rn wouldno' stir till they'd made booathe eaur Sal an' me as , fine as two foos. I'd ha' nowt to do ver coo; an' th' last ' mon ut coorne geet so auvish (impudent) ut I took my clogs to him, an' lifted him into th' fowt afore he knew wheere he're gooin' to. Well, I kept Join' my own till, in a while, I fiend it 1 eaut felk ,wurno for lettin' me quietly. My Uncle , Jammie kept comb', an' talkin' abeaut bad times', an' I 1 buildin' clubs, an' what little interest th' bank war 1 payin' ; an' neaw an' then he'd whisper summat abeaut ' folk livin' lunger when ther sanieb'dy waitie' for their shoon—summat ut I couldno' understand till one day, when he mentioned th' same thing, he winked at me, an' It made I me feel as if Id rayther ha' punced him eaut o'th' heause than harkened to another word. What surprised me an' put me on th' look-eaut, his owdest wench coome a-seem' us, an' wanted to aloud godmother for eaur Joe an' made sich a fuss abeaut th' childer at I thowt hoo ha' bitten a piece eaut o' tone on 'em same as bitia' a apple. Hoo said heaw mich they wur like their mother, an' wondeet if they're owt like their aronfeyther o'th' mother's side —if they our heaw preaud he'd be ! One day, abeaut Kesmus (Christmas), a chap coe.d, an' flung a goose i'th' middle o'th' heause-floor, an' said it would do for my Kesmus dinner. I towd him I couldno' afford nowt o' that sort, ad' ehouldno' pay for it. He said ther nowt to paw, an' banged off deawn th' fowt as if he're feeart I should throw th' goose after him. A day or two after that th' same chap coed agen, an' this time he browt a bottle o' whisky an' two bottles o' wine. He said ther nowt to pay for that, 'loather. When my Uncle Jammie wur towd on't he went very nee into fits wi' laaflin', an' said he knew what it would come to. But Pre as bewildered abeaut it as if l'd bin carried to owd Crusoe's island asleep, an' ne'er wakkent till I fund mysel roastin' o'er a fire, ern' a lot o' black fellys doancin' reaund me. But I very soon fund it cant at this wur nobbut th' beginnin' o' these strange dooin's. Things coome in ding-dong; an' folk at used to pass me as if I'd bin a stamp, took their hats off to me neaw, an' reminded me so oft abeaut th' weather, at I owl never ha' fcrgetten what sort it wur as long as 1 lived. One day th' pa'son coed—th' fast day sin' Pre wed, an' le! sit upo' my loom rail talkin' till he're as daubed o'er we . pooin's (waste) as ever a bobbin-winder war. He didno' talk so mich abeaut things one would ha' thowt pa'sons knew th' mooast on; but abeaut property, an' families, an' what Hezelwo'th war likely to be in a two-thri year.. What good wavther ther war for manufacturin' ; an' heaw hondy coal war; an' heaw it war likely at rents would goo up, an' mak' his livin' better, an' sick lice carnil things as my Uncle Jammie liked talkin' abeaut so wed. But what war th' capper of o—th' loomheause window wur one day darkened wi a carriage, drawn wi' two hosses, an' two chaps droivin—one i'th' front an' tin' tother beheend. I wondeet at th' fuel if it war a buryin', but couldno' think o'•nob'dy at war deead. Baur Sal went fairly o of a tremble, an' said summit had happent, an' at we should be carried away—heo oreuldno' tell wheere' for hoo're sure witchcraft had summat to do wi' it. Hoo'clhad her misgivin's ever sin' so mony things kept bein' sent, an' nowt said abeaut wheere they coome fro'. Hoo wished we'd never takken 'em in. Well, ther a knock coome to th' dur, an' thing, I thowt, Our lookin' very queer; but when I went to th' dur, an' seed owd Miss Rigby fro' th' Hazel Ho gettin' cant o'th' carriage, I felt a bit yeesier. "Does Abram Fletcher live here ?" hoo said; an' hoo- put her spectekles on, an' looked up at me: "I'm th' chap at our kessent so," I said, "though my neighbours coen me Ab-o'th'-Yate." . "May I coome in ?" hoo said. "Oh, ay," I said, an' I showed her to Wu' fire, an' set her a cheear ; an' after hoo'd sit deawn, an' warmed her honds a bit, hoo said— " Dost know me?" . "Ay," I said, "yo' come fro' th' Ho, danno yo ?" " Yoi," hoo said; an' hoo took some peppers cant ov her pocket. "Let's see," boo said, " warno' thy fey ther owd Sam Fletcher's lad ?" I said he writ. " Owd Sam at th' Knowe ?" " Th' same chap," I said. "Well then," boo said, "I'm a cousin o' thy feyther's o' his mother's side." I towd her I thowt as mulch, but I'd never sper'd into 't. "Theau'rt comm n in for some money, I yer," hoo said, "through thy wife, if I'm no' mistakken.' Just then my face fired nu like a breek-kiln, an' I felt as if I could ha sunken through th' floor. I could akeaunt et once for her comm n a-seemn me, an' for one or two things beside. It war plain to me that my uncle Jammie had been bletherin abeaut that skit I'd had with him, an' at it war gooin through th' neighbourhood at my wife would ha' theausands o' peauds left her when her feyther toped o'er; so I determined for e put th' best face on't, an' tell th' owd ii besom no lies abeaut it. munno believe o ut yo veto," I said. " Wheay, is it noane true ?" hoo said. "Nowt o'th' sort," I said. "I'st ner'er ha' nowt nobbut what I wortch for, an' no' mulch o' that." "Then folk tell lies," hoo said. " Well, I conno' help it," I said. With that th' owd Jezebel jampt up, an' givin me a lung look through her spectekles said— " Theau'rt an arrant Jackanapes I" Then hoo banged eaut o'th' heause like a waddlin soot- bag, an' scrambled int' her carriage; an' fro' that day noather presents nor relations han ever troubled us; so at I'm (loin' my own still, an' likely for doom' so eendway.—From Ben. As told in the New York papers the story of the crime has a singular interest. Mrs. Chapman aided the men to escape from a Turkish prison in which her husband was also incarcerated, on ccn- dition that they• also set him free. They deserted Chap- man, and on being afterwards threatened by the wife with exposure, they murdered her and fled to America. The murder was after a time added to the catalogue of Lon- don's "Undiscovered crimes," but there seems reason to believe that the assassins have, after so long an interval, been secured.

IMPERIAL PARMA HOUSE OF LORDS.—MoNDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after .four o'clock. ROYAL ASSENT.—The Royal assent was given by com- mission to the Consolidated Fund (No. 1) 1311, the Mar- riages Validity Bill, the Glebe Loan (Ireland) Acts Amend- ment Bill, and the Drill Grounds Bill. The Royal Commis- sioners we the Lord Chancellor, Lord Monson, and Lord

Sudeley. THE CULTIVATION OF Tgna.cco.—Lord HARRIS called attention to the penalties imposed by certain Acts of Par- liament on the cultivation of tobacco in the United King- dom. and asked her Majesty's Government if they would give facilities for experiments being undertaken in its cul- tivation and preparation.—Lord SIMELET, for the Govern- ment, said they proposed to allow a few experiments in some selected localities, under certaia restrictions. No legis-

_ lation would be required. TIM LAW OF EFIDENCH.—On the report of amendments to the Law of Evidence Amendment Bill, the Earl of MILL TOWN moved to strike out the fifth claue, which pro- vided that a defendant should not be required to answer any questions tending to show that he had committed or been convicted of any offence other than that with which he was charged.—On a division the amendment was lost by 31
to 14. - ' Their Lordships adjourned at 6-50. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--MoNDA.Y. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock, and sub- sequently went to the House of Lords to hear the Royal

assent. THE WRIT FOR BARROW.—Mr. ARNOLD MORLEY MCIVed the issue of the new writ for Barrow-in-Furness. in the room of Mr. David Duncan, whose election had been declared void —Mr. LEWIS said the House ought to know more about this case. The House had frequently suspended the issue of a new writ for a session, or a couple of sessions, and he there- fore moved the adjournment of the present debate—Mr. HANEL-RE seconded the motion.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said he hoped the House would see that there was no ground for suggesting that there had been any corrupt practice on the part of the late member.—The motion for the adjourn- ment of the debate was negatived, and the motion for the

new writ agreed to. EGIPT.—Mr. BRYCE, in reply to a series of qnestions from Sir George Campbell, said the Government were receiving from Sir H. D. Wolff reports on the condition and adneini- stratitm of Egypt, but pending the continuance of Sir H. D. Wolff's mission it was not possible to fix the date of

their publication. ARABI PASHA.—In answer to Mr. llabouchere, Mr. BRYCE said the Government were not aware that the Egyptian exiles received any assurance that they should receive pen- sins. The papers presented to Parliament showed the con- trary. THE ROYAL FAMILY.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Mr. H. Spenselev, said: It is quite correct that an intention was expressed in the course of last session to move the ap- pointment of a committee to consider the question of grants of money to the Royal family, and that intention is still entertained, but we are doubtful whether the present would be most convenient, when questions of great and absorbing interest and of serious difficulty are in immediate prospect. NEW MEMBER.—Sir W Cunliffe Brooks took the oath and his seat for the Altrincham Division of Cheshire. THE IRISH LEGISLATION.—Mr. GLADSTONE said : I slid I would to-day give the terms of the motion which I expect to make on the Bth of April. It will be for leave to bring in a bill to amend the provisions for the future government of Ireland. On the 12th the Chancellor of the Exchequer pro- poses to move the Budget, and on the 15th I shall prepose to ask for leave to bring in a bill to make amended provision for the sale and purchase of land in Ireland. (Ministerial arel Parnellite cheers.) THE CRorrens BILL.—On the motion to go into com- mittee on the Crofters Bill, Mr. M‘LAREN moved that it be an instruction to the committee to extend the bill to the whole of Scotland, but Mr. J. H. MACDONALD strongly objected to this. liointing out that the exceptional provisions of the measure had only been accepted on the understanding that they were to apply to those parts of the country which had been inquired into by the Commission; and the LORD ADVOCATE also opposed it, remarking that under the title of the bill it might be extended to any High- land county —After some discussion, the instruction was negatived by 287 to 91.—The [louse having gone into committee, it was occuppied until a late hour with the con- sideration of amendments to clause I.—The claue was still under consideration when the Committee adjourned till Thursday. MISCELLANEOUS.—Sir R. WEBSTER moved the second reading of the Marriages (Attend ince of Registrars) Bill, which proposed that marriages should be solemnised in Dissenting chapels in preseece of a recognised minister, who should see the certificate of marriage returned to the registrar. The bill would reduce the cost of marriages in Dissenting chapels by one-half.—Mr. ILLlNGwoarrt moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. BUCHANAN seconded the amendment.—Mr. CHILDERS supported.—Sir R. CROSS urged that the second reading should be agreed to.—The adjournment was agreed to.--The Marriages (Hours of Solemnisation) Bill was read a third time. The Labourers (Land Acts Amendment) Bill was read a third time. After other business, the House rose at 245. HOUSE OF LORDS—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. THE LUNACY LAWS.—On consideration of the Lunacy Acts Amendment Bill (on recommitment), the LORD CHAN- CELLOR stated that he had modified some of the clauses of the Lunacy Acts Amendment Bill which had been objected to in Committee, but he adhered to the view that it was neces- sary in order to meet the requirements of the public that private lunatic asylums should be abolished. He had deter- mined, however, to preserve all vested interests: and licences would onlybe granted for existing houses properly conducted and for no greater number of patients than were accommo- dated at present.—Lord SELBORNE sunported the proposed amendments. Lord GRIMTHORPR moved the rejection of the clause placing restrictions on private asylums, and said he failed to see why at the expense of the State Parliament should attempt to stop competition on the pert of the, keepers of such institutions.—Upen Lord CRANBROOK de- claring that he thought the Lord Chancellor had gone as far as he could have been expected in the amendment of the bill, Lord GRIMTHORPE withdrew hiakfitonotion, and the bill passed through Committee. MISCELLANEOUS —A brief discussion upon naval policy followed.—The Select Committee on the Parish Churches Bill was nominated.—The Consolidated Fund No. 2 Bill was read a third time, and passed. Their Lordships adjourned at ten minutes after six o'clock. HOUSE OF COIIIMONS.—TIIESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE TRADE COMMISSION.—Mr. J. F. HuTTON put a ques- tion on bi-metalism, and desired to know when the Royal Commission on the Depression of Trade would present their report on the currency question.—The CHANCELLOR of the ExeHRQuER replied that the commission had only just be- gun to inquire into it, and at present he could not put on anlepressure or hurry the matter. INTERNATIONAL POSTAGE.—Mr. J. HENNIKER HEATON moved that the time had arrived for our Government to open negotiations with other Governments with a view to the establishment of a universal international penny post- age system.—Mr. H. G. REID having seconded the motion, Mr. J. F. HurroN moved an amendment in favour of the establishment of a penny postage system throughout the British Empire.—Mr. MATHER seconded the amendment.— Mr. H. H. FOWLER, on behalf of the Government, oppose's:l both the motion and the amendment, on the ground that the adoption of either would involve a further increase in the burdens of taxation.—The amendment was negatived without a division, and the motion was rejected by 258 to 127. DISESTABLISIIMENT IN SCOTLAND. Dr. CAMERON moved a resolution declaring that in the opinion of the House the Church of Scotland ought to be disestablished and disendowed.—Dr. HUNTER seconded the motion.—Sir D. CURRIE moved as an amendment that, in Vi9W of the recent declaration of the PRIME MINISTER that the ques- tion should be left as much as possible to the spontaneous action and consideration of the country, the House declined to entertain a proposal for dieestablisliment and disendow- ment until the wishes of the people in Scotland in relation thereto shall have been ascertained.—Me. BOISEETSON sec- onded the amendment.—Sir J. FEROUSSON exprassed his surprise that the Prime Minister had no opinion upon this subject.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that the people of Scot- land were accustomed on ecclesiastical questions to think for themselves, and he was not prepaeed to depart from the statement of Lord Hartington some years ago that the Gov- ernment would not interfere, but would respect the genuine and clear convictions of the people of Scotland. He should act in strict consistency with the declara,ion he made at the general election. He could not vote for either the amendment or the motion.—The amendment was negatived without a division, and upon Dr. CAMERON'S motion being put it was defeated by 237 to 125. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Bankruptcy (Agricultural Lab- Wages) Bill was read a second time, and the Army adjournedth ir d time. The °ut Annualer s' at 20 minutes past twelve. HOUSE OF LORDS.—WEDNESDAY. Houseßii' a ROYAL ASSENT.—Their Lordships met at 25 minutes past twelve o'clock, when the Royal assent was given by com- mission to the Consolidated Fund (No. 2) Bill and the Drain- age and Improvement of Lands (Ireland) Provisional Order Bill. The Lords Commissioners were the Lord Chancellor, Lord Munson, and Lord Sudeley, who were the only peers in attendance. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty-five minutes to one o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS MT. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minptes past twelve. THE POLICE AND THE FBANCHISE.—Sir H. SELWIN. IBBETSON moved the second reading of a bill for confer- ring the Parliamentary franchise upon the members of the
TIMELY RESCUE OF A CHILD.

ihe Redcar and SaWarn Gazette says: The following I.nteresting facts regarding the timely rescue of a child have Just been brought to light, and are made public by due authority of the father of the little girl, who is Mr. W. Haw, the well-known baker and grocer at Redcar, and Whose place of business is at 53, High-street. We may add that tee publishers of this paper, being familiar with the facts, are in a position to personally vouch for the entire ac- curacy of the particulars given. As the incident is no doubt Of. decided importance to parents, we gladly become the me- dium of bringing it to the notice of the public. borne little time ago the young daught-r of Mr. 'law be- came the victim of an acute bodily affliction of a rheumatic nature, which attacked the arms and legs of the child, so , that these became alarmingly swollen and painful. Not- withstanding the steps which were taken to relieve the little sufferer. her case became so serious that she not enly Was confined to her bed, but was unable to turn her body from one side to the other. At this critical moment, every- thing having failed, Mr. Haw remembered having read in the Racar and Saltbarn Gazette regarding a medical dis- covery which it was claimed possessed almost magical Power to drive away pain. He procured a bottle of the same, and made an application in accordance with the directions. To his agreeable surprise and satisfaction, the pain and swelling began to disappear immediately, and in the aston- ishingly short time of twelve hours the child could walk across the room, and when only three applications had been made the pain and swelling had entirely left her, and she is now quite well. Mr. Haw very aptly remarked that a reedy Possessing such wonderful power as St. Jacobs Oil, which is the article he used on the child, should be made known by every legitimate means, as by its use no doubt untold suffer- ing would be avoided. While the foregoing doubtless confirms what has been Said and published recently, with reference to the marvel- lous pain-banishing and healing properties of this wonder- ful Oil, our attention has been drawn to a still more start- ling case than that above referred to, and the facts of which have likewise been carefully substantiated. Mr. George C. Coin, of 73, Newman-street, Oxford-street, London, Writes: "I desire to acquaint you with the marvellous re- (severe- of my mother, aged fifty-seven, who resides in Ber- Wick, Wilts, and who for many years has been a helpless cripple from rheumatism- She was unable to move without assistance, and continually suffering pain, much of the time enduring the most intense ag ny. Her hands were swollen to Such an extent that she had not been able to see her knuckles for a long time. Her feet likewice had become quite defore teed. During her long suffering she had tried many things Without obtaining any relief, and she gradually grew worse, Until she, as well as I, had given up all hope of her ever regaining her health. Hearing recently some of the wonder- ful accounts of how St. Jacobs Oil cured pain, I procured a bottle, little expecting he would derive much, if any, benefit from its use. But, incredible as it may seem, after the very first application of this surprising Oil, she could Walk about without feeling any inconvenience, and the ,Bw.elling of her hands had become so far reduced that they began once more to assume their natural shape. Continu- lag the applications, she was in a few days able to walk as Well as ever she could, and without experiencing any pain Whatsoever. She also regained the free and full use of 110 t hands, and she is, in fact, entirely cured, for she has had

JAMES repeated hie.objections to the proposal, but said that in face of the evident feeling of the Housn and the country, and in order that the question might not be made a burning one at any future election, he should not oppose the sectant reading.—Mr. CHILDERS, believing that the inclueion ef other classes of civil servants had worked-no harm, would not oppose the bill.—Mr. Creeeezota objected to the applica- tion of the bill to Ireland ; and Sir Selwin-Ibbetson having consented to the exclusion of the Royal Irish Constabulary from the measure, the bill was read a second time. QUARTER SESSIONS BILL.—Mr. J. POWELL WILLIAMS moved the second reading of the Quiirter Sessions Boroughs Bill, the object of which was to exempt from contributions to the county rates boroughs which at present make their own provisioqs with regard to matters for which they are now required to contribute to the county rates.—Mr. HAND- Bußy moved the rejection of the bill, and a long discussion followed.—Mr. HIBBERT, speaking en behalf of the Govern- ment, stated that there were so many anomalies and diffi- culties connected with the present system that the Home Secretary desired to inquire into the subject as aftecting all parts of the country, either by sending a commission to the various boroughs or by some other means. The bill as it stood was a somewhat crude measure, and would in certain cases inflict great hardships. In view of the fact that the Government had in preparation a measure dealing with county government, he trusted the motion would not be pressed to a division.—The bill was then withdrawn ALLOTMENTS AND SMALL HOLDINGS. Dr. FOSTER moved the second reading of the Allotments and Small Holdings Bill, the object of which was to confer upon local authorities the power to acquire and afterwards let land for the benefit of the poorer classes. The bill proposed that the allotments should extend to one acre of arable or three acres of pasture—The motion was neconfled by Mr. WINTER- MOTHAM.—Mr. CHAPLIN sympathised with the measure so far as it sought to ameliorate the condition of the agricul- tural classes, but he strongly condemned the machinery by which the bill sought to attain that end.—The CHANCEL- LOR of the EXCHEQUER thought a measure of this impor- tance ought to be in the hands of the Government, and questions of this kind would be dealt with in any measure of local government proposed by the Government.—The bill was talked out by Mr. AMBROSE. MISCELLANFOUS.—Mr. SHIRESS WILL brought in a bill to amend the Education (Scotland) Act, 1872, with regard to the voting at School. Board elections —Mr. C. KENNY brought in a bill to abolish prosecutions against laymen for the expression of opinion on matters of religion. The House adjourned at 5-50. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after 40 o'clock. MD,CELLANEOUS.—LDrd SIDMOUTH intimated that he in- tended on an early day to move that the Navy Estimates be laid on the table of their Lordship's House.—A long discus- sloe arose upon the motion of Lord HOUGHTON that the Electric Lighting Act Amendment (No. 3) Bill be read a second time.—The motion baying been agreed to, Lord Bray moved the reference of the bill, together with the other bills on the same subject, to a Select Committee, on the ground that the extension of time allowed in the Government bill was not sufficient, as it would prevent the cln-elopment of undertakings.—The proposal to refer the bills nov resisted by Lord HouciliToN, but was ultimately agreed to. Their Lordships adjourned at five minutes past six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. The Midland Itailway Bill was read a third time. MISCELLANEOUS.—Mr. BRYCE, replying to Mr. Bouree, stated that the departure of the Russian squadron from Suda Boy was only temporary. for tne purpose of obtaining pro- visions, and there was reason to believe that the vessels would at once rejoin the fleet.—Mr. MUNDELLA. announced that the Government would introduce a bill for the purpose of giving effect to the recommendations of the Copyright Convention, which included the sabiect of artistic copy- right. They hoped soon to be in a Position to introduce a bill dealing with the whole question of copyright. —Mr. GLADSTONE informed Mr. Magnaic that owing to differences of opinion that had sprung up the nomination of the East India Committee must stand over for a short time.—The House aeain went into Committee on the Crofters' Progress having been reported, Mr. JOHN MORLEY moved the second reading of the Poor Relief (Ireland) Bill, explain- ing that it facilitated the distribution by boards of guardians in Ireland of out-door relief, in the shape of food only, to distressed persons, till the end of this year.—Captain NOLAN, Mr. DILLPN, and other Irish members criticised the provi- sions of the bill.—The second reading was agreed to.-- Prison Officers' Superannuation Bill was read a second time. --The Cooyhold Enfranchisement Bill passed through committee.--'Mr. MACFARLANE introduced a bill to make Provision for the prevention of bydrophephia through the United Kingdom. The House adjourned at 25 minates past 2 o'clock.
THE DISTRESS IN WARRINGTON.
GENERAL RELIEF COMMITTEE.

The weekly meeting of too General Relief Corn- raittee was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair ; the Revs. J. Yonge, W. R. Parry, E. C. E. Carleton. S. Wilkinson, J. Drummond; Major Litton, and Messrs. J. Green- ing, T. Jolley, J. tsmetlaurst, S. Davies, F. Monks (hon. me.), and .a considerable number of ladies.
TIP MINISTERIAL CRISIS.
RESIGNATION OF MR. CHAMBERLAIN AND
MR. TREVELYAN.

Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Trevelyan have ten- dered their resignations, which have been accepted by the Queen. Her Majesty has approved ot`the following arrangement consequent on these resigna- tions ;—Mr. Stanstield, as President of the Local Government Board, will resume the position he held during the latter years of Mr. Gladstone's Ad- ministration of 1868-74. Lord Dalhousie becomes Secretary for Scotland. The members of the Cabinet will thus be reduced by one. Stansfield's ap- pointment will give general satisfaction. He may be said to be the founder of the Local Government Board. He succeeded Mr. Goschen as President of the old Poor Law Board in March, 1871; and in this capacity carried through the bill by which the Poor Law Board underwent evolutionary development into the Local Government Board. He was the first president of the new Board, and presided over it with conspicuous ability and success till the change of Government in 1874. Lord Dalhousie's appoint- ment as Secretary for Scotland is an official ad- vancement which he has well deserved. He made a gallant but unsuccessful fight for a seat at Liver- pool in the February before the last General Elec- tion, and was returned when the General Election took place three months later. His experience in the House of Commons was very short, as he succeeded to the peerage in August in the same year. It is a curious coincident that the number of Cabinet Ministers and ex-Cabinet Ministers on the Liberal benches in the House of Commons is now precisely the same. The members of the present Ministry in the House of Commons are Mr. Glad- stone, Mr. Childers, Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, Sir W. Harcourt, Mr. John Morley, Mr. Mundella, and Mr. Stanstield—seven. The Liberal members who have been in this or previous Cabinets are Lord Har- tington, Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Trevelyan, Mr. Bright, Sir Charles Dilke, Mr. Forster, and Mr. Goschen— seven. _

_ . The Press Association says that it is 'somewhat wide of the mark to assume that any league or covenant has been arranged between the seceding Ministers and the section headed by Lord Harting- ton. So far, at any rate, there is no such compact. Mr. Chamberlain and his supporters below the gang- way will oppose Mr. Gladstone's scheme; so also will Lord Hartington and his Whig followers, but the two sections have arrived at this decision from very different points of view, and when the ques- tion of an alternative scheme comes to be consi- dered, their accord, unless existing conditions undergo a marked change, will disappear. Lord Harting,ton, Sir Henry James, Mr. Goschen, and. their friends objected to the policy of inquiry and examination proposed by Mr. Gladstone as the initial step towards dealing with Ireland. Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Trevelyan had no objection to this, but they dissent from the conclusions arrived at by that policy. Shortly after noon on Monday summonses were issued for a Cabinet Council, to be held at two o'clock, at the Prime. Minister's official residence in Downing-street. Previous to the meeting of Minis- ters, Mr. Childers had a short interview with Mr. Gladstone, and left to visit the Home Office a few minutes before Lord Kimberley arrived to attend the Council. The Marquis of Ripon next arrived, and walked as far as the Treasury with Mr. Treve- lyan, who had been in conversation with the Mar- quis at the Admiralty for some time. Mr. Trevelyan left his lordship at Downing-street. Mr. Morley, I Mr. Mundella, and Mr. Campbell-Bannerman passed in almost together, and were followed by the Lord Chancellor, -Earl Spencer, Mr. Childers, and SW William Harcourt. Earl Granville had previously entered the Council Chamber through the private garden entrance. At a quarter past two Mr. Stans- field remained with the Premier for a short time after the other Ministers had left. Lord Dalhousie called at the Scotch Office and stayed a short time during the day. Later in the evening Mr. Glad- stone occupied his seat in the House of Commons, and made a statement (found in another column) as to the procedure of business. The Marquis of Salisbury will be present at the meeting of the Conservative party, which will be held at the Carlton Club as soon as Mr. Gladstone has made in Parliament his promised statements respecting his Irish measures. The noble Marquis, whose health has benefited considerably by his stay in the Riviera, will leave Cannes almost imme- diately for London, for the purpose of conferring with the Conservative leaders previous to-the meet- ing of the party. Lord Dalhousie and Mr. Stansfield will proceed to Windsor Castle on Saturday to be sworn to their respective offices. Mr. STANSFIELD'S ADDRESS.-Mr. Stansfield, who is seeking re-election on being appointed President of the Local Government Board, says in his address to the Halifax electors that Mr. Gladstone is about to submit proposals for the solution on an efficient scale of the vexed and critical question of the bet- ter government of Ireland. The right hon. gentle- I man adds that, agreeing with the principles of the I Midlothian programme, he has felt it a duty to ac- cept the grave responsibility of endeavouring to ' contribute towards their realisation. The nomina- tion is fixed for to-day (Saturday), and the polling, if any, for Wednesday next. The Cabinet was in council on Thursday afternoon from two o'clock until four, and in the evening from six to eight.

TOWNSHIP MEETINGS. HOUGHTON, MIDDLETON, AND ARBURY. The annual meeting of ratepayers of tke above township was held at the Plough Inn, Houghton Green, on Friday evening. Mr. Starier was appointed chairman. The over- seers' statement of accounts was passed as read, on the motion of Mr. Swinton, seconded by Mr. William Howard. Messrs. John Stanier and John Howard were nominated overseers, Mr. Stanier re-elected waywarden, and Messrs. James Swinton, George Jackson, and William Howard ap- pointed uurleymen for the ensuing year. Mr. Brimelow was reappointed assistant overseer. A vote of thanks was given to the chairman for presiding, on the motion of Mr. Brime- low, which terminated the proceedings. LATCHFORD.

The annual meeting of ratepayers of the above township I was held at the Black Bear Inn, Latchford, on Monday evening. There were present Messrs. W. Pierpoint tin the chair), W. Dutton, A. Kenworthy, Dinwiddie, I. Turner, and J. W. Booth. It was ar.nounced that the balance in the bank to the credit of the overseers amounted to .£596 12s 3d, as compared with £526 7s, the balance of the previ- ous year. It was stated that the whole of the rate had been co!lected On the motion of Mr. Kenworthy, seconded by Mr. Dinwiddie, the accounts were passed. Mr. Pierpoint and Dutton, the retiring overseers, having declared that they in- tended to retire from the office, Mr. John Lunt and Mr. John Fairhurst were nominattd to the post on the sugges- tion of the chairman. On the proposal of Mr. Kenworthy, a vote of thanks was accorded to the retiring overseers, and a similar compliment was paid to the assistant over- seer, Mr. Hawkins, on the motion of Mr. Dinwiddie, the

latter gentleman remarking that great cledit as due to the assistant overseer for his collection of the rate, of which there was not a penny owing. At a meeting of ratepayers of the extra municipal portion of Latchford township, L eld at the Black Bear Inn, on Monday evening, Mr. A. Kenwortby was re-appointed way- warden for the district. Mr. J. Shaw Green was also re- appointed collector of the highway rate. The ratepayers present were Messrs. W. Pierpoint, A. Kenworthv, I. Tur- ner, and J. W. Booth.

LECTITRE• ON THE _IRISH QI7ESTION.—Under the aus- pices of the Newton Polling; District Cosservative Associa- tion, a lecture was delivered in the Co-operative Hall, Ear- -1 estown, on Monday evening, by Mr. F. W. Deakin, of Manchester, on " The Irish question." Captain Seton pre- sided.—The Lecturer said the Irish question was a time- worn question. It was a subject that had been brought to the forefront again almost entirely through the action of Mr. Gladstone, and he believed had it not been for him we should have had some respite from this dreary question. Referring to the present scheme of Mr. Gladstone, he said the question of placing the constabulary under an Irish Parliament was, he considered, a wrong thing altogether. Before the industries of Ireland could be developed they must first see that order was established, and he asked them to stand firm in this crisis of our country, and it would be a shame if they permitted a Premier wad with vanity to un- do what their forefathers had for generations been engaged in doing. div.head: LETTBR FROM MIL BEAMONT.
div.p: LETTBR FROM MIL BEAMONT.

The 'MAron said that he had rsoeived a letter from Mr. Beamont, in which that gentleman stated he was precluded from attending through having taken a cold. If he had been present, the letter went on, he should have advocated a provident society instead of a relief or soup society. It would encourage thrift and habits of self reliance instead of leading a labourer to look there for relief the first moment he was out of work. THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE'S REPORT.

At a special meeting of this committee, held on the 24th March, at which there were present Messrs. T. Litton, T. Jotley, J. Greening, and F. Monks, the following resolu- tion was parsed, viz :—"That in the opinion of this com- mittee the time has now arrived for discontinuing the pre- sent system of relief, and that icstructions be given to discontinue the making and distributing of soup after Sun- day next." The committee also passed the following resolution :—"That the inquiry officer be authorised to give tickets for bread only in deserving cases and at the rate ef 6ne pound of bread per head of the number relieved." At a meeting of the committee held on the 26th ult, the follow- ing report was adopted :—"After carefully considering all the circumstances connected with the present relief fund, your sub-committee are of opinion that the time has come for discontinuing the present system of administering the fund as the necessity for it has passed away with the im- provement in the weather and consequent employment of a large number of people. We are, however, fully alive to the fact that in consequence of the partial and in some cases. total stoppage of work in the town, there must be much distress, which it is desirable to relieve, and we purpose to continue Mr. Sutor and Mr. Blease as Inquiry officer and clerk, but under somewhat altered conditions, and we sug- gest the follawina as the best plan for the future adminis- tration of the fund. An application to be made as at present. As soon as possible the inquiry officer to attend to each application, giving or refusing assistance as the circum- stances may determine. All cases se visited to be reported upon in the hook kept for the purpose. If assistance is Igiven, the amount per 'bead and for how long it is to be given, to be recorded so that the committee may see what is being done, and the clerk may be able to check off his own work and the accounts when presented for payment; this to apply to both food and clothing. As many deserv- ing cases will not apply personally, we shall be glad to re- ceive the name and address of such that they may be visited and dealt with as though they had applied personally, but it is not intended to visit any cases anonymously communi- cated. We believe by adopting this plan we shall be able to eliminate the bulk of undeserving cases, and more effectu- ally carry out the wishes of thei subscribers whose desire is relive the really deserving who shrink from parading their distress or clamouring for assistance, as opposed to the surface distress which meets the eve at every corner, and is very frequently the result of idleness, intemperance, and improvidence. If it be the wish of the committee that we continue the fund, we can only consent on the dis- tinct understanding that we have the full confidence of the committee, that we shall do so with firmness and courage, kindness and consideration, to alleviate the distress which unfortunately has overtaken many of our neighbours. The number of cases visited week ending March 27th, was 208, and of these 39 were refuse'. The accounts'submitted for payment were :—Food £5O 19s 7d, clothing £24 Os 61, total £75 65 ld.—On the motion of the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, seconded by the Rev. J.170..zGE, the committee's report was adopted.

div.head: CONCERT.
div.p: THE CONCERT.

The MAYOR stated that the proceeds of the recent concert in aid of the distress fund amounted to £2O 17s 10d. (Hear, hear.) Tie greatest credit, the Mayor said, was due to Mr. Alfred Perris for having got up this concert and car- ried it to a successful issue. (Hear, bear). This was all the business before the committee. PROPOSED PERMANENT RELIEF SOCIETY.

After the business of the committee had been transacted a meeting called by the Mayor was held "to consider the ad- visability or otherwise of establishing a Warrington Perma- nent Relief Society for the purpose of assisting those who from the result of a strict investigation may deserve and require it, and with the view of checking, if possible, the evil practice of giving indiscriminate relief." In addition to the ladies and gentlemen above mentioned there were present Mr. R. Davies, Dr. Mackie, and Mr. J. Walker.— The MAYOR, having again read Mr. Beamont's letter given above, said there was a desire on the part of some of the inhabitants of the town that a permanent organisation should be established as in other towns. In Hull they had a permanent organisation of a successful character, and he was told they had also one in Rochdale equally successful. The course adopted in Hull when the society was first founded was as follows :—A meeting of the inhabitants was called, a committee appointed, a permanent chairman elected, and subscriptions solicited. After a sufficient sum was obtained for the purpose, offices were taken, a perma- neat secretary was appointed, together with the clerk, and whenever any inhabitants of Hull met with any one in the streets who solicited aln:s he would at once give that indi- vidual a printed ticket and seed him to the society's office, where particulars as to the man's family, occupation, and in fact all the information calculated to inform the committee as to the individual's deservedness to receive relief were obtained by the officials. If the person was found deserving of relief it was within the province of the paid official to administer it as he thought desirable under the circum- stances. The inhabitants were also requested, instead of giving promiscuously, to forward their old clothes to the deo& of the society, and when applicants came who were in want of clothes they were served out to them. In this way the charitaole object was fully and fairly carried out with- out apparently any difficulty or confusion. There were many cases which a societa, like the one he had named could relieve but which a Board of Guardians could not. (Hear, hear.) Boards of Juardians could only relieve cases of absolute destitution, and if they kept strictly within the limits of the law they would relieve no person, even though out of emploi,roent, as long as he had any furniture. The Mayor also mentioned instances in which relief might be afforded by such a society as the one in question.—Major LerroN said there was a great difference between a society such as the* Mayor had referred to and a provident society, for in the latter case people would have to contribute to a fund which would be augmented by subscriptions.— He should also like to know whether the subscribers to the present fund would be willing that their subscriptions should be applied to the purposes of a permanent relief fund. —The MAYOR explained that he did not propose to use the present subscriptions in that way.—Mr. MONKS said he had not a particle of sympathy with a permanent relief fund. No one could walk through the town without seeing how much of the present distress was the result of idleness, in- temperance, and improvidence. If they could teach the I people how to make the best use of their wages, and how to I become provident and to strive to live within their means, they would do them a great deal of good, but if they carried out the former suggestion in many cases they would do more harm than good —Dr. MACKIE was in favour of such a society as "The Bolton Society for the Protection of the Poor" being founded.—The Rev. S. WILKINSON was in favour of an institution of the kind suggested by the Mayor. —The MAYOR at this point read a letter from Mr. John White, in which he stated that the present poor-law system failed to reach the most deserving poor, and he should be glad to see some other plan adopted.—Mr. ROBERT DAVIES pointed out that although Bolton was about three times the size of Warrington the subscriptions for a year only amoun- ted to about .£l2O. and VO of this went in rent and in the salary of the official, so that there had been only £6O dis- tributed by the society. He moved that the matter be re- ferred to a committee for consideration.—The MAYOR said the annual report of the Hull society showed that the total income of the organisation was £563 12s 6d, and there was only £259 16s 3d of it distributed in the shape of relief, leaving £303 16s 3d as the expenses of the work —Mr. SMETHURST seconded Mr. Davies's proposal.—The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON suggested that inquiry be made as to the societies of a similar character there were already in the town.—Mr. WALKER thought they ought to have the lines of both the charity and provident organisations laid before them. If there was anyone present who could explain the objects of a provident society it was very desirable that it should be tione.—The MAYOR thought that if Mr. Beamont bad been present he would have defined what he meant by a provident society in such a way as to take it entirely out of the scope of the provident societies already in Warrington. He (the Mayor) thought there must be 50 such societies, and there was tee room ior more.—After a little further discaeesion it was decided that the considera- tion of the subject of forming a permanent committee be postponed till that day three weeks. The following ladies were added to the Executive Relief Committee, viz. :—The Mayoress, Mrs. Pickmere, Mrs. Litton, Mrs. Reynolds, and Mrs. Fox. The proceedings then terminated.

THE COAL TRADE—The Forest of Dean coalmasters in- timated on Thursday an immediate reduction of Gd. per ton on household coals. The wages of the colliers will be reduced two and a half per cent, in accordance with the sliding scale. CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH—At Birfningham, on Thurs- day, Clara Price, a young single woman, was committed for trial for concealment of birth. She confessed to the police, but said the child was born dead, and that she had buried it in the garden. A search was made, but no body was found. Price then confessed, on being urged by her mother, that she had kept the body for a fortnight, and then buried it in the wash-house furnace. No trace of the remains was found. div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

The frost has made sad havoc amongst the vegetables, and a day or two after its departure there was a most offensive smell that filled the air in the neighbourhood of plantations of green vegetables. Autumn-planted cabbages are, in some instances, destroyed, and the sur- vivors are not more than one-fourth the size they were when planted last September. Broccoli have mostly escaped, especially where covered with snow, but all the heads will be extra small. Curled greens, cottae-ers' kale, and asparagus kale are none the worse, and are pushing their teller sprouts out rapidly; We know of nothing at this time of the year that is so delicious as the sprouts of the latter. Upon inspecting a breadth of autumn-sown onions, we could scarcely see a plant. The onion is not particularly tender, but these had been sown late, and possessed very little strength. Fortunately, summer onions are plentiful, and are keeping well; but, should any of them show signs of growth, they should be planted at once, and they will yield useful stuff for flavouring and making savoury dishes] till the spring- sown are ready to draw. A sharp lookout should be kept on the piece of ground intended for this sowing, and, as soon as it is in a fit state to deal with, the oppor- tunity should not be lost, as the sooner they are in the ground the better. Our earliest proceeding will be to fork the ground over three or four inches deep the first sunny day, with the view of warming it, which it must obviously do if we turn face downwards that which has been exposed to the sun for the best part of the day. We have repeated this process some seasons three or four times preparatory to sowing, and the rapidity with which the seeds came up was suggestive of a gentle hot-bed. We have managed to plant on a warm border a few kidney potatoes, where not one season out of six do they get touched by the frost. Earth is drawn over the stems as they progress, and by watching them for a week or ten days in this way they escape being injured. Wednes- day being a sunny day, we took the opportunity to draw drills for pea-sowing, and they were allowed to. remain open for a few hours, in order to warm the soil, and so hasten germination. In localities where mice and rats are troublesome, the sower should act on the advice given to a correspondent last week, and coat the seeds with powdered red lead. THE FRONT GARDEN.—We notice that the Clematis in sheltered places on walls has made two or three inches of growth, therefore pruning should not be longer de- layed. If the plants have 'filled the space allotted to them severe pruning may be practised, and all .weakly shoots should be cut back to one joint, and the stronger ones to two or three, or even one, where the shoots are prolific; for even at this rate the latter will be twice as numerous as they were the previous year, and can be trained to cover a large space during the season. With plants of old standing it may be found necessary to re- move long naked shoots, which should be cut off at their junction with another shoot. Beyond filling the gaps made in this way very little tying is needed now, but as they grow they require ati ending to every two or three days, or they get entangled and give much trouble. Dahlias should now be examined, and all dead portions . cut away, and if there is no frame or greenhouse for them they should have the warmest place in the dwell- ing, and till growth is visible a warm cupboard will answer to excite them. Several roots can be packed in a moderate-sized box, and if the soil that is placed round them is moderately moist it will not require any water till it appears to be dust-dry on the surface. There are two flowers that seem to have defied the snow and frost —the Snowdrop and the Winter Aconite. The first was partially in flower three weeks ago, and they seemed to have progressed under their mantle of snow, for they are now at their best; and the latter will shortly expand its bright yellow flowers. 'THE WINDOW.—In looking over the exhibits of window ! plants at the Preston .Spring Flower Show on the 17th inst. we thought it a matter of regret that cottagers had not selected more legitimate window plants, and not gone to forced Azaleas and others of doubtful window growth. We admit that. the subjects to select from at this time of the year are not numerous, and we would allow some concession in the way of hardy plants in preference to tender exotics or those requiring forcing to bring them in flower in March. The insertion of a note in the schedule that the judges will make the awards to those plants that they deem most likely to have been grown in the window Would have a wholesome effect.
