div.head: FOOTBALL IN WARRINGTON. [Br A SPECTATOR.]
div.p: FOOTBALL IN WARRINGTON. [Br A SPECTATOR.]

Lcoking over a newspaper published in a town not far from the Scotch border, the other day, I came across an account of a football match played in that locality. The match had been a successful one, the play being good, the spectators numerous and very enthusiastic, and the writer—obviously desirous of giving the highest praise—declared that the whole proceedings reminded him of a Lancashire football I field. This is good evidence that Lancashire is re- garded as the premier county of England, just as much in regard to football as in regard to manufac- tures and industry in general. Yorkshire may know ' more about horses and horse racing, and the Tyne and the Thames may be more famous for boating and other aquatic sports than the Mersey, but for the cul- tivation of football the palm is yielded to Lancashire. The correctness of this opinion, and the fact that Warrington is a typical Lancashire town in this respect, were impressed upon me on Saturday after- noon by the continuous stream of people who passed over the bridge in the direction of the field on Wilderspool Causeway, where the struggle for victory in the third round for the West Lancashire and Border Towns Union Challenge Cup was to take place between the Warrington and St. Helens Clubs. Both of these clubs have won some fame in the foot- ball field, and it was apparent that their meeting was the cause of no little excitement, though as might have been expected from local feeling and the recent achievement of the Club, it was very generally decided beforehand that the Warringtonians would again carry off the honours of the day. Not having any very pressing business on hand, I soon yielded to that gregarious or " follow-your - leader " instinct, which is so strong in men and sheep, and "went with the crowd." Tne gate arrangements being excellent, an entrance to the field was obtained without the pressing and squeezing that were experienced the previous week, when the rush for admittance exceeded what had been antici- pated. Being in good time, a place was easily secured on the renovated and improved grand stand, of which it may be said by the way that it would be none the worse of a few more uprights to prevent that oscillatory motion beneath one's feet, which was not particularly re-assuring to those who had shared in the misadventure of the Saturday before. A glance roun-i the field showed that all the places from which a view of the game might be had were being rapidly taken up, and before proceedings began there was an attendance seemingly little short of that of the pre- vious week, certainly one of the largest ever brought together in this neighbourhood. I do not know whether or not any of the matches of the Warrington Club have been dignified by the presence of the borough member, or the occupant of the Mayoral chair, but it is quite evident that football in Warrington is a democratic game. It draws together " all sorts and conditions of men." Amongst the spectators you find Town Councillors in profusion jostling with these bumble servants of the Corporation who wait upon and minister to the uncomely and suggestive, but at the same time necessary, vehicles which are a feature of Warrington streets; you find magistrates—adminis- trators of the law—in close proximity to some to whom gentle corrective doses of the law are occa- sionally administered ; and you occasionally find clergymen rubbing elbows with people who are very unfamilar with the interior of a church.

But to turn from the spectators to the players, the respective teams turned out well to time. The St. Helens men were the first to enter the ground and received an encouraging cheer, and the Warrington champions were similarly greeted, only "much more I so," as the phrase runs. It was at once seen that so ' far as outward appearance was concerned, St. Helens is very creditably represented in the football field. I In physique they displayed more uniformity than the 1 Warrington team ; they possessed no player of the , I Goliath-like proportions of Fair. Turner, and per- haps none quite so slim and wiry as Massey. It was quite evident, too, that if placed in the balance the ; Warringtonians would outweigh their opponents, the , differences in form and development being particu- larly noticeable between the two rows of forwards. I No time was lost before making a start. St. Helens having the full advantage of a strong wind, began in a very spirited manner and seemed fully determined to keep the offensive. In the first two or three scrim- mages they were notably successful, but after the first shock the Warrington men showed that this was more than they would stand, and gathering themselves together in a compact scrimmage in the very centre , of the field, after an unusually protracted struggle, , they by sheer dint of endurance and superior weight overbore their opponents. This was the turning point of the day so far as the scrimmaging was con- cerned, for almost without exception after that en- counters of this kind turned out to the advantage of Warrington. By the end of the first quarter of an hour or twenty minutes the differences in the quail- I ties and methods of the two teams also became very j apparent.' People began to see that the St. Helens men had the makings of a good, perhaps a first-rate team, about them. Their forwardsshowed pluck and determi- nation, some of the backs. andnotably Foreman, proved themselves to have unusual fleetness of foot, while Pennington won applause more than once by his bril- liant saving, the ball rarely coming within his reach without its being smartly remitted a considerable dis- tance nearer the home goal posts. But all these good qualities were to a great extent lost by a want of judicious organisation. The materials of a good team seemed to be there, but .they had not been developed and arranged to the best advantage. The consequence was that towards the end of the game the St. Helens play "fell to pieces," as it were. On the other hand the Warrington men worked together like a well-constructed machine, every screw, bar, and bolt of which had been thoroughly tested and put in its proper place. The very vigorous introductory assault of St. Helens was met with a steady organised resistance, before which it gradually but surely died away with the result that the assailants became the defenders, and continued so to the end of the game. It was this unity of motion which made the Warring- ton assaults when they took place so very dangerous. It was a weakness on the part of St. Helens that when the ball was carried forward by one of their players the player was apt to be left too much to himself, and the effort therefore invariably ended in- effectively. Comparatively little passing and ex- change took place amongst them. Warrington on the contrary played a remarkably inter-dependent game, notwithstanding that the wind made the motions ' of the ball somewhat eccentric and difficult to calcu- late. Their passing was extremely deliberate, and often appeared to completely non-plus their oppo- nents. At the same time the Warrington game was I not without its brilliant individual feats. The almost irresistible rushes of Fair. Turner, the unique manner in which Barnes piloted his way through a whole group of opponents without being laid hold of, the , splendid runs of Massey, the sure defence of Buxton on the rather rare occasions when defence was needed, and sundry other examples of individual good play were all noticeable and admirable features of the game. But were any one asked how it was that such a victory as that of Saturday last was scored against a club of the standing of that of St. Helens the cor- rect answer, in my opinion, would be that it was .due to skilful organisation, to the putting of the right man in the right place, and to the working of the team as a whole, and not merely as a group of. EO many individuals. And further, the prediction might sately be hazarded that if the Warrington team keeps up the form which it has hitherto displayed in this com- petition, the chances of any other club carrying off the trophy are small indeed.

Prince von Bismarck completed on Thursday his seventy- first year, having been born on April Ist, 1815. The captain and principal officers of the Cunard steamer Oregon landed at Liverpool on Tuesday. The officers con- sider the Oregon has not drifted into dcep water, and is within reach of divers. OXFORD AND CAMBRIDGE UNIVERSITY BOAT RACE.— This race comes off to-day (Saturday). Lively interest is daily exhibited in the practices of the crews, and the various points of each oarsman are narrowly criticised. In the last few days the crews have been working hard and constantly. ANOTHER PARIS TRAGEDY.—An Exchange Company's telegram from Paris states terrible tragedy took place at Belleville on Thursday morning. A carpenter named Vaubier strangled his mistress and then shot himself through the head. The coupleagreed to die together. and drew lots which should kill the other. . IPSWICH ELECTION PETITION.—The arguments in the Ipswich election petition inquiry terminated on NVednesday, when three persons were called before the judges to show cause why they should not be reported as guilty of illegal practices. These were some of the men called at an earlier stage, and who had been accused of giving or receiving money as a bribe. Their Lordships reserved judgment until next day. The petition has resulted in Mr. H. W.l West, Q.C. (Recorder of Manchester), and Ur. Jesse Col. I lingo (Secretary to the Local Government Board) being un- seated, on the ground of bribery and corrupt practices on the part of agents. The Judges. on Thursday, found that general corruption did not prevail in the borough. Sir Horace Davey (the Solicitor General) and Lord John Her- vey are to be the candidates of the Liberal party at the fresh election which will now have to take place. Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOi to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY APRIL 3, 1886

THE Liberal party in Warrington, having faith not only in their principles, but in the Strength of their fol Lowing, notwithstanding the defeat which (in common with Liberals in other Lancashire boroughs) they sustained at the General El: ction, have taken the right ourse in deciding at the earliest opportunity Who shall enter the lists on their behalf in the fle encounter. It was natural that they allould turn in the first instance to Mr. WIL- LIAM CROSFIELD, the late Liberal candidate and, as we recorded a few weeks ago, the *General Council of the party passed a unani- tons resolution to invite him to again be- c°lne their candidate. It was felt that he had IPade a good fight; that he had advocated Liberal principles earnestly, consistently, and With conspicuous ability; and that, as there reas an end to the unholy combination which d a :number of Liberals astray, there was an 1

excellent chance, if he would venture once kore, of his becoming member for War- lington. Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD has not, tllowever, seen his way to accepting the ~.nearty invitation which was offered him. tlis reply is characteristic in being perfectly I.trai2htforward. "I do not," he says, "con- fider that the present is a suitable time to I.3ind myself by a promise which must extend 'over an indefinite, and, it maybe, alengthened Period of time, during which the conditions of politics and of parties may undergo a • inaterial change." He is determined to leave himself free, and he is ,quite within his right in doing so. On the other hand the Liberals °f Warrington, while acknowledging that "a lengthened period " may elapse before they ate.caliedupon to relieve Sir GILBERT GREEN- ALL of the duties which already press too heavily -upon him, recognise that a dissolution aYicome as a thief in the night, and that they must be prepared for it. To this end, the meeting, after expressing its sincere re- ,gret that Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD had de- 'clined the invitation to become the Liberal candidate, proceeded to consider who should ezt be assked to take the position, and was not 4°lig in coming to the unanimous conclusion , extend the invitation to Alderman JOHN ; ‘-ltosnELD, 1.P., thc, cousin of the late candi- 'date. He retired from the room, on hearing his name mentioned; and was re- ceived with .enthusiacm on his return—an 'enthusiasm which was .heightened when he intimated that he felt it his dety, on this occasion, to accept the invitation. It will be remembered that nearly two years ago, when McMiNmEs, consequent upon failing , health, ,made it 'known that he should not offer himself for re-election, Mr. JOHN UROS- IZLID was the first gentleman thought of as "a, successor by the General Council of the: Liberal party. He, however, refused to yield 10 the appeals that were then made to him ; 'out this time he has not turned a deaf ear to ft/le voice of the charmer; and we need hardly claY that his acceptance of the position has glven the utmost satisfaction to every section c'f the Liberal party. Given two candidates °f,equal merit, it is always recognised that ,theone possessing local standing, in addition, 4as I.‘y far the better chance in a contested election. This holds good almost every- here—holds good under some circumstances 0, an evil extent—and Warrington, which, 'te most small towns, is clannish, is no ex- ,eption to the rule. The Liberal party may !herefore be congratulated on having secured 14 Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD a candidate who te12"38 sses all the qualifications that tend to ,-sure success. He is a townsman who has a great many years been identified with the l'olvth and government of the borough, and With the fortunes of the Liberal party. His ep2nduct as Mayor of Warrington in 1883 was 'arked in every act by a high sense of justice inkild fairness, and by benevolent regard for ze interests of all classes of the community. Was due to his generosity that the town was 13.,t°vided with a public clock which is a model 411ekeeper ; and it was owing to his initia-

tive, coupled with a subscription of no less ' than £i,ooo, that the movement was made which resulted in the new and handsome School of Art in Museum-street. But we need not dwell on a liberality which as to the CROSFIELD family is proverbial. As . Alder- man PICKMERE remarked in proposing th-, health of Mr. CROSFIELD on the occasion of a banquet given to him as Mayor, when a worthy object is placed before him, or when it is a case of distress, " his hand finds its way into his pocket without his knowing it." As a politician, he is ardent and strenuous without being extreme. He is essentially practical as to politics, as he is in the conduct of town's affairs—a feature in his character which, as revealing itself in municipal-matters, leading men otherwise op- posed to him always gratefully acknowledge. Not long since, as chairman at a lecture, Mr. CROSFIELD took occasion to express his dis- approval of a reckless and impractical scheme of Disendowment of the Church which had come under his notice; but as his observa- tions on this head left Disestablishment an open question, he took care on Monday night to define his position by saying that, as he believed in perfect ieligious equality, he was in favour of the separation of Church and State. But as to this and other ques- tions, he will in due time explain his views at various public meetings. Meantime we cannot do better than give- a brief quct ition from the speech he made at the Mayor's ban- quet in 1883. Proposing the health of Mr. MC - MINNIES as borough member, he said: "He always votes as he ought to do. He votes just as I should vote if I was sitting in the House of Commons myself." After this, it need hardly be said that he is in the right place as a Liberal candidate, and tha: he will be in the right place as member for Warrington.

THE meeting called by the MAYOR of War- rington for the purpose of considering the advisability of establishing a Warrington Permanent Relief Society brought together a considerable number of ladies and gentlemen on 'Tuesday afternoon. There is evidently a lively feeling of benevolence among a consider- able section of the community; and although no active steps were taken to form a ' erma- nent Society, it was not because there was any lack of inclination to aid those who may require aid ; it was because the meeting, with such infcrmation as was before it, could not see its way clearly as to the best course to take. The MAYOR opened the proceedings with a succinct statement of the objects of such an organisation, which was to render assistance to deserving people who were in distressed circumstances, and who had a whole- some dread of becoming paupers. He gave some interesting details of the work of a Society at Hull; but it transpired that at Hull, as at Bolton, the cost of inquiry and administration absorbed about half of the funds subscribed; and this, as Mr. ROBERT DAVIES pointedly remarked, could hardly be regarded as satisfactory. Mr. BEAMONT had written suggesting a Provident Society; but as to this the MAYOR remarked that Provident Societies involved contributions on the part of the ultimate recipients; and what they wanted was to render aid to those who were so poor as to be unable to contribute anything. The Rev. E. C.E. CARLETON observed that there were provident organisations in several of the parishes of the town; but, if this be so, it is extremely desirable that whatever is done should be done with a full knowledge of the objects and work of all other agencies for assisting the poor. After the question had been considered from various points of view, it was resolved to adjourn the matter for three weeks, it being understood that in the meantime those present should institute inquires as to the working of Charity Organisation and other kindred Societies. There can be no harm in thus delaying a decision. It is not a case of the horse starv- ing while the grass is growing, for the Dis- tress Fund Committee have funds in hand fully sufficient to relieve such distress as there is likely to be in the town for the next five or six weeks. With an improvement in the weather, there will be an improvement in the condition of even the poorest of the poor.

LORD EBRINGTON, as will be seen from a letter Avhich we publish, has been taken to task by Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., for misrepresen- tation in an article just published in the "Nineteenth Century." His lordship quoted a few lines from the Election Address of the member for Northwicn, to the effect that "the reforms which he desired for Great Britain he also desired for Ireland." To an ordinary mind this meant that Mr. BRUNSIER was not in favour of giving Englishmen benefits which Irishmen were not to be privileged to enjoy; but Lord EBRINGTON saw in the expression something quite dif- ferent; and made use of it with the view of showing that Mr. BR'UNNER had changed Iris mind, if he was now disposed to give a favourable ear to Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule project. How he couid flounder to such a conclusion is puzzling, especially if he has ' had the whole of the Election Address be- fore him, for immediately preceding the phrase in question Mr. BRUNNER says:— " Ireland ought to have the full power to deal with all .affairs purely Irish." Lord EBRINTG- TON is not of course to be accused of wilful misrepresentation ; he is simply a bungler. He should not write articles for high-class magazines; he should 70 to school again, and learn this time to summarise correctly, or produce a "fair copy."

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
The Newton Division of the Liberal Army are drilling so as to be ready for the conflict; but they must go a little further—they must insist on being led again by "the Colonel." He will win next timeS

On Monday the Manchester Ship Canal Bill was read a third time in the House of Commons, and the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Bill' a second time. We are glad to be able to "report progress" so far as this part of the country is con- cerned.

The Soiree of the Viaduct Institutes near Earlestown, was "a big boom." No fewer than 1,500 persons sit down to tea, and then there were a concert, and ball, with an entertainment. thrown in on the night follow- ing. Everything was well managed, for they do not order these things better in France.

There would seem to be plenty of work cut out for the Footpaths Preservation Society. In addition to the case mentioned by a cor- respondent the other week, a report reaches us of two public footpaths being appropriated in the neighbourhood of Grappenhall The land-grabbers must be required to give an account of themselves.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
THE WIDNES MANSLAUGHTEFIC, PETITION.—The petition for the relrale of William Percy, formtrly a farmer's con- tractor in Widnes, has been forwarded to the Home Secre- tary.
Sr. PAUL'S WESLEYA.N CHAPEL, BUNCORN.—The re-open- lug services will take place on Thursday next, and we would again draw attention to the advertisement in our columns.

ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION, INTBNES.—About 30 members of this association were examined on Tuesday night at the National Schools by Brigade-Surgeon E. Nicholson. The result is not yet known. NELSON-STREET BAPTIST CRAPEL, WIDNES.—On Sunday the Rev. R. Yeatman preached two special sermons to large cocgregetions. The titles of the discourses were " Walking with Goi " and " An invaluable discovery." MR. AND Mas. lIMNRY ViTIGOAN concluded their mission at the Hetchinson-street Primitive Methodist Chapel on Sunday. There was a crowded congregation at the evening service. The proceedings have been altogether a success. RATE'PAYERS' MEETING AT ITALTON.—Lt the annual meeting, held under the presidency of the Rev. J. Lock- wood. the following appointments were made: Waywarden Mr. J. W. Haddock; burleymen, Mr. J. Rztter and Mr. rc. Baguley ; constables, Messrs. a. Riley and T.. Potter. HALTON BURIAL BOARD.—A. report of the labours of this Board since June last has been presented to the ratepayers, and states that the contracts fer the melting of a cemetery., have been signed, and the contractors had engaged to com- plete their work by the end of May. Three members have now to retire, viz. :—The Rey.er. Lockwood, and Messrs. 3. Rutter and H. Lowe e but they offer themselves for re- election. BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.—In aid of the funds of this chapel a tea meeting was held on Thursday night. There were 120 persons present. Subsequently the service of song " an Dabberton's dream " was given by the choir and several friends from Runcorn, under the leadership of Mr. Edwards. Miss Passey was the accompanist. The solos were capitally rendered by Mr. Fox (of Rurcore), Mr. Ed- wards. and Miss Priestnall. Mr. E. Carey read the narrative, and Mr. W. Clarke, of -the Hollies, presided. SAD •FATALITY AT RUNCORN.—Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, on Tuesday, held an inquest at the *Royal Hotel, Runcorn, on the .body of Daniel Jones, 70 years of age, who lived at 38, Penketh-lane. Mr. Thomas S. H. Briggs, assistant to Mecers. P. Smith and ,Co., chemists, said on Saturday morning he saw the deceased commence to walk across Bridge-street at the bottom of Penketh-lane. At this time a phaeton was approaching, and the deceased was stepping back, when his foot slipped on the kerbstone ani he fell backwards on his head. He was picked up in an unconscious condition and taken home, where he died on Sunday afternoon. A. verdict of accidental death was re- corded. WITK4RS LACROSSE CLVB.—The Widnes team went down to Wavertret on Saturday to meet Fairfield in the first round of the Liverpool and District (Seaforth) Cup Cempetition, and won by three goals to two. Neither club had its best team, Fairfield starting with only ten men. One of thel vacancies, however, was filled a few minutes after the start, i thus making Widnes 12 to Fairfield 11. Widnes played well together in the first half, and scored three goals to 0. In the second half the game was more Nasal, Fairfield, how- ever, having slightly the best of it. For the winners, For- shaw and Gossage played best, while Fairfield was best re- presented by Taylor, a prominent member of the Liverpool Lacrosse Ciab. Tetras :—Widnes J. R. Wylde (captain), J. Wvlde, G. Halsalt, R. Helsel!, F. H. Gossage, G. Thomp- son, J. W. White, T. Forshaw, J. Thorburn, Longton, Ham- mill, and Parkinson. Fairfield : Hill, Taylor, Pressley (captain), Haddock, Day, Mason, S. Barlow, Nicholls, Brunt, Brooke, and A. N. Other. RUNCORN SCIIOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held yesterday at the Town Hall. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were present the Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. .3". Pritchard, G. S. Hazelehurst, E. Laeison, W. Handley, and F. Rigby (clerk.)—The resignation of Samuel Inglestield as assistant visitor was accepted, and he was ap- pointed caretaker of Greenway Board Schools, at a salary of £26' a year.—A letter was read from the Rev. W. Preston, vicar of Holy Trinity, in which he stated that at a meeting of the managers of Trinity Bay School, he laid before them his (the clerk's) letter of February fifth. In reply they de- sired him to say that Mr. Annett did not consult them when writing his communication, the style of which they could not approve of. Mr., Annett had explained that what he wrote was not intended for the Board, but for their visitor. He (Mr. Annett) desired to treat the Board with proper re- spect. A complaint enclosed was referred to the Attend- ance Committee. RUNCORN BOARD or Guerantews,—There is no contest in the Union except at Runcorn, where eleven gentlemen have been nominated for five scats. The list is as fol- lows :—Samuel Coventry, 12, Church-etreet, Runcorn, tailor and draper; William Farrell, South Kink, Runcorn. buil- der and contractor; William Fisher, Highfield House, Runcorn, gentleman; Henry Joseph Urine, Bridge-street, Riincorn, saddler, &c. ; Edwin Imison, Church-street, Run- corn, pawnbroker; John Wilson Lightburn, Rockfield, Higher Runcorn, accountant; William Mellor, Church- street, Runcorn, grocer; Robert Shaw. The Highland!, Higher Runcorn, alkali manufacturer; Philip Speakman, The Mount, Runcorn, lime merchant; Samuel Taylor, Halton-road, Runcorn, merchant and canal carrier; William Whittaker, Castle View, Motighlands-lane, Runcorn, gentle- man. Mr. W. Handley, who has done admirable service on the Board in past years, does not seek re-election : but Messrs. Whittaker, Fisher, and Speakman again seek the suffrages of the ratepayers. Misers. Lnison, Mellor, and Coventry have withdrawn their nominations, but the re- maining eight will go to the poll.

in London a few days ago, \vas a rich man. It is stated that he has left property to the value of four million pounds. It would be interesting to know if he ever stumbled upon the passage—" Flow hardly shall they that have riches enter into the Kingdom of God !" and what he thought about it.

They build tall chimneys at St. Helens— that is one good thing. The Corporation Gas Committee, who.are about to extend the works, have just given an order for the erec- tion of a chimney 150 feet high. They have got to thinking about erecting taller chimneys at Warrington. Meantime the smoke black- ens everything—always excepting, of course, the character of the inhabitants.

The Tories were disposed to make a fuss the other day in the House of Commons, because Mr. Duncan had been unseated, at Barrow, for an illegal act. What will they say as to a Conservative like Mr. Bullard being unseated and rendered unable to sit for seven years, because of being found guilty by his agent of corrupt practices? Perhaps they will think that is an apple off another tree, and say nothing.

The Tories of the city of London—which is but a comparatively small portion of the metropolis—declared last night against a separate Parliament in Dublin. They were aided by certain of the Liberals who have thus behaved badly; they, at any rate, ought to have waited to hear Mr. Gladstone explain his proposals before they condemned them. Having resolved in haste, they may perhaps find occasion to repent at leisure.

The Royal Commission on Trade Depres- sion has just begun to inquire into bi-metal- lism and the currency. In answer to a ques- tion put to him, the Chancellor of the Exchequer said "he could not put on any pressure or hurry in the matter." Just so; why should the doctor hurry up when a patient is suffering? Give him plenty of time to inquire, to read up, and think about the case (at the public expense), and in the mean- time the patient may—recover.

The Allotments and Small Holdings Asso- ciation, of which Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., is president, have just commenced a paper with the title of "Land and People." The land wants labour, and the labourer wants land, and the object of the journal is to help, to bring the two together upon the best pos- sible terms. After trying pheasant preserving with such poor results, it is time to turn to peasant preserving. The motto of " Land and the People" is" Three acres and a cow."

It has long been a grievance with Irishmen that they were not allowed to grow tobacco, the impression with many being- that the pro- hibition applied to Ireland only. As a matter of fact the whole Kingdom is under the ban in this respect, with a view of course to rev- enue, from the imported article. It is doubt- ful whether "the weed" could be grown in any part of the United Kingdom with profit, having regard to the tax; but the Govern- ment are about to permit experiments in selected localities. What will it end in- smoke?

OAKLAND-STREET GOSPEL TEMPERANCE bOCIETY, WID- RES.—An exceilent entertainment was given in the Wes- leyan school-room on Tuesday evening, and .six persons signed the pledge. LECTURE AT WIDNES.-11;Ir. H. Wade Deacon on Thurs- day evening delivered an interesting lecture on "Seeing" to the members of the C.E.T.S. in the National School. The wonderful structure of the eve and its mode of work was illustrated and explained. The Vicar presided. SALE oy WORK AT WIDNES.—Mi. J. G. McMinmes, formerly M.P. for Warrington will ,on Wednesday next per- form the opening ceremony.of a sale- of work at Simm's Cross Primitive KethOdist Chapel. Dr. MacLennan will officiate on the following day. • ,Full particulars in our an- nouncement,columne. FIRE AT WIDNES CO-OPERATIVE STORES.—Shortly before six o'clock on Tuesday evening a fire was discovered in the 'helves of the drapery department of the Ditton-road shoo of the Runcorn and Widnes' Co-operative Society. The flames were quickly quenched with several buckets of veto:. , The damage done was not extensive. . ASSUILT ON A WiDNES CONsTLBLE.—At Widnes Police Court on Monday, James Qninn, was charged with resist- ing P.C. Chambers in the execution of his duty. On Sun- day afternoon the constable was taking the names of several youths for playing pitch arid toss 'in Back Carlisleestreet, when the prisoner came up and struck him several times, on the head and face. In striking again prisoner sent his hand through a windew. He was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. THE FREE DINNERS A.T WIDNES.—A football match in aid of the funds for providing free dinners to the poor school children at Widnes was played on Lowerhouse-lane ground on Thursday evening, the contending teams being Widnes (first) versus Eighteen 'of the District. The Eighteen seemed to have the best of the game, but were 'unlucky in scoring, the result of the match being—Widnes, two tries, got by Farrell and S. Bingham, to four touchdowns for the District. • The GALE AT Tirmsras.--A gale of great violence swept over Runcorn and Widnes during Tuesday night and Wed- nesday motning, but both towns escaped any serious damage. A woman walking along Mersepst., Widnes, was se- riously injured by one ot . the numerous falling slates. At the Central Hotel the roof of a wooden shed belonging to Mr. Edward Connor. the cab proprietor, was bodily lifted off, and carried against a building a short distance away; demolishing a chimney. A shooting gallery on the mar- ket ground was overturned. NELSON-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.—The annual meeting of the teachers Of this school was held on Monday evening. A DRUNKEN ULACKSISITE AND lIIS MONET.—At Wid- nes Court, on Monday, Mary Ellen Winstaniey was charged with stealing 2s 6d from Ralph Gaunt, a blacksmith, Hale. Between five and six o'clock on Saturday evening Gaunt was at Ditton Junction, but he was\so drunk that the railway officials refused to book him. The woman proffered to get him a ticket and he gave her 3s 6.1. She only returned him is change' and bad no ticket. She was taken into cus- tody, and MrsCootea, wife of P.C.,Cootes, found 2s 6d con- cealed in her boot. The prisoner was remanded.—The pri- soner was brought before the Bench on Thursday, and again remanded in consequence of the non-appearance of Gaunt.--Superintendert Barker said he should ask for a summons to compel his attendance. DRUNK AND TICKETLESS AT WIDNES.—Joseph Downe. apparently a labourer, was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, charged with travelling on the London end North-Western Railway frost Warrington to.Widnes without having previously paid his fare. Mr. Ferranti. of the solicitors' department, Lime-street Station, prosecuted.

The prisoner was awn to alight from the Warrington train due at 3-10 on' Friday by William? Henry Lee, a newsboy, who called the station master's (Mr. McConnell) attention to him as he was going into the porters' room. The station- master asked him for his ticket, and the prisoner who was drunk, used very foul language in reply. He mentioned St. Helens' Beasley Cross, and other places as his starting point, and he was given into custody. The prisoner, who pleaded not guilty, called a man named John Blake, who said he was with the prisoner in Widnes until two o'clock,
and that he had not been out of town. The Bench con- sidered the charge prayed, and imposed a fine of l'Os and vests, or 14 days' hard labour. lio3tz RULE AT WIDNES.—Under the auspices of the

Widnes Liberal Association, Mr. Roger Fogg, on Tuesday evening, read a paper on the History of Ireland. with 'especial reference to self-government, in the Baths itssemblY Rooms, Whines. The room was tilled_ Mr. E. Carey pre- sided. 11,e Lecturer, in an able manner, reviewed the history of Irelaed from the earliest times, and

referred to the eminence the island attained in the world as the home of learning and religion. He concluded with expressing the option that when at the last general electic,cl36 members out of 103 wero returned pledged to advocate and vote for Henn Rule, there could jbe no doubt that it demanded the earliest and be attention of all who wished for the peace atd welfare of the Irish .people and the safety and prosperity of the Eatpire.—Mr. Joseph Morresou, Rev. W. Vause, Mr. B. Kniveton (of Runcorn), and Dr. O'Keeffe delivered speeches in favour of Home Rule.—Mr. Fogg and the speakers from Dcncorn were cordially thanked on the motion of the cbairman.—A.

_ "smoking concert*" was subsequently held. Songs were contributed by Mr. F. Scott and Vir. F. Roves, and Mr. Nicholson gave a solo on the bagpipes. Mr. Brown gave a recitation, and Mr. John Betney a reading. The concert was much enjoyed. THE WIDNES WESLEYAN LIBELEE' SCHRAIE:—The scheme for extending tbe Library of Lacey-street Sunday School. an-. 1 providing a reading-room is in process of being carried out. The present library contains 693 volumes, and a snot of £5O has to be expended in the purchase of additional books. Mr. Thomas Sadler, who has the voluatary assis- tance of several teachers and scholars is engaged in erect- ing a new room in the main school-room for the purpose of the library, it is to be situate between the two main en- trances of the school, and will afford ample accommoda- tion for the numerous volumes. One of the class-rooms is ,

to be utilized as a reading-room, ad this branch is to be open every evening. The scheme it expected to cost £l2e, and the whole of this amount is being raised amongst Wesleyan Methodists, who have reeerved the use of the library and the reading-room to the riembers of their con- gregations, and those connected with their Sunday schools. A concert in aid of the funds was riven in Lacey-street School on Monday evening, when Mr. B. Browr presided, and a good audience assembled. A capital programme of vocal aod instrumental music was stiamitted. Under the

leadership of Mr.iroseph lobinson, a string band—p-eif-o; med several selections very creditably, and directed by Mr. John Helford, the Runcorn Choral Society sang several part songs in a fashion that called forth hearts, commendation. Miss Sadler and Mies Kiddie contributed a duet '(pianoforte and violin) with skill; and a pianoforte duet was given by Uiss J. and Miss M. Sadler with succesg.. Miss tones and Mr. J. Ho'ford, and Messrs. W. Rigby and H. Neild sang duets that were very 'favourably received. Songs were given by Misses A. Kilsall, E. S idler, and Curzon; Messrs. Arthur Fox, W. Rigby., and John Holford, in good style. The library and reading-room will ba open in a few weeks.

TIER AFFAIRS or MR. S. Bum, OF RUNCORN.—At Run- corn County Court, on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, an interpleader was heard, in which a houseful of furniture was in dispute. The elaimants were Messrs. Samuel Ravenscroft and John Frodsham, the debtor Mr. Samuel Blair, formerly grocer, Church-street, and the execution cre litors Messrs. Williams and Co., to- bacconists, Chester. The furniture hid been seized by the high bailiff, acting on Messrs. Williams' instructions, but Mrs. Blair was called, and deposed that she was married to the debtor on the 9th April, ISM, and that the goods were then hers, having been left by her former husband, de- ceased. The only addition was a piano, for which she was paying out of her private means. She made a settlement of the goods to the trustees for the protection of herself and children.—Mr. Tetlow, solicitor, Chester. acting under sheriff, who appeared for the execution creditor, said he could not dispute this evidence, and his Honour gave a ver- dict accordingly, with costs. M-. Mulholland (instructed by Mr. Hitchen) represented the debtor.— ['here was a second interpleader summons with regard to the stock-in- trade, which had been seized at the same time. The claim- ant of the goods in this case was Mrs. Flophe Barrow, of the Royal Oak Intl, Weston.—Mr. Mulholland stated, being in difficulties, Mr. Samuel Blair, on the 11th March, called his creditors together, and assigned to Mr. Arthur Thraves, accountant, Liverpool, in trust for the creditors the goods which were in dispute. Mr. Blair entered into an arrangement to pay a compositicm of lOs in the X; and Mrs Barrow secured it by giving three pro- missory notes at three, six, and nine months, the amount being X 360 The debtors liabilities were £OBO. Upon this

. . Mr. Thraves assigned the stock-in-trade to Mrs Barrow._ When called, Mr. Thraves slid creditors representing £6OO had agreed to the assignment.--Mr. Tetlow entered into a contention that there was no bonafrie asssignment, when the court rose, and the case will be concluded on a future occasion.

BRUNNER, M.P.—The following letter appears in a London contemporary: I see that Lord Ebrington, in his article in the "Nineteenth Century" for April, has made an ex- tract from my election address, which gives an in- correct idea of my view on the question of Irish self-government. The noble lord's wish seems to be to prove that a large number of Liberals will, in fupperting Mr. Gladstone's scheme to amend the provision for the future government of Ireland, be putting party before principle, because, he alleges, they denounced or threw cold watei upon projects of Home Rule during their contests. The extract given by Lord Ebrington reads as follows: "The reforms which I desire for Great Britain I also de- sire for Ireland." If he had taken the first words which appear in my address, instead of, or in addi- tion to, the last, it would have been clear that I declared my opinion with no uncertain sound. The whole of my declaration will take but little space: —" Ireland ought to have full power to deal with all affairs purely Irish; but I will be no party to any .enactintent which 'would make the two millions of Irish people living in Great Britain foreigners among us. The reforms which I desire for Great Britain I also desire for Ireland." If Lord Ebring- ton has taken no more care in making extracts from the addresses of all the Liberal members, it would be well that his work should be done over again.— Yours, &c., JOHN T. Batustrtnn. House of Commons, March 31. •

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—Mr. Leonard Courtenay has returnea the following report on the Manchester Ship Canal to the House of Commons: "The bill does not authorise the construction of any new works. The object of the bill is to authorise the Manchester Ship Canal Company to pay, during- the period of seven years, interest to the share- hoblers of the company on the amount from time to time paid up on their shares from the respective times of such payments. A report from the Board of. Trade with respect to the object of the bill was laid before the committee and considered by them. The report states that the provisions of the bill with respect to such payments are in accordance with those required by Standing Order 167 to be inserted in the railway bills, seeking the like powers, and are simi- lar to those contained in the Regent's Canal, City and Docks Railway act, 183. The report further stated that the provisions of the bill with regard. to the mode of raising the capital for the construction of the canal appeared to the Board to be deserving of the favourable consideration of Parliament. There are no other circumstances of which, in the opinion of the Committee it is desirable the House should •

be inioi•M-ed". Mr:'do-u-r-t-e-n-a-3,7iui:iher--ie-P-C-rts from the Committee that they have examined the allega- tions of the bill, and found the same to be true. and directed him to report the same without amend- ment. The bill was read aithird time on Monday.
-TOppositiol-i iti the Lords : The opposition to the bill, which was withdrawn in the House of Corn-

mons, will, it is understood, be renewed now that the bill has reached the House of Lords. The Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company, the Corporation of Liverpool, and the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board will again deposit petitions Praying to be heard before a Select Committee against the merits of the bill, but the.first attack
will, it is stated, be made by a motion to reject tha bill on the second reading. This motion will receive the support of Lord Itedesclale, the chairman of the . .
committee, who, it is not improbable, will himself move the rejection of the bill.

- , I HAGENBECIeS CEYLONESE EXHIBITION.—This ex- hibition, which has made the tour of Germany, 1 Austria, and Switzerland, with such marked success during the 'last three years, is announced to visit ' Manchester during Easter. The Agricultural Hall, Pomona Palace, has been specially engaged for the exhibition. The attractions comprise fourteen large working elephants, sixteen zebu cattle, troupes of devil dancers, Nautch girls, a Tamil , comedian troupe, snake charmers, monkey performers, jug- glers, dwarfs, &c. MOORE WESLEY.A.N IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— The closing meeting of this society, which has had a very successful session, was celebrated on Monday evening by a tea and public meeting. A fair gather- ing of the fends took place at six o'clock in the schoolroom where teaowas providtd, the tables be- ing decorated by a display of choice flowers, the 'arrangements of the tea being made by Miss Dutton, 'Miss Bessie Dutton, Miss Stelfox, and Mrs Silcock. After tea a public meeting was held in the chapel, presided over by Mr. Shaw Green, of Warrington, and an excellent programme of songs, readings, and addresses was gone through, the various items giv- ing great satisfaction. Mr. William Silcock, the secretary, read a well prepared and humourous re- port of the society's proceedings during the session, which evoked much laughter and considerable ap- plauSe. SERMITS A CCIDENT AT E ADT:ESTOWN STATION.— OnWednesdiyafternoon a serious accident occurred at Earlestown Station which should act as a warn- ingto those who are in the habit of leaving trains while in motion. A: young man named William Wright, a farmer at Alder Root Farm, near Vulcan, was a passenger by a train leaving Warrington for Newton Bridge and Manchester at 4-40, but which does not stop at Earlestown Station. The train is an express from Chester and Warrington, but while passing Earlestown the speed was slackened to about 10 or 12 miles an hour. Whilst the train was run- _ ,

fling ,rOntid the .` curve" at Earlestown, Wright at- tempted to aliglt by jumping upon the platform. The velocity of the train, however, threw him tiio- - forward on his face, and he sustained , serious injuries. His .body was bruised, while his face was one mass of cuts and lacerations. He was rendered unconscious, and under the di- rections ef Mr. Young, stationmaster; the wounds were attended to. The injured man was afterwards conveyed to Vulcan on one of the railway engines, and was removed to his home, where he Was atten- ded by Dr. J. W.' Watkins. of Newton.

ALLEGED WRONGFUL PAYMENT OF ACCOUNTS. STORMY SCENE.

Mr. Meadoweroft drew attention to two accounts passed on the 22nd Meech. One related to the expenses in connec- tion with the Manchester Ship Canal Bill poll, and made out to the returnicg ()dicer, and not the Commissioners ; and the other had reference to the account in connec ion with the erection of the building in the Town Hall yard. He alleged that one account had not passed the committee interested, and that the other, which was made out to the returning otficer, had net been passed by that gentleman, butsbotla by the Finance Committee, which committee had no right to deal with the accounts at all, according to the rules. He complained that the accounts were brought before a special Board meeting without explanation, and stated that the gentlemen who signed the cheques had no conception that they were signing cheques which were of a debateable character. He thought some explanatior should have been vouchsafed.—Mr. Fisher said a full explanation was given why the accounts were brought forward when Mr. Meadow- croft was present. and Mr. Meadowcroft replied that he was not in the room until after the accounts were dealt with.--.-Mr. Shaw: supported Mr. Meadoweroft's contention that the accounts ought to pass the committees of the Board before they were sent to the Finance Committee. It was a convenient way cf dealing with money belonging to the ratepayers to smuggle it through in that way.—Objec- tton being taken to that. remark, Mr. Shaw said he thought the term was justifiable because of the want of explicitness and straightforwardness.—Mr. Grice said he was one of the persons who signed the cheques, and he was not at the meet- ing of the Finance Committee. He did not hear anything of the matter at the Board meeting. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Mellor stated that he also signed the cheques. He had not the slightest knowledge of what they were but thought they bad passed the committee and were in order. Mr. Lake said that the discussion that day shooed the ab- solute necessity of the cnramittee appointed to consider the question of the law clerk's remuneration dealing with the matter at once. Until that question was finally settled he did not think the Board were justified in passing accounts to which there might be bona fide objections.—The Law Clerk real the section of the Public Health Act under which he held that the account could be paid.—Mr. Shaw said that up to the last election of Commissioners it was quite right to pay the law clerk two guineas per day when the returning officer kept him in the book; but at the last election the returning officer did not keep him in the booth, and there was nothing pail—The Law Clerk pointed out that Mr.

Shaw, as the returning officer. sent the secretary to him to obtain certain legal advice. He (the law Clerk) drew up all the forms necessary, and the secretary, who was in the -sole- employ of the Board, and was paid ioe. the extra services rendered. Mr. Breokes was paid £4O fer his extra services, and after he had paid his disbursements he would be able to have £2O as his remuneration. He did not see why Mr. Shaw, after paying the secretary for . extra work_ should make a distinction in his case and decline to pay him anything.—Mr. Shaw contended that the agreement with the law clerk covered the extra services which he per- formed on the taking of the poll. Out of the £4O Mr. 'Brookes had to pay various assistants engaged with him.— The Chairman said that the discussion was out of order, and Mr. Meadowcroft differed, remarking that his object in rais- ing the question was to protect the members of the Board. lie did not wish to move a vote of censure, but contended that ho was perfectly justified in introducing the matter either by resolution or otherwise. The Chairman said that he could not listen to Mr. Meadowcroft, and should leave the chair. He thought it very ungentlemanly for Mr. Meadowproft to go on in that way.—Mr. Shaw rose to a point of order and asked what the chairman's ruling was —After further and rather perrnal discussion, the Ctiairman held - that as long as there was no resolution before the Board no member had a right to reply. If Mr. Meadowcroft had wished to move a vote of censure it would have been within his power What he (the chairman) wished was that the Board should be not what it was in the past, a bear-garden, but he wanted it to be a meeting of gentlemen, who. were prepared to discuss a question on its merits without pique. Mr. Meadowcreft -said that he could put himself ia order by moving the adjournment of the Board, and to this course the Chairman offered no objeceion, but sutseanently added that he was informed by the law clerk that as there was no. business before the Board no adjournment could be moved. The discussion, however, did not then cease, and assumed a somewhat heated character. Mr. Meadowcroft rose and put on his hat, and the Chairman asked hi.n to take it off. Ha complied. The Chairman then held that the proceedings were wholly irregular. The word 'smuggle," he said, used by Mr. Shaw would have a tendency to make people believe that the Commissioners were a dishonest set of men. He maintained that a direct charge of dishonesty had been made, and it would go to the public that nefe had been a connivance to pat money into Mr. Linaker's pocket by smuggling his account through the committee. He had been a member of that Board for 14 ar 15 years, and he had never been charged with smuggling before. The Board had always considered the small salary received by Mr. LinOer and his accounts for extra services had always been paid. Mr. Shaw had not withdrawn the word "smuggling," but persisted in its use, and he regretted that a gentleman who hqd so recently held the position of chairman of that Board should have made such a charge against gentlemen who had conducted their business honestly. Mr. Shaw: I am not obliged. to take any interpretation you may put upon words that I use. If I understand the word smuggle it means doing something without letting those know who ought to , know.—The Chairman: Oh no.—Mr. Shaw (continuing) said smuggling tobacco on shore meant bringing tobacco without the proper authorities knowing, and bringing accounts in the way they had been brought was not a manly way.—The Chairman said be.cou'd not Haien to any further disoussion, and the meeting then broke up.

SETTING: THE SCHOOL BOARD AT DEFIANCE. *On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, sen., and P. H. Gossage, john Keenaghan, labourer, Lee-street, Lugs:lade, was charged with neglecting to send his stepdaughter, Elizabeth Burke, to school.—Mr. Denby, clerk to the School Board, said defendant bad been fined twenty-four times in that court for a like offence. The defem,ant did not appear, and, in fact, he declined to attend the ceurt.—The Chairman: What reason does he assign? —The Clerk: Simply that he was going to heat the School Board. The child is about eleven years of age, and de- fendant pays the 5s every time he is summoned.—Attend- ance•officer Rowe said the girl had made thirty' six attend- ances during the year out of a passible 450.—The Chairman: Is the child earning anything P—Witness : No, sir.—The Chairman : What is it doing, then ?—.llr. Denby Playing aboat the street.—The Chairman: Bid' it locks like mere insanity to let the child play about the streets under such circumstances. If they were makisg money by keeping the child away from school the matter would be very dif- ferent. It seems a very singular proceeding to throw away Sc per week.—Mr. Danby : We have to take out cemmit- ments against him when he does not pay. Defendant paid one guinea the other week.—Superlatendent Barker: He was fined twice last montb.—Tbe Chairman : Is he an Irisletnan P—Mr. Danby : I don't know, sir. (Laughter.) —The Attendance-officer: lie is an Irishman. sir.—The Chairman: Cannot the police say something in this mat- ter ? It seems that he objects to send the child to the school selected by the board.—Mr. Danby : Certainly the child ought to be going to school.—The Chairman : Has not the priest any influence over it P—Mr. Denby: The priest is agreeable to his being summoned in this case.— The Chairman: Well, we must try what we can do. He chooses to pay Sc per week rather than send his child to school. I think he will get tired of that. He will have 5s to pay in this case.—Mr. Denby explained that the de- fendant had not yet paid the fine inflicted upon him about a week ago, and the School Board asked for a commitment. —This was granted. •

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The neual fortnightly meeting of this body was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon, when the chair was occupied by Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton. There were also present the Revs. J. Lockwood, J. J. Bryant, J. W. N. Tanner ; Messrs. J. Knowles, J. Warburton, Mclntyre, Stokes, Lewis, Parr, Hall, Percival, R. Ashton, Weir, and Mounfield.—The Deputy Clerk read the follow- ing letter from the Public Works Loan Cotnnaiesioners, viz. :—"I am directed to inform you that the Public Works Loan Commissioners having had the application of th. 2 Run- corn Rural Sanitary Authority for a loin of £163 under , consideration, have resolved that a 'loan not exceeding .£166 be granted for the purposes mentioned in the applica:ion, upon the security of the rates author7eed under the Public Health Act, 1875, snob loan to be repaid with interest at a per cent per annum, at the same dates and within the same period, as the loan of £lO9 granted 21st May. 1383, and to be consolidated therewith, subject, however, to this Board's solicitor being satisfied that the requirements of thie Board, and of the Acts of Parliament applicable to this case, have been sufficiently complied with." The letter was simPlv received.—The Rev. J. Lockwood said he felt sure that thci would all agree with him when tic said that in Dr. Joseph Adams they bad had an excellent Medical Officer of Healths.. and he had very great pleasure in movinc: his re-wpoint- ment for the year ending Lady Day, 1877, at a salary of £I2O. If he dwelt upon the work Dr. Adams had done in connection with the Union as its medical cfficer be was sure that it would only occupy needless time. He had great pleasure in proposing, and that most heartily, that the re- appointment be made.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded the proposi- tion, which was carried without diecussion.—The Chairman said that the next business was to fix the salary of the clerk for the year lust past. For the previous year the salary was £llo.—The Clerk said that for the year when the surn of- £l.lo was paid, a certain sum was allowed for extra services in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal.—On the motion of the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, seconded by Mr. Hadtield, the sum of £B5 was voted to the clerk for his ser- vices for the past year.—Mr. Farringten, nuisance inspec- tor, reported on various matters of minor imprtance, which concluded the business of the meeting.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.

The voting papers in this contest were delivered yesterday, will be collected on Tuesday, and counted at the Board's offices on Wednesday. The Returning Officer (Mr. F. H. Gossage) will attend at the Local Board offices on Tuesday from twelve o'clock to four for the purpose of supplying voting papers to persons entitled to receive voting papers, but who have not received such papers in the usual courses. Any papers not collected on Tuesday may be delivered by the voter to the Returning Officer at the Board.Reem. on Wednesday in the fornoon. On the surface there is comparatively little interest in this year's contest. There is a total absence of mural literature; but the addresses of the candidates may be perused in our ad- vertising columns. The Owners' and Occupiers' Association are conducting a vigerens campaign, and are confident of success. Dr. O'Keeffe and Messrs. Dutton and Houghton have served the ratepayers on the Board for the past three years, and the ratepayers have had an opportunity of forming an estimate of the value of their labours, but Mr. Cook and Mr W. W. Gossage, though well-known, are untried men in any public capacity. The honoured name of Gos- sage, however, is almost suffieient in itself to ensure the last named gentleman's return. Their interests are attended to by an efficient stel: of canvassers. Mr. Midwood, who was defeated at the last election, had previously occupied a seat on the Board for three years, and taken a prominent part in the town's con- cerns with which he is intimately acquainted. Messrs. Martley, Webster, and Horrabin have combined to- gether to fight the battle against the opposing forces. They ineau to go in on the "purity ticket," and personal merits and ability, unbolstored by the "wiles and smiles" of canvassers, are the only pass-ports they would put forth for the favourable consideration of the electors. Mr. Martley and Mr. Webster have a past record as local legislators to appeal to, but Mr. Horrabin is not so fortunate. As usuel, the election is non-political, the one expressed intention of all the candidates being to serve their fellow- ratepayers with a single eye to the town's welfare.

THE LAND LAws.—The Lord Chancellor, replying on Tuesday afternoon to a deputation from the Fee Land League, said he was generally in agreeinent with the views of the chiputation in regard to tl.e ab‘plition of primogeniture, of ccpyhold, and customary tenure. He also agreed with them in regard to the registration of titles and the enfran- chisement of leaseholds. On the latter poir.t, hoTeever, he - must point out that the provisions of a measure dealing with existing leases would have to be less str!ngent than those applicable to future lets,s. The many existing leases bad been granted at low rent in order that the landlord might have the benefit of the works carried out by tbe tenant whenever the leaee should fall in.

MONDA.Y.—Before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell, Messrs. Jas. Handley. and G. L. Davies. A DOG ClSE.—Phoeb% Barrow, of the Royal Oalr., Wes- ton, was summoned for having, on the 18th March, at Wes- ton, failed to comply with an order of the justices, made on the 20th October, 1884, requiring her to keep a dog be- lonaing to her under proper control. Mr. Hitclaen appeared on defendant's behalf. P.C. Breeze proved seeing the dog at large. A man named Jones, who lodges at Mrs. Burrow's house, was called for the defence, and stated that the dog was his, and had been for two years. He produced two licenses.—Case dismissed.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TCPSDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenell (chairman), C. Broadbent, W. Long, and J. Marson. Srarcers CHARGE AGAINST A HUSBAND.—James Pickup, a young man, was charged with having assaulted his wife, ' Harriet Pickup, at Whitley Superior, on the 16th February. —Mr. Harris, of Altrincham, represented the complainant; Mr. McKeand, barrister, defended.—Mr. Harris stated that the defendant was a man who did not work, but he had an income of from £5 to £6 a week. The two parties were married on the 18th August, 1884, and almost from that period there had been a series of gross cruelties on the part of the husband, culminating in that of the 16th February. —The complainant having stated that there had been one child of the marriage between her and defendant, went on to give particulars of the assault in question. She said that on the 16th February her husband was very unpleasant throughout the day, and at night, after they had gone to bed, the baby was rather noisy, and because she could not quiet him he struck her on the shoulder three or four times. tihe then screamed out for her sister and the servant to come, and having opened the door to let them in her hue- band knocked both her and her sister to the floor. and palled their hair with so much violence that a consWer- able quantity of hair was pulled from her head. After this she was so taint that a cup of tea was brought to her, but the defendant seized it, flung the contents over her, and then dashed the cup against the wall.—Hennah Law, sister of the complainant, and the servant, Ellen Parkinson, gave corroborative evidence.—ln defence, Mr. Mclieand con- tended that the assault had been very much exaggerate The Bench, after a short retirement, decided that an aggra- vated assault had been committed, and aned defendant £5 and costs.--A judicial separation was then applied for on behalf of Mrs. Pickup. In giving evidence in support of this application, complainant said that the illusage of her husband commenced about a month after their marriage. , On one occasion be threw a hammer which just missed her head, and on another occasion he fastened her I and the servant into a bedroom and threatened that they I would be burnt to ashes before the morning. Defendant, she also stated, kept a loaded rifle and revolver in his house, and she was afraid of her life. After evidence had been given as to defendant's means, a separation order was granted, and defendant was directed to pay 25s per week towards the maintenance of his wife. WARRINGTON LIBRARY.

BY LANCE CIIESELYRE. Stimulated by the recent controversy in the columns of the Bxaininer respecting the Warrington Library, I the other evening paid a visit to the institution and was much gratified by the improvements which have been effected there. Notwithstanding all that may be said in favour of the "good old times," young people in Warrington have every reason to be thankful that ,1 they live in the latter part of the Nineteenth Century, I and there are grounds for the belief that the younger generatioos will have need to be grateful that their ,4 lines" have fallen to them in more •‘ pleasant places" still. For nothing will their gratitudeneed to be greater i than for the alterations and improvements that have I been effected at the Library darj.ng even the last de- cede, and the gratitude of future generations will be unbounded if the Library and Arts Committee, in their efforts to meet the public wants, will just go a step further and make the .institution all it ought to be. For a town of its size, Warrington offers very few facilities for the xecreation and improvement of its inhabitants But what few there are are fully ap- preciated; and none of the public places have given , more gratifying evidence ot increasing in popular favour than the Reading Room, a circumstance due, no doubt, to the extended accommodation for, and greater attention paid to, the comfort of frequen- ters during recent years. Indeed it is difficult to realise on entering the Reading Room u w that you are in the building used for that purpose some time ago. It does not seem long since the iustitution had a most dismal appearance, so much so that even the librarian seemed to be affected by his surroundings, and the contagion appeared to have spread to his feminine assistant who was a terror to all the small boys with a taste for reading who ventured into her presence. But a p'eaeant change at length came over the place—a change of which the public were not slow to take advantage. The windows, through which hitherto the light bad had hard work to penotrate, admitted the full light of day, which found its way into the furthest corners; and the solitary table and half-dozen straight-backed forms were re- placed with furniture of a more suitable character. The building was lighted by three large windows on the west side, and round the other three sides of the room were ar- ranged the books in the Lending Library, which i 3 a credit to the town. On twelve long shelves running round the the three sides were placed thousands of volumes from the pens of the most eminent writers in various walks of life. Here were to be seen the exquisite producCons of pohte, the brilliant narratives of historians, the charming fictions of novelists, the most startling tales of travel and adventure, the works of theologians and philosophers, the researches of naturalists and scientists, the writings of satirists and humorists—in fact, books of every kind. The coverings of the volumes also were of as varied a character as their con- tents, and amongst t`-em were sore,e excellent specimens of the bookbinder's art. Some of them had a serviceable every- day appearance, and shoxved signs of constant usage; Where, of more respectable exterior, suggested lees frequent consul- tation; while a few looked as fresh in their elegant bind- ings and letters of gilt as they did on the day they werelfirst put on the shelf. The books were protected from the public by a rail, except at the top end, where the librarian's counter acted as protector. At one end of this counter was the lib- rarian's desk„..fnd at the other near the door was a notice board on which large illustrations were exhibited. In the centre of the room were four light, though substantial pine tables, each with chairs for twelve persons. One of these tables seemed to be devoted to weekly newspapers, one to literary and trade journals, the third to the illustrated and comic newspapers, the fourth being used by general readers. Behind the two latter and immediately beneath the windows were shelves containing dictionaries, books of reference,-and the monthlies. The room was further adorned with several busts, and a portrait of William E mart, " who originated and carried the Act which gave free libraries," with a number of "rubbings "of monumental brasses in local and other churches, and with a check which hung over the door. Anyone who of late years has visited the Reading Room on Saturday or on an evening could not fail to have noticed the number of working-men who frequented the Institution ; and on wet days, too, it was pleasing to notice the number of men who followed outdoor occupations who turned in there in preference to the public-house. It was interesting when there was a full attendance to study the facial expressions of the various readers. At the first table a working-man, reading one of the " POpular Educators" with which it was furnished, leaned back in hie chair with a self-satisfied air; at another table one of the Upper Ten, who had come to exchange his book, had token a seat and was hurriedly glancing through one of the literary journals, while beside him was a mechanic engaged in studying the description of a new invention in an engineering organ. At the third table, always well attended by persons young and old anxious to look through the illustrated papers, an old soldier was gazing with admiration at an engraving of some military spectacle; near by a young fellow viewed with evident pleasure the reproduction of some scene in a far-off land; and next him was a youth with a comic paper before him who was Irving to suppress the laughter which had been provoked by some caricature or witty remark. Atten- tion was directed to the fourth table by an outburst of laughter from a boy who had buried his head on the book that had caused his mirth, and who broke out again as his companion a3ked Jinn what was the matter. There also was a Youth who as you watched him turned quite pale as he read of a bair-breadth escape of some daring adven- turer, but in a while he breathed more freely, and read on with intense interest; and occasionally gere to be seen amongst the readers members of the fair sex who would remain awhile to get an insight into the plot runninn• through the last "three volumes" they had obtained from the Librarian. In this excellently managed Institution, there was little to which exception could be taken, and under the most recent improvements readers seem to have all they could desire. The structural alterations of the place have been very striking, and the Institution has very little to remind one of ite former self. Immediately on entering the visitor's attention is arrested by a blaze of light which at night il- lumines a compact little office devoted to the use of the Librarian. Notices in front of the door indicate that books can be obtained at the left of the office, and that! the Reading Room will be found on the right. Fol- lowing the latter direction the visitor will soon find himself in a large, newly decorated room. Save the paint there is little in the way of embellish- ment about the place. As before, three sides of the room are adorned with book shelves, and what little space is left by the windows on the fourth side is devoted again to the books of reference, etc. The librarian's counter has now cnanged sides, for instead of being at the top of the room it is at the bottom near the door. Though book shelves are placed in the Reading Room, with a few exceptions they are vacant, and the room presents a marked contrast in this respect to what it did before. A slight attempt to hide the nakedness of the shelves is made on one side by the exhibi- tion of drawings of a proposed bridge over the Mersey at Rowley, and a plan of the town; while close by coloured illustrations from the illustrated papers are affixed. The centre of the room is occupied as before with the reading tables, which as usual were crowded with readers, and if the numbers continue to increase it is difficult to see where the readers will be put. The room is only' just large enough now, and if there is any great addition to the number of frequenters, the committee will have to let the readers take the books home. it looks as if, in making the new arrange- ments, the committee had kept this fact in mind, as the books, instead of being placid in inaccessible positions all over the Institution, are now concentrated in one apart- ment, and are so disposed as to be got at with the least de- lay from the librarian's office. The latter appears to have been specially designed for meeting the requirements of a Free Library, and when we have one the Institution will be much more useful than it is at present. While surrounding towns heve adopted the Free Libraries Act, at Warrington a subscription is required, and it cannot therefore be said Ithat the Library is free, in the usual acceptation of the term. It is desirable in theas days that no obstacle be placed in the way of the intellectual advancement of the people, and it is worthy the consideration of the Town Council whether the time, has not arrived when the rite- payers should be put on a par in this respect with those in I other towns, and the literary treasures of our splendid Library placed at the disposal of the humblest individual.

RUGBY RULES. WIDNES V. WALKDEN.—PIaved on the ground of the former, the home team being without Gouldon and Gandy, ' the rosult being a draw. Walkden scorimg two minors to Widnes on,. RUNCORN WATERLILIES V. WESTON SHANTERs.—This return match was pl3.y,!d on the ground of the former en Saturday, and a very pleasant game ended in favour of Weston by two tries and five minors to one minor. The tries were obtained by Molineaux. For the home team the brothers Nicholls played a good game. receiving assistance from Gibson, Meeres, and Woodwar.i. For the visitors, the backs played a sterling game, their kicking and passing be- ing done with judgment, while forward Austin, Molineaux, Lawrinson, and Farrell played well.

EARLESTOWN V. COLBORIsTE.—The roturn match between I thes cluhs wee played at Golborne on Saturdty afternoon. The late holders of the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup were represented by only three members vf their cup team, and as a consequence thu home team bad matters entirely their own way. The result was a victory for Gol- borse by six goals to none. The Etrlestown team com- prised the following :—T. 0. Roberts, goal ; T. Siddeley and J. Howard, backs; J. Whalley, A. Harrop, and W. Saul, half-backs ; Whitehead and G. Bowker, left-wing; J. Jones, centre; J. W. Sims and H. Holcroft, right-wing.

NOTES BY THE WAY. On Saturday the Warringtonians again demonstrated that a vast amount of improvement has manifested itself in their play. The Saints, previous to the mata, thought highly of their chance, owing to their success over Warring- ton last season. Having the assistance of the wind in the first half, they made strenuous efforts to register a respect- able seers, something beyond the home team's ability to wipe off. This enticipition, however, was not realised, as the men in " white " prevented the leather getting loose, and so robbed the opposing backs of any opportunities to kick with the strong wind. Manfully the home representa- tives performed their task, as, besides having a clean sheet, they recorded 12 points by the time ends were changed. Failing to score with the wind, it seemed impossible to do so against. 'l'bn visitors never looked dangerous nor even threatened the home citadel,and 40 points were scored against them, totalling 52, all told. Their play had no distinctive feature to characterise it, simply a forward game assisted by wing men to hamper the movements of opposite half-backs, who play the passing game. The display afforded by the home players was beyond question a more interesting game, though perhaps not so exciting as the one against Widnes. The passing was good, nonplussing the visitors at times, and the forwards showed they had lost none of their smart- ness and tackling powers. Runcorn faced Wigan (A. team) at Runcorn for the other tie in the 3rd round, and vanquished them by 46 points to nil. The performance is scarcely so good as the above, St. Helens ranking as a rising club, beating such clubs as Wal- ton, Wavertree, Blackley, and giving Atipull a very good game. Cestleford were defeated by Ruucoria on Wednesday,l but no criterion must be attached to it, as the Yorkshiremen lacked energy and were indifferent how they played. Just to show how careless they must have been and how their form is superior to Runcorn the following will prove, via —On Saturday they met Llanelly on their ground and played a drawn game, and Runcorn were beaten by the same club and on the same ground by 2 goals 2 tries to 1 try, last November. Rochdale Hornets sustained another to their already long , list of;reverees on Saturday, Wigan being the executants. The all-absorbing topic this week is the semi-final with Runcorn at Widnes. There will be 12,000 people present if , the afternoon proves fine, and the party feeling will be very high and exciting. If Warrington exhibit the same quali- ties, unselfishnees and harmony with each other, that they have hitherto shown, they will, no doubt, come out of the ! ordeal with credit to themselves and to the town they ! represent. The draw far the semi-finals gives:—Warrington v. Run- • corn, at Widnes. Umpires. Messrs. Wilcock and Ansaale. Referee. Mr. J. Jackson, Salford. Aepull v. St. Helens, at i St. Helens. Umpires, Messrs. Ireland and William*. Referee, Mr. A. Dewhurst, Broughton Rangers. Special arrangements will be made for the accommodation of the spectatoes at Widnes. A bumping gate for the West Lan- cashire Union is sure to be the result.

VEST LANCASHIRE CUP TIES. Run:ollN v. WIGAN.—The Union Committee having thrown Leith out of the competition for refusing to play oil the drawn game at Runcorn, the Runcorn team had an easy thing on on Saturday when they met Wi,,an. With the sordid motive of getting two gates, Wigan Club kept their best team at, Wigan to play the Itcchdale Hornets, an sent "A "team to Runcorn. 'file "A " had to retire de- feated by three goals, five tries, and four minor points—or 413 points—to nil. Lunt was in splendid form, and obtained three tries, whilst Spe4man, "the demon," as he is termed, , dropped a beautiful toal, and did some capital passing. The captain, H Hughes, and his brother, W Hughes, and Wainwright each obtained tries. Woods was in tine form at back. In fact all the Runcorn team played in admirable fashion, the passing being a real treat. Teams :—Runcorn : T Woods, full back ; E Lunt, H C Speakman, and T Johnson, three-quarter backs; 11 Hughes and H Andrews, half backs ; W Wright, W Hughes, J Lewis, J Clarke, J Gettley, J Dean, J Barns, W Faulkner, and Wainwright, forwards. Wigan : R Crompton, back; P Clarke, Mit- chinson, and B Wilson, three-quarter backs ; Aspinwall and Worstoy, half backs ; Sim. Peck, Harris, Carey, Swift, Wa.dle. Harris, and Scholeneld, forwards.
WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS.

On Saturday Warrington bad to meet the above club to try conclusions who should go into the semi-final for the above cup. The Sr. Helens team have not been so success- ful this season as the leen so the excitement was not of so large a scale as daring the previous week. In Warring- ton Warren's lads were the favouritee, whilst the St. Helens supporters were pretty confiient that their team would win. If St. Helens did beat Warrington lest season, they forget that Warrington had only a moderate team against them, and between that time sad the present Warren's lads have made wonderful strides towards the tor of tee ladder. Just now they are ielayiog a good combined game. Their for- wards are strong and fest, and it would be difficult to find a better set of backs in the county. Just a remark or two about passing, for it is owing to this that the boys in white have attained such fame during the present season. A few months back their passing was erratic, but during the last three or four weeks no fault can be found with it. Selfish play has been abaudoned, and if they continue in the seme form a grand career is before them. This was the most im- portant fixture for the above round,four clubs onlycompeting, St. Helens Recreation and Aspull being the lucky recipients of a bye, thus getting into the semi-final without • playing. Wigan chose to send their A team to Runcorn, thus throw- ing away their cuence rather than lose their gate against Rechdale Hornets.
