PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, when there were present Mr. John Leatherbarrow (chairman), the Rev. ; T. Chambers, J. Barnacle, Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. Joseph ' Ellison, W. Birchall, J. Jackson, J. Buckley, W. Gerrard, E. Syde, W. G. nshton,,J. Matthews, w. Tyrer, J. Griffiths. J. , Kenwright, T. Dobell, J. Fisher, R. Leigh, J. T. Hill, R. Tuson, W. Swift, H. Hnlme, P. Longton, W. B. Longton, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF Szemenes.—The Workhouse Master reported , there were 512 inmates this week, against 543 last week,. land 435 in the corresponding week of last year. There had been 46 vagrants relieved during the week, and also 46 last year. A DISABLED POST.—It was reported that a finger past be- longing to the local authority was hanging over one of the walls, and it would be a help to vagrants who wished to scale the walls_ The matter was referred to the Visiting Committee. THE MILL. Ctsesreoer.—The Visiting , Committee called attention to the inferior quality of milk supplied to the Workhouse by Mr. 0. Ward.—The Rev. T. Finegan thought something should be done in the matter.—The Clerk said the contract expired in June next, and the question was left over. THE naII•RANT CHILDREN.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board requesting the Guar- dians to obtain the names and addresses of the persona with , whom had been placed out the orphans and deserted child- ren who were assisted to emigrate to Canada last year. The ' Clerk said he had written to the Rev. Father Whelan, of Canada, who received the childrenebut he had reeeived no reply. He promised to again write, and the question dropped. TIM RafersTnevole of Vcanns.—The Clerk reported the receipt of ;£7B lie from the Local Government Board, being the amount payable towards the expenses of the overseers with regard to the reeistration of voters. APPLICATION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY.—Mr. 0. M. Barton, relieving officer for the Sutton district, wrote ap- plying for an increase of salary. He remarked that he had held his present appointment for two years, and he trusted he had elven satisfaction. The letter was referred to the Finance -Committee. THE WATER k•UPPLY.—Mr. William Longton, of Eccles- ton Grange, wrote on March 20th in respect to the water supply to the Workhouse, remarking that as the matter had been a long disturbed question he should like it to be settled for ever, and in justice to himself he must ask for some, definite arrangetnent to be come to. He had no wish to de- prive the Workhouse of the present supply, but just now another body was inquiring the price he would take to sell. Before entering into any proposition, however, he would sell the whole freehold, with all pumping arrangements and water rights to the Beard. He awaited their decision on the matter.—lt was decided to leave the question over for the consideration of the new Board.—Me. Dobell rel take it that the Board does not wish to prejudice Mr. Longton's Chairneln : Oh, no. ASSISTANT OVERSEER FOR WOOLTON.—The Local Govern inpnt Board wrote, under date 22nd lrch, enclosing copy of a memorial addressed to the Board with reference to the appointment of Mr. 'Laster, as assistant overseer for the dis- trict of Woolton, and reeked for the observations of the Guardians thereon. The memorial was a lengthy docu- ment, and was signed by the following :—Mr. Jos. Griffiths, euardian for Hale; Rev. Thomas Chambers, MA., rector,

and guardian for Halewocd; Mr. Ralph Leigh, guardian for Speke ; Mr. Henry Hulme, guardian for Little Woolton ; and Mr. John Kenwright, guardian for Tarbock. It stated that the office was rendered vacant by the defalcations and absconding of Mr. Wood, the late officer, and observed that it had unfortunately happened that the last five assistant overseers had all been defaulters. The memorials pointed out the steps taken to fill the post, and said the appoint- ment at last rested between two candidates, Mr. Spencer and Mr. Bakter, and at the Board meeting held on the 15th ult., it was decided to vote by ballot. That way of voting had never been taken previously on any occasion. The Chairman declared there were 11 votes for each candidate, and thereupon gave his casting vote verbally in favour of Mr. Baxter, and declared him elected. The memorialists were dissatisfied, but could not examine the voting papers, as they were informed they were burnt immediately after the balloting. The memorialists, the whole of the Gnardiane of the Woolton district except Messrs. Teams and Hill, the Guardians of Much and Little Woobon were unanimously in faiour of Mr. Spencer and Mr. Baxter had not their confidence in regard to his qualifi- cations for the post. They submitted the mode of election was irregular and illegal, that in a ballot the chairman had no casting vote, a casting vote declared verbally being in- consistent with the secret ballot, and that the papers ought to have been preserved and open for examination by any member of the Board. They believed the statement of the voting was erroneous, and teat there was a majority for Mr. Spencer on the ballot. They asked the Local Government Board not to confirm the appeintment of Mr. Baxter, and order a new election to be made in a regular manner.— A lengthy discussion ensued, during the course of which the Rev. J. Barnacle said he was surprised at the memo- rial. The comparison of the character of the candidates was quite out of place.—The Chairman explained the ac- tion he took in the voting, and said if his casting vete had gone the other way there would have been no. application to the Local Government Board at all.—Mr. Hill strongly denied several of the assertions in the memorial, and alleged that in favour of the unsuccessful candidate there had been five or six influences at work ; there was the territorial, the landlords', the clerical, the mggisterial, the publia house, and the corn market influence. Mr. Dobell, the Bev. T. Chambers, and Mr. Jackson ques- tioned Mr. Hill as to the influences which had been exer- cised, and it was stated that letters in favour of the candi- dates had been written by several persons.—lt was ulti- mately decided that it should be left to the clerk to forward to the Local Government Board what he considered a true statement of the facts.—The Clerk said he would be very sorry to grieve one section of the Board by saying anything for the otber.—The subject then dropped. ATTENDANCE or GUARDIANS.—The Clerk submitted a return giving the attendances of the various members of taae Board at committee and Board meetings during the ensuing year, from which it appeared that Mr. Eatock had attended 40 meetings out of a possible 97a Mr. \V. B. Longton 17 out of 100, Mr. Newsome 144 out of 166, Mr. E Johnson 1 out of 81, Mr. Ellison 34 out of 00. Mr. Griffiths 77 out of 148, the Rey. T. Chambers 55 out of 144, afr. J. Barnacle 61 Out of 110. Mr. Heald 22 out of 72, Mr. Leigh 24 out of 100, Mr. Fisher 83 out of 'lOl, Mr. P. Longton 20 out of Si, Mr. Lowe 70 out of 125, Mr. Kenwright 71 out of 124, Mr. Leatherbarrow 139 out of 108, the Rev. Father Finegan 27 out of 110, Mr. Gerrard 16 out of 68, Mr. Matthews 36 out of 110, Mr. Sadler 22 out of 96, Mr. Swift 31 out of 100, Mr. Birchall 84 out of 125, Mr. Marsh 2 out of 81, Mr. Hulme 20 out of 81, Mr. Hill 80 out of 139, Mr. 'ruson 28 out of 86. It was decided to have the same printed.
THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.—On the recommendation of this committee, the Clerk (Mr. Hartley) was granted a salary of £l5O for the past year.

div.head: LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WARRINGTON. SELECTION OF. ALDERMAN JOHN CROSPIELD.
div.p: THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WARRINGTON. SELECTION OF. ALDERMAN JOHN CROSPIELD.

On Monday evening there was, an important meeting at the Liberal Club of the Liberal Two Ilundred of Warrington, the principal business being to consider the reply to an invitation to Mr. William Crosfield, J.P., to become the Liberal can- didate at the next election. Mr.. J. G. McMinnies, J.P., President of the Association, occupied the chair. There was a large attendance, amongst those present being Messrs. John Crosfield, C. Broadbent, P. Monks, William Long, J. 11. Gornall, Ziba .1..-mi- tage, William Pierpoint, J. Bonnell,. Frank A. Roberts, Henry Roberts, and others.
MR. WILLIAM CROSFIELD'S REPLY.-

The CHAIRMAN said the first business they had. to consider was the reply of Mr. William Crostield to the invitation they had sent him to again become their candidate. It was as follows :- "National Liberal Club, Trafalgar-square,. London, March 19, 1886. "My DEAR FRIEND,—The period of grace which your Liberal Council has beei good enough to allow before requiring any answer to their offer-again to place me in the honourable position of Liberal can- didate for your borough has now so nearly expired that I cannot longer delay my reply. I regret that I cannot, under existing circumstances, accept the flattering invitation, as I do not consider that the present is a suitable time to bind myself by a promise which must extend over an indefinite, and, it may be, a lengthened period of time, during which the condition of politics and of parties may undergo a material change. "1 cannot sever the agreeable connection with the Liberal party in Warrington without again ex.-, pressing what I have already said to many:of your- number individually, the pleasure which, it has, given me to tight the political battle with so many: comrades whose loyalty and devotion will ever re- main a bright memory with yours truly, " WM. CIIOSFIELD.

"•J. G. McMinnies, Esq. The CHAIRMAN then moved, and Mr. C. BROADITNTi. .J.n, seconded, the following resolution, which was unanimously carried :—" That this meeting hears. with sincere regret that Mr. William Crosfield has. declined the invitation to become the Liberal candi-H date at the next Parliamentary election.'' . 1

SELECTION OF MR. JOHN CROSFIETID, The CHAIRMAN said it was now forthemeeting, to4ook elsewhere for a candidate, and he thought they could no; do better than try, as they:had done. before, to • fina a local man to accept the' position. Mr. F. MONKS, J.P., concurred in this view of the. matter, and moved—" That Mr. . John. Crosfield be requested to accept the position of Liberal can- didate for the borough of Warrington at the next Parliamentary election." The resolution was seconded by Mr; Itimmar, JEFFREY, and supported by Messrs. C.',Broadbent,, J. H. Gornall, F. Roberts, Samuel aulow, John Craik, William Long, Thomas Birchall, William Stirrup, H. Whitham. Thos. Flood, and others. While this business was being considered, Mr. John Crosfield left the room, and on re-entering was greeted with the most hearty applause:. The CHAIRMAN informed Mr. Crosfield of the nature of the resolution which had been so my' ni- mously carried

Mr. 'JOHN CRosrIELD, in reply, mitt he accepted the position, as he believed it to be his. duty to do so, although at the same time he must say that it would involve considerable personal! sacrifice on his part. (Applause.) Having accepted the position they had been kind enough to offer him, he should do all in his .power to secure the object of the association in regard to his candidature. (Cheers.) He was in favour of disestablishment, and also of perfect religious equality, and thought that the Church would he better, and the State would not suffer, if • there was a separation. (Hear, hear.) He should give his support to any. motion brought forward for the abolition of tithes, and should be in favour- of the exclusion of the bishops from the House of Lords. He should 'also, be strongly op- posed to. the establishment of a- School Board in Warrington. (Applause.) Hs knew that they would not agree in every respect; but they should not allow their disagreements to interfere with the great objects they desired to secure fOrtheir party at the next opportunity. (Loud applause.) Mr. John erosfield then resigned his position cf treasurer of the Liberal Association; and, after some other business, the proceedings were 'brought to a close by a hearty vote of thanks being accorded to Mr. McMinnies for his kindness in presiding over the meeting.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, TIII7RSDAY,, . We are now within Measurable distance of dis- closure of Mr. Gladstone's scheme dealing with Irish policy. On Thursday next the cat will be let out of the (Gladstone) bag, and the world will know where now it only conjectures. The event is looked forward to with unusual interest. Members are be- sieged by their constituents for orders of admission to the House. The extraordinary and, as far as I know, the unprecedented course has been taken of ballot- ing for orders for the Speaker's and 'the Strangers' -galleries. In olden times the Strangers' gallery was a pitfall for the stranger. Every member had the right to issue an order for admis- sion for every night. As there Were then 658 members and less than three score seats in the gallery there used to be exciting scenes outside on important oc- casions. If a member had given away his own order he borrowed from his friends, gave the,ticket to his constituent, who went away happy in the. thought that he had secured a; seat. But the seats were balloted for, and frequently there were two hundred strangers balloting. Fox' the Speakers Gallery the situation was more assured. The Speaker's order was issued, and if there was room the holder of the ticket had the right to take his seat without balloting. On Thursday every seat will be balloted for, only in this case the balloting will be done by members them- selves, and as only as many tickets as there are seats will ,be issued, every ticket will have its billet.

Mr. Gladstone intends to speak three hours if his - voice "holds out, and in respect of this important condition, as of all others, he feels certain of suc- cess. Doubt does not disturb his mind, even in view of the withdrawal of Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Trevelyan. "Put me face to face with the House of Commons and the country," he says, "and I will undertake to recommend my scheme to their acceptance." Everyone who comes in contact with him is infected by his enthusiasm,. and speaks as confidently of success as the Premier himself. His scheme is, one gathers from nods and hints of those in the secret, nothing like the proposals variously attributed to him. As far as the land scheme is concerned, the difference between rumour and fact , may be instanced by a single illustration. When conjecture first grew busy with the subject the sum of £200,000,009 was, with a light heart, put down as the cost. The scheme actually involved a maximum guarantee of 0E120,000,000; and this is merely nominal. Not a single penny of the British • taxpayer's Money will be spent. As to Home Rule, all talk of subserving Imperial interests in the desire to conciliate national feeling in Ireland will be proved to be groundless. MT. Gladstone looks for the advantage of a strong reaction in his favour when his scheme is actually before the public. It has been, painted, in such dark colours that when the facts are known the public will make haste to acknowledge its simplicity, and the soundness of its construction. In the meantime all the efforts of the Conserva-

tives are strained to bring about an alliance with the recalcitrant Liberal chiefs, Every morning the Times, which upon occasion really makes itself very ridiculous, comes out with an article urging, beseeching, cajoling, and threatening Lord liar- tiugton and Mr. Chamberlain to join hands with Lord Salisbury and defeat the designs of the wickedest of all Ministers. It is quite touching to observe the discovery made by this journal of ex- cellent features in Mr. Chamberlain's character. In fact, if he would only go over bodily to the enemy and join in the attack on Mr. Gladstone the ad- miration and respect of the Times for him would be unbounded. The Standard urges the same plea, though with less trace of the excitable old woman in it. It would indeed be a grand thing for Con- servatives if this juncture could be effected. But the hope is plainly futile. Mr. Chamberlain has a future before him which he knows he has imperilled by the course already taken. To join hands with the Conservatives in inflicting a last defeat. upon Mr. Gladstone wciuld be his political ruin, and Mr. Chamberlain knows how to take care of himself.

Various opinions have been expressed of the rela- tive character of the present House of Commons. Mr. Bright. is reported to have said that it was the best ever summoned. But Mr. Bright is so little there that his opinion on this subject does not carry its ordinary weight. Another observer, hid- ing his identity under the flowing title of "The Provincial Press Agency," has evidently come to the conclusion that the House of Commons are

mostly fools. A member has forwarded me a cir- cular received from the Provincial Press Agency, which is one of the most astounding things in its way I ever saw. For the trifling consideration of ten guineas a year the P.P.A. proposes to assist ruembefs of Parliament in keeping touch with their local. press; to popularise their work by constant references in leading articles ; to interest their constituents by notices in a weekly London Letter; to procurepublication of speeches not repor- ted in the daily press, to republish speeches in a series of popular London newspapers; to influence dis- cussions in hostile journals affecting inenibers of Parliament; to secure the support of newspapers circulating in the constituency; to keep the personelle (thus this mighty agency prefers to spell the word) of members constantly before the constituency; to give technical advice for acquiring press support to members dParlieiment :. and much else. Here, surely,

is enough for ten guineas a year, though this Of course is not the full expense that may be incurred. For example it will cost the aspiring M.P. three guineas a column "for procuring insertion of his speech in the London newspapers: I should- like ta see the P.PA- 'going to 'the ofßces of one of the London dailies with the man.useript of two or three eolurn.ns of a speech by Admiral Field, ftir example, and the three guineas per column. (less commission) his hand. The circular looks like a joke, but it is undoubtedly pat forward as a. serious matter of business. ' , ,1

London society will miss iii the coming season' one of its most picturesque habitues. This is the Maharajah Dhuleep Singh. There were few hcuses of the better kind at Which the Maharajah was not met. His great idea was to be an English gentle- man. To this end he bought a large estate near Thelford, where he had a notable preserve, and wite sometimes in. shooting. season visited by the Prince of Wales. He IS a very handsonie.man, with the most beautiful set of .teeth I ever saw,' and being in his company there is full oPportunity of admiring: them, for the Maharajah is -always sniffing. His father liras Runjeet, singh, Lad of- the Panjaub,, whose -name is writ . large in the history' of British struggles for supremacy in India. Dhu- leep Was in infant When his father died..' The Indian. Government of the day; With that prompt decisioni which Was wont to mark its procedure, bought • out the Maharajah for a pension of £40,000 a year. The child was brought to England, where he has since lived in princely state. But his Highness, who in spite of all temptation 'resolved to be an English,. man, has foiind that he must take the good with the bad; As an English landlord, he finds rents have decreased, and on the wholediscovers that he is. naft i rich enough to live n London, so he is going *back to India,. and his white teeth will no • more gleam in London' drawing rooms:. It is not often we find an English Bishop on his travels. Bishops' are supposed to find plenty of work to keep them 'within. touch of their flock throughout the year. Rut. Dr. Thorold- has found time to get away and see something of the • world. He made a tour a the, *United -States, ,and- went south as far as Meiico.' He' waS last heard oi from Jainaie,a, and is ekpeeted home before Easter,

Mr:, Toole is one of the kindest of men as well as the most humourous of actors. If a brother is in trouble, "Johnnie's " purse is always open,, and no charitable entertainment .proposed in dramatic circles is complete Without his hearty and generous co-Operation. Much that ha does in this way is necessarily known. But there is. much elSe, the knowledge of which is confined to:the recipient. I Ihear, of a delicate little kindlxaction he has just !accomplished. Henry J. Byron, to the. Surprise of • many who knew him, died poor. How this came 'about it would be.. hard,fo say; The only mark of extravagance that I knew abeut Byroli was that he kept a carriage and a couple of horses., and that cer- tainly did not seem out oi properrtion. to his in- come. One oth2r extravagaucehe had was a passion for changing his place of residence. lie would go to a new house, spend much meney on embellishing it, get his furniture in, and within a year take a ' dislike to the place and goto• live somewhere else. Put he was an industrious man, got big prices for his work;, and might well :withstand these little excesses. Still he died poor. The hat went round for the support of his wife and children. nut his ! grave was left neglected till it occurred to Toole to ' look at it. Thole had the spice railed in, a garden ground made of the mound, and a monument erected to the singular genius with whom he had cordially worked through so many years. DEPUTATION ON DONKEYS.— Much amusement has beer created in Glamorganshire by a remarkable speech by a lkt,L7 John Jones, delivered before the Mumbles Local Board. appears that a deputation presented themselves before tter Board to protest against the ill-usage the donkeys at the Mumbles Head received at the hands of their driver The deputation was introduced by Mr. Jones who *AO the a uestion was a peculiar one, but one which he coir sidered it was within the province of that Board to diet with. It might be said that as an assembly of asses thet might approach the question with a certain amount or brotherly love. (Laughter.) They knew from Holy WO that in the days of the Judges of Israel the valiant ssmeelt slew a multitude of Philistines with the jawbone of an as,' and he bad often thought that the inhuman treatment the poor asses received was due in a great measure to the dead' Philistines calling upon posterity to avenge them—(laugh ter),—for since the *arum episode the vendetta had gone' on, to the disgrace of humanity. (Hear, bear.) Mr. Jbnar continuing, said: i presume the deputation selected Me to plead the cause of the poor asses as the biggest ass on the. Board—(laughter) but whether this is so or not I care nothing. All I ask is this—Let us ply our jawbones tia'niglit' P.O that we may.determine to do all we can to improve the condition and lighten the distress and suffering of our fel' low-crsatures—(load laughter)—the asses outside the Board (renewed laughter) and prove the truth of the poet's words, " A fellow-feeling makes us wondrous kind.° (Roars of laughter Let it not be said that we are care less or unfeeling in this matter. (Cheers 1 I have mach pleasure in introducing the deputation, whose labours I hope' will have the effect of ameliorating the condition of the asses inside and outside this Board. (Loud laughter and air plause.) A fire broqe out on Monday morning in some farm build- ings near Dundee, and spread with suca rapidity that before the animals could be extricated 14 cows,*two oxen, and two calves were burned to death. NORWICH ELFCTION PETlTlON.—Jastices Denman and Cave delivered judgment in this petition on Saturday. Mr. Justice Denman said that of 52 cases of bribery only one was proved, that of Walter Banham paying a florin or half-a•crown to Charles Wigger. That being a case of bri- bery by an agent—for though Banham was no voter he was in and out of the committee room, and cinvassed—the elec- tion must be voided. It was hard that a candidate who desired a pure election should be unseated for the single act of folly of an enthusiastic or unscrupulous supporter, but it was important to the nation that an election should not ba carried on by br bery.—Mr. Justice Cave concurred generally, and gave his reasons at length. He said that out of 55 cases of bribery alleged only one was established; out of 77 cases of treating only four had been proved:. and out of 81 cases of illegal practices none had been proved. Under those circumstances the petitioners ought not to have their costs.

Sigh of the seamstress.--hem! Waist of time—The middle of the hour•glase. A flourishing industry—Ornamental penmanship. Domestic pursuit—Chasing the gudeman with a broom- stick. 'the working horse takes his meals at 'table d'oat awidoes his work a la cart. A student of human nature • says anything can be sharpened. Pat a lead pencil in a woman's hands and see. Worth, the dressmaker, may not be long rememberedafter his death, but it can't be denied that few men have made more bastle'in life. Ages will come and g 3; but woman will not be perfectly happy until she can have eyes attached to her shoulders, so that she may look up to criticise her own back hair. "Have you any reason to offer why sentence should not be passed upon' you ?" asked the Judge of the female pawn- broker, who had been arrested for extortion. "Please, your Honour, I throw myself on the mercy of the court. lam a poor loan woman." BEDAD !—An old Irishwoman at Birmingham, when the Inniskilling Dragoons entered that town some time ago, ex- claimed .witharreat delight," Well, boys, it's , mighty well ye look, considerin' it is over a hundred years since ye were here before !" • < " Undle James," said a young lady who was spending a few dayi in the country; "is that chicken by the gate a Brahmin ?" "No," replied uncle James, "he's a Leghorn." "Why, certainly, to be sure !" said the young lady. "How stupid of me! I can see the horns on his ankles." WHAT HE MINDED.—An incautious American traveller was exploring certain parts of Polynesia. The natives, not being acquainted with white men, killed, cooked, and ate him—not from cruelty, but just 'to see what kind of an animal he 'was. "1 dotft mind his being killed," said the friend of his bosom, commenting afterwards on the incident; "but r hate to think of his being' fooled away over a darned experiment." A gentleman, being threatened with An, infectious fever, said to his little son, who in aia affectionate mood wished to embrace him, "You mustn't hug me; you'll catch the fever." Willie, standing back, looked in amazement upon his papa, who, by the way, is a pattern of propriety, and quickly asked, "Papa, who did you hug ?" BROWN'S DISCOVERY.—Brown (newly-married) : "I tell you what it is, Merrit, I've learned e. great deal about women that I never knew before."—Merrit (smiling) : Well, I should say you had."—Brown (naeasuredly) : " Yes ; before I was married I always thought that if a woman was kept up later than usual, and, was anxious to get to bed, she would never stop to pat her hair in papers." , —Merrit (who had been of the same opinion) : " Well, I isn't' that what she does P—llroien (confidentially) : "Not a bit of it, my boy; she just cuts her prayers short." WORSE AND MORE OF h.—Fenderson (who has just been introduced): "Delighted to meet you, I'm sure. My , friend Jones often speaks of you. ' It was only the other' day he said, Mrs. Louisburg is such a fine, motherly lady !'"—Miss Louisburg (with a faint smile of annoyance on her smiling face) : "How droll! ' Your friend Mr. Jones .was probably speaking of my mother. lam Mies; not Mrs., Lonisburg."—Fenderflen (much agitated) : "Oh, I beg your pardon! but, really, is it possible that you have a mother living?" IT WAS MUTUAL.—TWO men who were rail-fencing along Michigan avenue under the influence of drink the other day met at Rowland-street. After a long stare at each other one turned away with the remark :—" Too bad! Too bad! Zhat feller'd be one shn3artest men in er country 'fee didn't git zhrunk." The other looked after him and mournfully soliloquised :-"Poor man! Might go to congress as well as 'not but for this awful habit. It's really too bad. I must shee him and tell him of 'er degrading 'fluences of zhrink." Apropos of the unconsciously funny speeches occasionally made by the late Mrs. George Hudson, wife of the million- naire railway-king, a 'correspondent sends the following story. It seems that on the occasion of some very grand dinner-party, when Mrs. Hudson was being piloted from drawing-room to dining-room, she noticed a marble bust on one of theepillars in the hall. "Do you know who that is ? " she inquired affably of her attendant cavalier. "Vat is Marcus Aurelius," was the answer.- " Oh, is it now!' ejaculated Mrs. Hudson. "But can you tell me," she ad- ded promptly, "whether it is the present markis or the late warkis ?" A !Urn! WOMAN'S REVENCM-*-A marchioness, who resides in the Legitimist faubourg of Paris, and who avoids the Napoleonites as " low " gives grand parties, To one of these an English lady took, we are told, uninvited a pretty Frenchwoman, a friend of the Empress. The pretty woman made herself conspicuous by her prettiness, but the marchioness found out who she was, and was disgusted. She , said to her, "I am so conscious of the honour you have done Me that I dare not expect a repetition of the unexpected compliment." The pretty woman grew pale, but smiled, and requested an attendant to order her carriage. The pretty woman was clever, and finessed a revenge. She bribed the marchioness's femme de clutmlwe to give her the list of guests invited for the next soiree.- Armed with this, she prepared a circular note, which she despatched to each of the invited late in the afternoon of the appointed day—" The marchioness presents her compliments to So-and-so, and regrets that a domestic calamity will prevent her," &c. She then went to a great "mad doctor," representing herself as the daughter of the marchioness, and acting with the consent of her ladyship's family. She told him that her mother, the marchioness, was afflicted with insanity, and that her mad- ness lay in the delusion that she was always having great parties. For instance, if monsieur the doctor would go to her ladyship's hotel that evening, he would .find her dressed in great splendour, with the salon illuminated, adorned with flowers, and buffets covered with refreshments. The doctor went on the understanding that he was to obtain the proper police authority to take the marchioness to a maison de sante in the event of the representations made to him being con- firmed by his own observation. He arrived at ten in the evening. He was the first—the only guest; and, though the marchioness did not remember his name, she took it for granted that she had invited him, and was profusely civil. His manner puzzled and his questions startled her, and, as he grew more abrupt on his perception of her lunacy becoming more clear, she was at last offendea, and rang for her servants. At the sanze time he gave due intimation of his police authority; the climax being that she was taken off by the doctor in hysterics. She was detained as a prisoner in his asylum until the whole truth came out, when all Paris was in roars of laughter.

div.p: GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Darbyshire, Bonnell, Ratcliffe, Brown, 'Greening, Foster, Wm. Hough- ton, Blackburst, Gibson, Humphries, John Houghton, It. nwtn, Kilshall, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assis- tant clerk). TILE PADGATE SCIIOOLS. The Schools Committee recommended, on Mr. owen's ad- vice, that the sum of £45 be paid to Messrs. Collins and Sons on account of their contract for stable and piggeries leaving a balance of £l5 on the contract.—On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Greening, the minutes were adopted. SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that fees had been granted in 111 cases, 84 of which were old and 27 new.—On the motion of Mr. BrAcKnunsr, seconded by Mr. BRowzr, the minutes were confirmed.

HODSE COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that six beds for the Workhouse, which had been ordered by Dr. Spinks, should be obtained from Mr. Mounfield, his being the lowest tender.—Confirmed. REVISING THE TENDERS. The CLERK said that it had been found on examina- tion of the tenders that instead of that of Messrs. Stead, Simpson, and Nephews being the lowest, that of Messrs. Roberts and Sons was the lowest. Messrs. Roberts' tender, calculated upon the probable requirements of the half-year, came to £64 12s 6d, while that of Messrs. Stead, Simpson, and Nephews was £7O 193 ld.—Mr. BROWN moved, and Mr. BONNELL seconded, that Messrs. Itoberts' tender be therefore accepted, and this was agreed to.—lt was also agreed, on the motion of Mr. BROWN, seconded by Mr. OWEN, that Mr. Wm. Lawless should continue to provide the workhouse with fish. VACCINATION AT NEWTON. Mr. GREENING, in accordance with notice of motion given at the previous meeting, moved that a gratuity of £lO be given to Mr. Cooper for extra work in connection with the arrears of vaccination in the township of Newton. He (Mr. Greening) had no doubt that the £lO had been very well earned, and the fact that they were in favour of vaccina- tion or opposed to it had nothing to do with the fact that Mr. Cooper had had a very great deal or wotk to do in getting together information and bringing people before the m3gistrates. That was not only so, but when Mr. Cooper was appointed, some few years ago, it was distinctly promised that he should have some recognition of his extra services.—Mr. JOLLEY seconded the proposal.—Mr. RAT- CLIFFE considered that that was a proposal to increase wages, and as it had been said the time was come when they should reduce labourers' wages, they should reduce all wages alike, and not pick out one class of men from amongst the rest. Re must say the Newton people were Very much obliged to that Board for their kindness in looking after their interests. Some gentlemen had looked after the interests of Newton so much that he was afraid they had neglected their own, and he therefore should be glad it a meeting were called at Earlestown for these gentlemen to attend and have votes of thanks passed to them. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He concluded by moving that £5 be given to Mr. Cooper instead of £lo.—Mr. UthsoN seconded the proposal.—Mr. OWEN said be was sorry they could not mule.: Newton with the whole of the £lO. He did not think it was fair that ether townships should have to contribute to pay for the extra trouble in vaccination caused by Newton aione. (Hear, hear.)—Several other Guardians supported Mr. Greening's proposal, which was carried, only Mr. Ratcliffe and Mr. Gibson voting against it. THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICERS. Mr. DARLYSHIRE moved the reappointment as attendance officers of Messrs. Shearer and Garnett, at the previous salary.—This motion was unanimously agreed to. THE NEWTON REGISTRAR AGAIN. A communication was read from Mr. Cooper, vaccination officer of the Newton district, stating that in several cases Mr. Appleton, the registrar of that district, had neglected to give parents the notices of vaccination at the time the births of their children were registered.—The CHAIRMAN

Sir,—Allow me to call the attention of branch com- mittees, political associations and clubs, and any other bodies, to the rourteenth Triennial Conference of the Liberation Society on May 4th and sth, in Loudon. These Triennial Conferences afford the opportunity for fresh men to join the movement, fresh methods of work to be sugg.s- led, and fresh spirit to be infused into the workers. It is not necessary that either the delegates to the conference, or the parties appointing them, should have been previously connected with the society. the only lualiticatioc required being an inaplie:i concurrence in the society's objtc s, and in the propriety .4 f organised efforts to obtain for them legis- lative sanction. Diset.tablishment ha,. now become a ques- tion of practical politics, and will come forward for settle- ment as soon as the work of the present Parliament is com- pleted. Every organisation ot Liberal principles ought therefore to be represented at this conference. I shall be glad to forward the arrangements circular to any person dcsiiing to know hew delegate's should be ap- pointed, and only add that all elections of del/gates must be notified to the London secretaries, or to myself, on or before April 24th.—Yours faithfully, J. F. ALEXANDER. 4, ht. James'-square, Manchester, March 31st, 1886.

div.head: ELECTION OF GUARDILNS.
div.p: THE ELECTION OF GUARDILNS.

Sir,—l am sorry to hear that some of the ratepayars of Grappen'nali have determined to oppose Mr. Darbyshire 's eitection as guardian. The office of guardian appears to be a very thankless one indeed, for after holding that office 15 or 16 years, and devoting a great deal of time and energy to the interests cf the ratepayers, Mr. Darbyshire is accused of seeing no further than Morris Brook. and of being extrava- gant wit'a the money of the ratepayers. Another strong ob- jection to him is that he voted against the inmates of the werkbouse having beer on Christmas Day. As regards the first charge, if ha had looked after Morris Brook more, and the affairs of the Union less, it would have been much better for his own interests. The charge of his having from the first supported the great and extravagant expenditure at the Padgate Schools is untrue, for Mr. Darbyshire was a strong opponent to the scheme when it was first brought for- ward, and voted against the schools being built, but after it was decided to build the schools he very wisely tried to make the best of a bad bargain; and his worst enemy cannot truth- fully say that he has not always tried to keep down expendi- ture in every way. I nincerely hone that the ratepayers of Grappenhall will think twice before they turn off an old and tried friend (and a ratepayer who pays rates on several hundred pounds) for one whose chief recommendation is that his father was a gocd Guardi.in several Tears ago.—Yours truly, A GUARDIAN.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

Sir,—ls it altogether advisable for a friend of the Eieuse of Lode to put on the guise of an enemy, and while ap- parently denouncing that chamber to be slyly pointing out its uses and advantagee ? "An Elector," whose letter ap- peared in your columns last week. evidently has a weakness for tactics (If this sort. On a first perusal one would al- most think he was fulminating very vigorously against the Lords, but a second look convinces one tiiat he is poking e little fun at their enemies. The gist of his letter, for in- stance, is contained in the following sentence, "One bears daily in political conversation that should Mr. Gladstone succeed in passing his measures of justice to Ireland through the House et Commons, they will undoebtedly be shelved by the Tory majority in the Upper Chamber ;" and after this he goes on to suggest the dreadful consequences that might result to the Upper Chamber from this action of theirs. Now, there are one or two considerations which convince one that all this is really exquisite irony. In the first place "An Elector" cannot possibly know anything about the " measures " he speaks of, and therefore be can- not say whether they are " measures of justice to Ireland " or measures of injustice to England. In the second place if he did know all about the " measures " I don't suppose he is possessed of any patent specific for ascertaining whether they would commend themselves to the majority of the people of this country as " measures of justice" to Irish- men or to anybody else. And, again, when momentous measures are suddenly brought forward in Parliament what is the most tlesiraile and most constitutional thing to ko ? Clearly to give the country an opportunity of pronouncing its opinion. And according to "An Elector" the House of Loris is bent upon giving the country an opportunity of pronouncing its opinion on these "measures of justice to Ireland," and therefore doing what is most desirable and constitutiona,. It is when we look at "An Elector's" let- ter in this way that we see he is, under the guise of a vie- mous assault. really bringing under people's notice the fact that the House of 'Lords may be relied upon to perform the most useful and most essential function of a second Chamber. —I am, sir, HOW) E.
WARRINGTON DIS FRES3 FUND. TRE MAYOR'S REPORT FOR TRE WEEK ENDING APRIL 2ND, 1856.

Sir,—l have the honour te report that the Ladies' Sew- ing Casa has met every day during the week at the Town Hall, and witla a val and energy worthy of the highest admiration, have employed themselves in making up gar- ments for the poor recipients. The following have been made and distributed :—Forty-seven skirts. 42 under gar- ments, 21 shirts. 32 children's garments, 2 jackets, 2 shawls, S pairs of boys' trousers, 7 pairs of stockings, 31 pairs of clogs, one poor girl a complete outfit for service, and a quantity of coals of 1 cwt. given to each fareily where sickness was known to exist. The distribution of bread and soup was continued on Saturday and Sunday last, but, as I intimated in my last week's report, the" Sub-Relief Committee " had decided to discontinue the soup and simply to give away bread, clothes, and (in case of sickness) coals. The numbers re- lieved were. on Saturday, the 27th March, men and women 325, children, 853; Sunday, 28th, men and women 313, chit- siren 1.072; rylonday, 29th, men and women 150, children 264; Tuesday, 30th, men and women 98, children 408; Wednesday, 31st, men and women 158, children 373; Thursday, let April, men and women 206, children 463; Friday, 2ud •April, men and women 192, children 583, making a total of persons relieved, 5,458, as compared with 11.498 last week, showing a de- crease of 6,040. It must not, however, be inferred from there figures, that the necessity for relief has dimin- ished materially, except to the extent of out-door workers who were frozen out, and who are, it is to be hoped, new wholly or partially employed. hat the distress arising from -trade depression is still extending, as the Relieving Officers of the Gnardians can testify—their relief lists being steadily en the increase, (le die in diem, and week by week. The only fresh contribution I have received to the fund -since my last wEek's report is a sum of £2O 17s 10d, the proceeds of a ccucert got up by Mr. Alfred Perris and his friends, but that is accounted for from the -fact that we are not in immediate want of funds as will be seen. We have a balance in hand (including promises) of 260 18s id, as compared with £341 15s lid last week, but there are plenty of large-hearted people liv- ing amongst us who will, ungrudgingly contribute to tho "Distress Fund," as the necessity for doing as may arise.
Total receipts to date £533 4 0 Total payments to ditto 323 5 11
I am, sir, yeur obedient servant, J. HARRISON, Mayor, Treasurer to the Distress Fani.
SOCIAL EQUALITY:
Sir,—l have come to the conclusion that " Jaques " has got a "political economy," a theory of evolution, and an ideal communism of his own. In that case, 'tis useless to

contest with him, because he has simply to discuss from premises laid down by himself in order to refute his oppo- nent. Badger-like, he refuses to be. drawn into a direct answer to my original queries. In his last, he admits in a lame halting fashion that a man done not "create his own fortune." He tells us that " the essential office of capital is to aid labour." Exactly so. But why dces he not stick to his original term "capitalist" ? Why has he shifted his ground? My whole argument has been to show that the capitalist—as we know him—hinders labour by pocketing the labour formed wealth of others, which is simply legal exploitation. As co-operators, we can dispense with your rich fortune making capitalist, and amply provide for the wants of each member of the 'community. Your capitalist who is possessed with "fortune and distinction," is as great an evil as your rich landlord, and therefore I again repeat , that "both extract a luxurious living from the poor," and the sooner we educate our fellow-men to co-operate for their common good, the sooner we shall have "social equality." We are informed by " Jaques " that "the vat majority of men, taking into consideration their own natures and the conditions under which they live, scout the very possioility of such a mode of life" as Communism. [The italics arc mine.] Who "takes" into consideration their own natures ? Dees one in a thousand? I unhesitatingly affirm that that Is the last thing they consider. The wiseet amongst us take too little trouble on that score, much less "the vast ma- jority." I am inclined to regard "Jaques" as in a "Rip Van Winkle" dream, and therefore pay no attention to his phraseology (I mean the sense of it). With reference to borrowed capital, all I can say is that interest on money, and rent on land, are equal abominations, and are part and parcel of our iniquitous conditions of eociety. But that is a question I don't mean to enter into in this discussion. Referring to the "vast majority," &c., they may well "scout the possibility of Communism" under existing• "conditions." Why the ' whole argument hinges upon that word " condition ; " I pointed that out in my second letter. Sir, I apprehend that "evolution" affects not merely the physical part of man, but the 'mental also; if not, we should just be one with the lower animals. As it is. we improve mentally, and thus recognise " evolution " in society ; in other words, sociology or the science of society, and from my study of that science, I recognise Communism as the outcome of sociology or "evolution." That the experi- ment has not been trieit on a large scale, is no argument whatever against it, or any other phase of social evolution. I doubt not a sprinkling of "Jaques'e" type existed in the great stone and bronze ages, ere iron had been used; and I could imagine a seer in those ages dimly predicting a better age, and forthwith up rose your "Jaques" to utter his crude notions about impossibilities, arising from their not being able to discern anything beyond that necessary pro- jectien of their physiognomy. The following grandiloquent paragraph on nay quoting

" Oneida" as an illustration—' was ever so mighty a super- 1 structure raised linos so minute and frail a foundation ?" I —reminds me of the juvenile act of firing a small train of gunpowder ; plenty of smoke. but little substance. Now I ; quite admit one swallow does not make a summer; but it is invariably the harbinger of the season. Here again our i friend dreams; I'll try and wake him. What about Buclh- I ism, Christianity, and Mahomedanism ? Again, what of the great Republic of America? Also the co-operative system, spreading its network of stores throughout Great Britain? The latter started fifty years ago in Toad-lane, Rochdale. Ah ! how the "shopkeeping " Jaques" laughed those twenty-seven poor working-men toscorn. To-day the united turnover of the Industrial and Civil Service Stores with kindred soci.2ties, reaches nearly if not quite thirty millions annually, and numbers thousands of memb.rs. .

" JAques's," "apex," and " weathercock" was a most infelicitous illustration, he had better try another. If I had chosen I could have given a score and more of kindred in- stitutions. I could name them in America, England, France. and Germany; a goodly number of " apex's " and " weathercocks." However smme people may mistake foundation stones for top stones, till they are better in- formed.

" By the way" how comes it that a whole nation— France to wit—does not allow its population to increase as other nations do? They seem to understand VA " great natural law of evolution" in one of its aspects. Perhaps they may yet comprehend that it is not impossible to apply that law in other ways, and thus one phase may be under- stood in one nation, and another phase in another nation, and so the world goes on. W. H. CHAPMAN. March 25, Warrington.

div.head: FREE LIBRIRY FOR, WIDNES.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRIRY FOR, WIDNES.
GOVERNMENT INQUIRY.

Mr. Stephen H. Terry, C.E., an inspector to the Local Government Board, held an inquiry at Alforde Chambers, on Wednesday, into an application of the Widnes Local Board to borrow £7OO for the purposes of a Free Public Library. There were present Messrs. Carey, Wright, Gatkell. Dr. O'Keeffe, and the Clerk (Mr. J. T. Allen). The Clerk explained that under the Public Health Act the Local Board had sanction to borrow £70,150. They had borrowed £51,150, and, the annual sum required to repay principal and inter- est within the various times specified was £3,153 163., equal to a rate of 7-88 d. in the £ on the present rateable value. If the Board borrowed the other sums for which they had sanction they would equal a rate of 2-361 in the £, in addition to the sum men- tioned. The surveyor's estimate for the Library was £9OO, but they had only proposed to borrow £7OO, because a surplus was expected ,from the Public Offices.—A representative of Messrs. F. & GoiHolme, the architects, stated that the dimensions of the Library would be 37 feet by 42 feet, and the height I 15 feet. The room would be lighted on two sides, and partially on a third. Sitting accommodation would be found for about 120 persons.—ln reply tol Mr. Wright, the Clerk said the Library would form , a permanent part of the Town Hall and Public ' Offices. When the Town Hall was built it might bel necessary to remove the roof of the Library, but this was not certain.—The Inspector: Is it not your in- tention to proceed with the Town Hall at present ? The Clerk: No, sir. It has been decided by the Board and by a public meeting not to proceed at present with the Town Hall.—Dr. O'Keeffe said at the public meeting there were only two of a majority against the erection of the Town Hall, and those two were not ratepayers —There was no opposition to the application, and the inspector went to view the site.

div.head: FRODSHAM•
div.p: FRODSHAM•
TRANSFER.—The license of the Commercial Hotel, Frod- sham, was transferred from Samuel Clarke to William Hen- shaw, at Eddisbury Petty Sessions on Monday.

KEEPING DOGS WITHOUT LICENSES —On Monday at Eddisonry Petty sessions Elizaheth WilsAl, of Froclsham, was summoned for keeping two dogs without licenses. Defen- dant's son appeared, and:said the getting of the licenses had been neglected. Fined lOs and costs. RELIEF CommirrEE.—The Honorary Treasurer to the Frodsham Relief CAnmittee, Mr. Henry Linaker, has sub- mitted a statement of accounts to the committee, from which It appears that daring the recent prevailing distress in Frodsham and district, extending over a period of seven weeks, some 70 or 80 families, representing from 350 to 400 persons, were relieved with provisions and coal to the value of about £66

RATEPAYERS' MRETnic).—Tbe annual meeting of rate- payers in Frodsbain Lordship was held at the Ring o'Bells, Overton, Mr. James Percival presiding. The following ap- pointments were made for the ensuing year :—Waywarden, Mr. .Robt. Ashton ; guardian, Mr. Thomas Lewis; overseers, Mr. James Percival and Mr. Rilpti Bate. It was resolved that the Assistant Overseer be allowed £lO for making and collecting each special sanitary rate in addition to his ordinary salary.

FROD-SHAM AND FRODSHAM LORDSHIP PAROCHIAL COM- MITTEES.—the usual fortnightly meeting of these committees was held at the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Friday evening, when Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., presided. It was resolved that tenders he obtained for sewering Barley Groves and proper- ties near thereto, and That the sanction of the Local Govern- ment Board be obtained to the surplus from Overton drainage loan being applied to defray the cost of the work. The Inspector was directed to make a further examination of the length of sewer at Overton. The Inspector of Nuisances reported that the public pump at Overton was still out of use, owing to the drainage of the cottages belonging to the Marquis of Chohnondeley not having been remedied. The notice for such drainage expired on the 11th inst. It was resolved that the Inspector press for the work to be carried out forthwith. Plans were submitted for the erection of two cottages in ship-street, Frodsham, by Mr. John Darlington, and the same were passed as complying with the building bye-lays.

A FRODSLIAM WILL DISPUTE His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes was occupied for six hours at Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, hearing an application for the grant of probate of the will of Mary Storer, late of Frodsham. The testatrix died on the 18th Jul v 1.885, at the age of 82 years, and the beneflcary under her mil was Hannah Wharton, a widow, who lives at Fro& sham. The application was opposed by Mrs. Harriette Storer, Kingsley Bank, Newsham Drive, Newsham Park Liverpool, sister-in-lawi to the deceased lady. The defen-, dant alleged n the pleadings that the will of the deceased was not duly executed according to statute? that at the time the deceaFed was not of saund mind, memory, and inderstanding, that the will was obtained by undue influ- ence of Hannah Wharton, and that the deceased did not know the contents thereof. The defendant also set up as a counter claim a prior will dated October, 1879, and asked for probate of that. Mr. Mulholland (instructed by Messrs. Linaker and Linaker), appeared for the executor of the will, George Wharton, labourer, Frodsham. and Mr. Shand (instructed by Mr. B. H. Newman, of Liverpool), appeared for the defendant.—After Mr. Mulholland bad detailed the facts of the case, Dr. Robinson, Frodsham, was called, and said he had practised in Frodsham since 1858. He had attended the deceased lady at intervals during that period. Be described her condition, and gave his opinion that she was quite com- petent to make a will at the time she did so. She was well nourished and well cared for by Mrs. Wharton. Mrs. Wharton, the plaintiff, was called, and bore out the counsel's statement. In cross-examination, witness stated that the deceased for the last twelve months of herlifepaid her 118, par week for board and lodging, and previously 15s per month and found her own food. The deceased bad furnished her bedroom, and partly her parlour. She was not present when the will was made ; she kept away pur- posely so that she could say that she had heard nothing. John Bethel, Frodsham, deposed to making her will. When she gave him instructions she was quite rational, and stated that she had no blood relations.
Enoch Aston, one of ih;w-iin.e-s;e-sTo the will, eaid when

the deceased had signed half her name she stopped, and asked himself and Rutter it she was doing right to leave all the money to Mrs. Storer. They said she bad a perfect , right to do as she wished with her own, and she then I stated that as Mrs. Wharton had had all the trouble and the mess, she ought to receive all the benefit.. The will was then signed and witnessed. John Rutter, who lives in Runcorn, said at the time in question he lodged with Mrs. Wharton. He corroborated the previous witness's statement. Mr. Shand entered into a long criticism of the evidence, and contended that there had not been clear and satisfac- , tory proof given that the will propounded the wishes of the testatrix. He called

Harriette Storer, the defendant, who deposed that in 1879. the testatrix made a will in her favour, and never intimated that she had revoked it. She frequently visited her at Frodsham. They were on the most friendly terms. She described a money transaction she had conducted for her, and said their relations continued of the warmest charac- ter.

His Honour, in a lengthy summing up, said be was of opinion it was deceased's wish and intention and indepen- dent action to make the second will, and she did it withou being driven or impelled to it by interference or improper influence being exercised over her by Mrs. Wharton, the plaintiff. He pronounced in favour of the plaintiff, the de- fendant to pay costs of the day.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURD4Y. APRIL 3,1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURD4Y. APRIL 3,1886.
THE ELECTION OF GUARDIANS AT
WIDNES.

For the four seats on the Present Board of Guar- dians, to which Widnes is entitled, there were nine gentlemen nominated. Mr. Thomas Sadler and Mr. Richard Kent, both old guardians, have withdrawn, and the issue now lies between seven gentlemen. In the Rev. Father Finegan, Messrs. Waring, Mathews, and Rock, the Owners and Occupiers' Association have four strong champions for their cause. They are gentleman of ability and probity of character and well able to deal with the business of the Union. Their address (given in another column) is the only one issued, the remaining candidates, Messrs. William Gerrard, a retiring guardian, J. H. Lea, and W. J Hargreaves having as vet made no sign. It has long been felt that as Widnes contained nearly due half of the population of , the Union, it was very inade- quately represented at the Board, and it is stated that during the next twelve months an effort will be made to obtain an additional two members for the township. At Ditton, Mr. Joseph Longton has retired, and Mr. R. White's nomination is invalid, so that the issue now lies between the Rev. C. W. Wooll and Mr. Jno. Hunt, licensed victualler. At Halewood, the Rev. Thos. Chamhers is unopposed.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

On Tuesday afternoon the usual fortnightly meeting of -I this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, when the chair I was taken by Lieut.-Colonel Ashton. There were also I present the Beys J. J.. Bryant, J. Lockwood, J. W. N. Tan. I ner, and Messrs. Hewitt, Knowles, Warburton, Mclntyre, Stokes, Campkin' Haslfield, Lewis, Parr. Hall, R. Ashton, Pickering, Weir, Hamilton, Aaron, Mounfield, Speakman, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).—The Assessment Committee recommended that the sum of £ll5 be paid to Mr. Linaker for his services during the past year as clerk, and a resolution that that amount be paid was car- ried without dissent; in seconding the proposition Mr. Speakman said the committee had carefully considered the work Mr. Linaker had done, and the services he had ren- dered to the Board and to the county, which had been well carried out.—On the proposition of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Percival, it was decided that the clerk for the School I Attendance Committee be paid £35 for his services, as hitherto.—The Deputy Clerk read a circular letter from the , Local Government Boald with reference to pauperism and distress.—The Clerk said that as a matter of fact they had had no increase of pauperism in that Union. There bad been no extra amount of distress in that Union.—A mem- ber ; And the works are in full employment.—Mr. Hadfield remarked that the Thirlmere water scheme had not proved a benefit, as it had brought a large number of paupers into that district. That would be the case with the Manchester Ship Canal; instead of takin away surplus poverty it would bring more paupers into the neighbourhood. The subject then dropped.—A circular letter from the Local Government Board was read by the Deputy Clerk, stating , that £5O 7s 41 had been allowed from the Parliamentary grant in respect to the registration ef voters, and the Clerk explained that he was requested to credit each parish with a certain portion of that sum. The money, he presumed, was , paid under the new Act—The following tenders were ac- cepted by the Board :—Clothing, Mr D H Jones, Runcorn ; shoes, a London firm ; drugs and oil, Mr Isaac Speakman, Runccrn ; drapery, Mr Thomas Wright, Halton; flour and groceries, executors of Mr Samuel Collier, Runcorn ; ; tea and coffee, Mr J 0 Jacason, Runcorn ;- coffins, Mr William Lightfoot, Aston ; meal and butter, Mr Samuel Basnett, Newton-by-Daresbury ; coal, Mr Thomas H Spender, Runcorn; wines, spirits, and beer, Mr Thomas E Price, Runcorn; butchers' meat and bacon, Mr W Gill, ' Warrington; cartage, Mr William Grounds, Aeton.—The following is a list of the attendances of the Guardians dur- ing the past year, concluding with this weak :—Thomas Hewitt, 15; Henry Lowe, 1; J W N Tanner, 23 ;Joseph 'Knowles, 10; James Warburton, 5 ; William Wilkinson, 6; Joseph Hoiliday, 0; Enoch Jackson, 2; John Mc Intyre, 14 ; Joseph Stokes, 13 ; James Whittle, 2 ; John I Campkin, 7; John Ashton, 21; Thomas Hadfield, 20; I Thomas Lewis, 17; John Lockwood, 23 ; James Parr, 10; John Arrswsmith, 8 ; H T Lowe, 1 ; Peter Hall, 8; John Harrison, 0; Peter Snelson, 0; Thomas Fors- ter, 9 ; Henry Percival, 7 ; Robert Ashton,, 12; Henry Pickering, 4; Jcseph W Baguley, 8 ; William Whitlow. 4; William Fisher, 11; William Handley, 0; Thomas Norman, 9; Philip Speakman, 15; William Whittaker. 11; John Highfield, 8; Joseph Smith, 9; Edward Vial- ! lington, Ii; John Weir, 22; J J Hamilton, 13; Edward Aaron, 21 ; J J Bryant, 18; Charles Mounfield, 4; Henry Neild, 1; -officio W V Fox and Charles Reynolds,.one attendance each. Twenty-five is the full number of attend- ances that could be made.—The Board then proceeded to-re- lief business.

div.head: WARRINGTON UN lON RURAL SAM-
div.p: WARRINGTON UN lON RURAL SAM-
TARY AUTHORITY.

The ordinary monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse yestirday morning. There were present Messrs. C. Broadbent (chairman), W. Long, Darbyshire, Owen, Jolley, Foster, Brown, Jaw. Houghton, Wm. Hough- ton, Kilshall, Humphries, Grange, Gibson; S. Sutton (clerk), J. C. Sutton (clerk to the Guardians), Dr. Seplston (medical offeer), W. Owen (surveyor), and G. Rawlins (nuisance inspector).
INACCURATE REPORTING : A CHARGE AGAINST A CONTEIIPORART.

Mr. GassoN called attention to the manner in which the proceedings of the Authority were reported in some news- papers. In a report of the previous meeting he was sur- prised to find that he had stated that his pasture land was half a mile from the Massey Brook works, when in reality he had said that his pasture land ran half a mile alongside the stream. Then again that—what ceuld he call ie?— " burning and shining light," "The Observer," did not re- port the clerk correctly, for he distinctly said he would not vouch for the truth ef a certain statement. And then it tried to make matters worse the previous Saturday when it said that at the meeting in question it was stated that &large quantity of arsenic was used at the Maesey Brook works. Now he (Mr. Gibson) must say he never said anything of the sort about what quantity was used, because how was he to know? "The Observer's" remarks of the previous Saturday he considered to 1 i downright lies.—The CHAIR- MAN: Incorrect, Mr. Gibson.—Mr. Grasratt t Well, incorrect we will y, but I call it a lie all the same. Mr. Gibson then went on to say that if tbe members of the Authority could not say asword in committee about the interests of the Authority without being in danger of having a writ served on them certainly he did not intend being a member. —The CHAIRMAN said it had always been a matter of sur- prise to him how very correctly they were reported on dif- ferent occasions, and how very clever the reporters were in catching the meaning of what was said, though sometimes mistakes would happen. But perhaps Mr. Ullman by call- ing attention to that would do good, especially as he (the chairman) understood that the repor- ters were present at those meetings on sufferance and that if they represented anything incorrectly or of a libellous character incorrectly the responsibility would rest with them and not with the Guardian who might be repor- ted.—Mr. Jettatr was sorry that any member of the Authority had to find fault with the reporters. He agreed with the Chairman that the reports were generally very correct, but, of course, a mistake might creep in. He did not think Mr. Gibson or anyone else need be afraid of bay- ing a writ served upon him for any error a reporter might make.—Mr. DARBYSIIIRE said that sometimes when the Clerk or a Guardian made a guarded statement that state- ment when it came before the public was robbed of the words that fenced it round, and it did, to some extent, an injury either to the Clerk or to the member who may have made it. The reporters ought to be particular in that respect, and he thought they generally were, but in the case of the paper referred to the editor had not been editor very long, and perhaps the mistake might be made through ignorance, or something of that sort. But certainly to his (Mr. Darbyshire's) knowledge Mr. Gibson was not the only person that had had a writ served upon him, and they ought to protect their members as occasion might require. He thought harm was occasionally done by reporting con- versations of a private character, and it was for the repor- ters to use discretion in that respect.—Mr.Gresox was then requested to state whether the other paper to which he referred was tbe Examiner or Guardian, but he replied that he could not say from memory which it was. [We may state, however, that no such statement as he reters to appeared in these columns.—ED. Ex.l SURVEYOR'S REPORT. Mr. OVVEN reported with regard to Lovely-lane drainage that he had obtained estimates for the laying of the drain from the houses in Lodge-lane, Bewsey, to the Sankey Brook. The estimate of Messrs. Hough and Son amounted to £4l 19s, and that of Mr. Robert Heaton to £43 189. If permission could be got for a short cut across the fields the estimates would be—Messrs. Hough and Sou, £36 4s; Heaton, £39. As the matter required immediate attention, he should be glad if they would give him instructions to accept one of the estimates and proceed with the work.— It was agreed that the tender of Messrs. Hough and Son be accepted.

MEDICAL OFFICHR'S IMPORT. Dr. Sephton reported for the month ending March 31st that the births were—males 14, females 16; deaths, males 8, females 8. The death rate from all causes was equal to 14 8 per 1,000, against 17 1 for the corresponding month of last year. The Nortality returns for Sankey were incom- plete, as be had not heard from the registrar since March 17. Two deaths from zymetic causes were due to whooping cough and diarrhcet (infantile), and occurred in Howard and Dale-streets, Liverpool-toad He had to rerort several cases of whooping cough at Hollins Green, and he had heard of a case of typhoid fever at Fernhead-lane. The case would be attended to at once.

div.head: CONTBACTS.
div.p: CONTBACTS.
The contract of M. Benjamin Grimabaw, of £44, for the removal of nightsoil in Liverpool-road for the ensuing 12 months was accepted ; and that of Mr. P. Winstauley of £lO, for Winwick-road.

div.head: PEZIKETIT DRAINAGE.
div.p: PEZIKETIT DRAINAGE.

_ The CLERK said the Penketh Parochial Committee had considered the letter from the Local Government Board on the above subject, and they recommended the Authority to send the following reply :--" My Lords and Gentlemen,—l am instructed by this Authority, with reference to your honourable Board's letter of the 6th January last, upon the subject of the Penketh drainage, to say that, after consulta- tion with the Penketh Parochial Committee, they desire to submit that the plan proposed and laid before General Scott upon the occasion of his recent visit would ineet all re- quirements for at any rate some years to come; and at the same time the sewage would be quite sufficiently purified to prevent any pollution of the brook. Intermittent filtration through land was shown open the plan submitted, the only difference between these plans and General Scott's proposi- tion being the extent of land proposed to be taken for the purpose. The committee are strongly of opinion that the existence of a filter bed, as suggested, would, from its, close proximity to dwelling-houses already erected, prove a still greater nuisance than now experienced, and would also deter persons from building upon what are now very favourable sites. It is also considered that the cost of the scheme proposed by General Scott would be far heavier than the committee's scheme, inasmuch as the annual rent of the land would be very much in excess, and the working empenses would also be heavier. For these-reasons the Authority therefore would again press the original scheme for adoption by your honourable Board. Should this, how- ever, not meet with approval, an alternative scheme has been suggested, which, if carried out, would intercept all sewage flowing from every source into the brook._ The sew- age would be carried by means of a special drain and cul- vert under the L. and N..W. Railway, near Penketh into the river, near the present outlet of the brook. Should this course meet with approval the necessary plans will be prepared and submitted. Before taking any further steps in the matter, the Authority wish to take the opinion of your honourable Board as to the alternative scheme proposed.— It was resolved that the above letter should be sent to the Local Government Board.
