div.p: COMPLI RENT& RY.

Mr. DARBYSHIRB moved, and Mr. 'POLLEY secondei a vote of thanks to the chairman for the kind and courteous man- ner in which he had presided over the Authority during the year.-1 his was unanimously agreed to, and the Chairman, in acknowledging ttle compliment, referred to the assistance be had obtained from more experienced members than him- self, and also to the efficient assistance from the very excel- lent officials connected with the Authority. This was all the business of public Interest.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT
COMMITTEE

The monthly meeting of this committee was held at the Workhouse yesterday morning. There were present Messrs. C. Broadbent (in the chair), W. Long, W. Darbyshire, J. Greening,.BlackhurstrJohn Houghton, J. C. Button (clerk), W. Owen (valuer), and J. L. Tunstall, and othevassistant overseers.

- VALUER'S REPORT.—Mr. OWEN reported; with•regard to the works of Messrs. Rylands Brothers, Limited, Church- street. Warrington, that the alterations had been very con- siderable, and he had made a valuation of the whole as now existing as follows : Gross, £1713 ; rateable, £1,329. The Penketh Tanning Company,. Limited :.Additions to works, gross £l7, rateable £3Bl total assessment on works, gross £lB5, rateable £152. Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Hope Mill premises, Dallam-lane Messrs. Walker appealed at the previous meeting against an assessment of gross £689, rateable £584. It appeared that in 1875 he (Mr. Owen) valued the works, and sutsequently in.lBBo+the ad- ditions, at gross £564, rateable £479 103, and he fund the addition over and above his valuation was put upon the property by the overseers; there being a minute to that effect. He had again been through the premises, and was of opinion that they were not worth more than his valua- tion, to which he thought the assessment should be reduced, and that that amount should cover the occupation of land round Hope House, adjoining the Hope Mill property, inas- much as the malt kiln was not occupied so fully or for the purpose it was when he valued it. Penketh School Trus- tees : The present assessment, exclusive of' the land, is gross £B7, rateable £BO. He had gone over the additions and found that they consisted of, portion of ths buildings, having been made two stories instead of one. A. large ex- penditure had been gone to, but it had been in taking down entirely an old wing and rebuilding it, one portion which was hitherto one storey being now raised to two.. He was of opinion that no addition shoeld be made to :bat assess- ment in convquence of these alterations.—Mr. Derbyshire said, with regard to Penketh School,.that the.steare superin- tendent, Mr. Gumersall, had found the assessment to be very high, and he (Mr. Darbyshire) thought as - the assess- ments of the other schools in the locality were low, and the Warrington Blue Coat Schoel, which mighl be consi- dered a parallel case, was free altogether, the acsessment of the Penketh School should also be reduced, as no one had ben,ficial use of it in the shape of profit.--Mr. OWEN mentioned that in all the townships of the Union he had visited he found that the schools were assessed at a nominal rate. The Wesleyan Schools at Penketh, if he-remembered correctly, were assessed at £s.—After a short discussion, it was agreed, on the motion of Mr. HOUGHTON, seconded by Mr. GREENING. that the assessment of the schools be fixed at £5O gross, £42 103 rateable. RE-APPOINTMENT OF VALUER, &o,—Mr. GREENING pro- posed, Mr. LONG seconded, and Mr. DARRYSHME and the the CHAIR3IAN supported, the re-appointment of Mr. Owen as valuer for the next year at a salary of. L2OO. Each of the gentlemen named spoke in eulogistic terms of the ser- vices of Mr. Owen.—lt was also, resolved that the clerk's salary for the past year should be £125; COMPLIMENTARY.—CordiaI votes of thanks were passed to Mr. Ryiands, the chairman, and to Mr. Broadbent, the vice-chairman, of the Committee for the able services ren- dered by them during the year. This was the prinoipal businessk
LYMM.

MisstoN Wonx.—Dnring the week the Rev. T. R. Wil- lacy, of York, has been conducting a very successful mis- sion in connection with the Parish Church. Several services have been given each day, and all have been very well attended.

ACClDENT.—Yestuday afternoon, as a waggon belonging to Mr. R. Heaton. contractor, Warrington,. which was laden with a number of long poles of timber, was passing over the bridge spanning the canal, near the Conservative Club, when a chain att4ched to the brake slipped as the vehicle was going down the incline. Three horses were at- tached to the waggon.. A man in charge of one of them, being in danger of being crushed against the wall, let go his hold, but was knocked down and rather seriously inj;ued. He was removed to Warrington Infirmary in a cab. Local, BOARD ELEOTION.,-Tho voting papers for the election of three members on the Lymm Local Board, were collected yesterday, and, the counting will be commenced this (Saturday) morning. It is expected that the result will be known between three and, four o'clock in the after- noon. The following are the candidates :—Wm. Brazen- dale, Bridgewater-street, Lymm, builder, nominated by Jas. Holt ; Hugh Cameron„ The Chestnuts. Lymm, agent. ROllll-- nated by Peter Stubs •,; Frederick Holt, The Cross, Lymm, agent, nominated by Mr. John, Fairelough ; Frederic Aloston, master fustian cutter„Newfield, Lymm, nominated, by Edwin Brown ;-Daniel Rogers, Stathatn,Cymm, commission agent, rrominated by Mr. Gr. C. Dewhurst ; John Thomason, Bridge- water-street, Lymm, bootrnaker, nominated by T. P. Norris. Messrs. Cameron, Thomason, and Rogers are the retiring members.

RATEpAyERS? MEETING.—Oa Monday evening a meeting of ratepayers was held at the Spread Eagle Hotel, Lymre4 for the purpose of selecting three candidates from those be- fore the electors to represent the interests of the ratepayers on the Local Board. Mr. James Holt presided, and took exception to many things that members of the Local Board had done. He thought the Board did not properly represent the ratepayers of Lynam. (Hear, hear.) Many of their would-be profus, by mismanagement, had turned out ta be losses. For instance, the Gas Works had not turned oat to I be such a source of revenue as some members of the Board had contended. Ht did not agree with borrowing money from private members of the Board. His opinion was that the only straightforward way to have met the gas account was to have raised the price of gas. He blamed the Board for delaying the question of the Massey Brook Works until after the election. The meeting was not called to benefit any particular class, but the ratepayers at large.—Mr. Ed. Burrows considered that the working-classes were not fully represented on the Board. It seemed to him tbat the mem- bers of the Board took no interest in the Massey Brook Works at all. The works had been there for the last 40 years. and now when Mr. Gibson came forward asking for powers to carry on exactly the same works, the Board seemed to be taking no action in the matter. He did not wish to set class against class in Lymm, nor to cause ill- feeling, but it was only fair that the Board should look after the interests of the poor as well as the rich. He proposed that the meeting should de its best to return Messrs. W. Brazendale, F. K. Holt, and F. 0. Moston as their represen- tatives on the Board.—Mr. Gibbon moved, as an amenkl- ment, "That this meeting do its best to return the retitlng members—Messrs. Cameron, Rogers, and Thomason."—Mr. G. F. Leigh seconded the amendment, which only bond one supporter.—Mr. George Hall trusted that the ratepayers of Lymm would sink small party differences, and do their utmost to return their selected candidates at the head of the poll.—The original resolution was then carried, and the pro- ceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chair- man.

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room, Lymm, on Thursday evening. There were

present Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Dewhurst, Rogers, Woolley, Forster, Gibbon, Appleton, Thomason, Hall, T. J. Ridgway (clerk), and Dr. Fox (medical officer.) THE RATE.—The Chairman, in accordance wirb notice of motion given at the previous meeting, moved that the rate for the ensuing year be 2s. in the L.—Mr. Hall said it run in his memory that at one time they had a certain sum allowed by the Government from the carriage tax. One year, he believed, it amounted to £12,9, and then it came down to £BB or £9a —The Clerk said be bad never heard of 1 any such allowance ; there was an allowance by Govezn- ment on account of main roads, and another in respect of ' the medical officer's salary, but there had been no other whilst be had been clerk to that Board.—Mr. Hall then re- ferred to an increase in the cost of gas lamps, and Mr. pew- Must pointed out that Mr. Hall would find that there bacr been an increase in the number of lamps.—Mr. Hall : Ido not say anything about that.-Mr. Dewburst : No, you never mention anything that does not suit your purpose. He thought if Mr Hall would attend the Finance Committee's meetings he would be of more service to the Board. He did not think Mr. Hall had been at a single committee meeting. —The Clerk also pointed out that the resolution as to the cost of as lamps bad bean confirmed at a meeting of the Board at which Mr. Hall was present.—Mr. Dewhurst said Mr. Tall came there after the minutes were passed and wanted to keep the Board waiting. If Mr. Hall would at- tend the committee meetings he would know all about the figures.—The proposition of the Chairman that the rate be Zs. in the £ was then agreed to. Mn. HALL LECTUREIN—The Chairman said he believed Mr. Hall had so arranged that he (the chairmanytahould not , again sit in that chair, and he should jest like to say that as far as his experience went Mt. Hall came to that meet- ing and talked to the reporters, but as soon as the reporters were gone Mr. Hall vanished. He never appeared at com- mittee meetings, and had not been at a Finance Committee's meeting this year. At the previous meeting of the Board Mr. Hall was preeent,whilst a certain subject was discussed, but when that was done with be scurried out o the room like a terrier after a rabbit to carry the news outside. He (the chairman) thought he would like to say that for the protection of b's successor, because it was expected that men who knew how to behave themselves would arms suf- ficient respect to the Board and the chair. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Hall came there pretending to protect the ratepayers, but be came to no meetingt that reporters were nat,present at , and at which he couldn't make a big noise.—Mr. Thoma- son said he was glad that the chairman had spoken out on the matter.—The subject then dropped. MESSRS. GIBSON'S' APPLICATION.—The application of Messrs. Gibson 'or permission to commence soapeboilino• at Massey Brook was again considered.—Dr. Fox presented a somewhat lengthy report on the subject. Haying dealt with the law relating to works of the kind in' luestion, and referred, to tke character of the Lymm district, the report concluded with the following words-: -" Lymm has got a pure water. Health, sentiment, interest, alike combineln saying let LpLerm, have also, as far aapractic- able, pure air."—Mr. Hall argued that the medical officer had not shown that the proposed works would be injurious to health or vegetation. In.the course of his remarks, he said Lymm Local Board had been compared to a flock of sheep. but that night he wanted them to think-for them- selves. He further contended that the opposition to the application had not come from the people interested in Lymrn, but from outsiders, the Rylandses. He moved that the application be granted.—A rather animated debate fol- lowed, but it was ultimatery decided, no the motion of Mr. Rogers, seconded be Mr. Gibbon, that the application be not granted.
TELEPHONY/ POLES.—A request for permission+ to erect 14 telephone poles on land belonging to the Board at fleatley was granted, subjeetrto conditions suggested by the Clerk.

Tam G3SI4VORKS.—A abort conversation took place with regard to the gas works, and it was stated that tbe leakage had been reduced from over 30 per at the and of the Sep- tember quarter last year to about 121- per cent:. Tho Chair- man remarked that the gas works were in a fair way of re- covering, and Mr. Dewhurst said that in about three months tinle they would finilthe place in very gc work- img order. This was all the business of public interest.
new writ for Norwich was moved in the House of Corn- monayesterday.

At the last moment, William Martin Edmonds (National- ist) was also nominated for Barrow. An unusually violent atorm burst over Thurles en Thurs- day night. Several bouees were unroofed by its force. The Daily, News says Mr. Jesse Collings has forwarded his resignation of office upon the decision of the election judges..
- Tile remains of the late Archbishop Trench were interred in Westminster Abbey on Yriday, in the presence af a large assembly.

There was.a revival of activity in the shipping business on the Tyne, on Friday, shipping office officials being busily eng,aged signing on -3sewS; The Oxtord and Cainuridge University sports took place at Lillie Bridge grounds on Friday afternoon; Oxford win- ning six and Cambridge three of the events. THE. QtEEN.—The Queen left Windsor shortly after ten o'clock on Friday. morning for London, to pay another visit to the Duchess of Connaught at Buckingham Palace. On Thursday afternoon Her Majesty attended a free dinner at the Windsor Guild Hall for poor children and unz-m- -pinged people.

-CITY OF LONDON IND Hom RULE.-4 largely at- tended and enthusiastic meeting of electors of the City of London, called by Lord Mayor Staples in response to a re- quisition,..was held on Friday afternoon, at the Guildball, London, to protest against the establishment of a separate Parliament at Dublin. A resolution to this effect was car- ried with about 200 dissentients amidst great cheering, fol- lowed by cheers for the Queen. It was resolved to send the resolution to Parliament. Several City Liberals were amongst the speakers, and the meeting was attended by be- tween 2;000 and 3,000 persons,

CoNnRmATION AT NEWTON.—The Bishop of Liver- pool held a confirmation at St. Peter's Church, Newton, on Friday afternoon, when the Rev. H. Monk, vicar, Rev. W. H. R. Pugh, curate, Rev. Canon Whitley (Wargrave), and Rev T. R. Matthews (Earlestown), took part in the service. About 140 candidates presented themselves for confirmation. They were under the care of their respective pastors, and were seated before the general congregation was admitted. The church was well filled. The Bishop delivered a short address to the candidates before the ceremony, and on its conclusion his Lordship again addressed them. He called upon them to beware of the downward step, not to give vp good habits, and to attend more regularly to their religious dutiea than they had ever done before.

div.head: BRUTIRH NAVAL PREPARATIONS.
div.p: BRUTIRH NAVAL PREPARATIONS.

In view of the alarming aspect which the Grecian diffi- culty has assumed, the Polyphemus steam torpedo ram was ordered to leave Devonport •on Thursday for Soda Xly, to reinforce the allied fleets assembled there. Should hostili- ties break out, this vessel will prove a formidable adver- sary.

div.head: BRITIONATRATJa IN FOREIGN COUNTRZELS.
div.p: BRITIONATRATJa IN FOREIGN COUNTRZELS.

On the motion to go into Committee of Supply, Mr. McLeonel called attention to the successful, efforts of the' German and other foreign Governments in pushing the trade of their respective cauntries in foreign markets in competi- tion with Eng:ish mantefacturers, and move& That, in the opinion of the House, the Governmen ought to consider the desirability of appointing properly ounlided diplomatic agents in all the foreign capitals or seats a government for the express purpose of promoting the eenelon of British commerce." He believed that, notwithstanding the cheaper labour and longer hours of work on the. continent, English manufacturers would still be able to bold their own and command • the. markets of the. world if they had but fair play. At present the. Englishmao. was met at eveey point with unfair competition of foreigners, assisted by the diplomatic representatives 0 the countries to which they belonged. He considered that our oreign Office did not exert the influence it posseseed, and if that department should spend a little money and ince:ease its energy good results to British trade lvould ensue.—Mr. C. PeLregre seconded :dr. McLaren's motion, and expressed the hope that the .Gevernment would energetically take up the subject e He coosidered there ought to be a minister of commerce in this country, and that. to our embsseles abr,4ad there ought to •he commercial men attached ii order to transmit information regarding trade and labour, to this country. He thought, without something was done to pre- vent capitalists leaving this co:retry, the present depres-. We sho.ald do our bestrto increase the Information of our mennrac- turers and workmen as to what was going an, abroad, and 'should endeavour to remove• impediments trade, but he did not think it would be welt for our console to imitate foreign contorts with regard. On trade and commsece.— , Lord W. Compton, Mr. Baker, Mr._ W. Lawrence, Mr. Sutherland, Mr. Seton-Xarr, and Mr. McLean , generally supported the amendment.—Mr. NOWELL, did not , believe British workmen need fear any fair competition as the output now per head by the British workmen was. greater than that of any of their foreign. competitors.—Mr BRYCE said the whole of the facts steted wouid be well weighed and carefully considered. Ile would not object to that resolution if it was so amended theet it ehouldezen as fol- lows :—" That the Henze hears with, satisfaction that the Foreign Office is preparing a scheme /or the greater effi- ciency of the diplomatic and consular staff, and for the collection and diffusion of information with regard to trade of foreign countriee.",—Mr. Bounxrecould na accept that suggested amendment of the resoltetion, as that amendment • for which the present Government wished to take credit was iritiated by their predecessors..—The raeolution of Mr. Laren was negatived without division, aedi the motion for 'going into supaly was withdrawn. PEASE explained that by the bill houses would be open in the country on Sunday from half.past twelve to half-past two and from seven to nine, instead of from six to ten.—or the eezond reading there voted 101, against 41.

WIDNES OWNERS' AND OCCUPIERS' ASSOCIA- TION. ELECTION OF GUARDIANS FOR WIDNES. TO THE RAT PAYERS OF WIDNRS. The Widnes Owners' and Occupiers' Association has pleasure in annowncing that the following gentlemen are nominated as candidates at the ensuing Election of Widnes Members for the Prescat Board of Guardians : Rev. THOS. FINEGAN. Mr. JOHN 1.11 ATTHEWS, WILLIAM ROOK. ~ J. W. WAREING. Considerlng the enormous funds under the control of the Guardians, and the large proportion that Widnes bears of the total expenses of the Union, it is highly desirable that the town should be represented by men of the very highest ability and business experience, In 1884, one committee alone spent, in legal expen es, nearly £7,000, or 2id in the £1 on the whole rateable value of the Union, the greater part of which might have been avoided if due consideration had been given to the depressed state of trade in Widnes. The well-known abilities of the gentlemen named above are a sufficient guarantee tkat every attention will be paid by them to the control of the funds of the Union with due regard to efficiency and economy; and the Wld.aes Owners' aid Occupiers' association appeals with confidence to the Electors to return Father Finegan and Messrs. Matthews, Rock, and Wareing at the head of the poll. FRANK GA SICELL, March 22nd, 1886. Hon. Secretary.

LOCAL BOARD ELECTION, 1886. Ratepayers ef Widnes. The time has again come round for yon to select members to represent you during the next three years. Having been nominated to serve you we cheerfully comply, without res- pect to any clique or party, and thus are Independent Can- didates, and, if elected, we prorn.se to study your interests— yours being identical with our own—that is to say: Efficiency with Economy. We do not believe in "penny wise and pound foolish." but we call your attention and ask you: Are you satisfied with the Board as it ri,w con,ists ? Are you satisfied that the Sewerage Scheme, which cost the ratepayers some £20,000,18 a success? We say at present that its largest drain is upon the pockets of the ratepayers. Your streets are now, as heretofore, full of filth and mud : and all for the want of Sewerage Extension. Notwithstanding tte promise of an Infectious Diseases Hospitil the lives of the in- habitants are being sacrificed. Look at the state of your roads and fo-tpaths, and ask yourselves. Where is your money being spent? We now leave the matter in your hands, and may say that no Canvassers will be employed by us; and we would ask you to Vote Straight for men who live in your Township, these being the men who know your immediate wants. Two of us have already sat as your representatives, and have not vet "Changed our Colour." We ask you to vote straight for JOHN HORABIN, EDWARD M ART I;EY, RICHARD WEBSTER. Your Townsmen.

LOCAL BOARD ELECTION, 1886.—T0 the Ratepayers of the District of Widnes. In compliance with the urgent requests of many friends. I have consented to stand as a candWate for a seat at the Widnes Local Board, and have therefore been nominated by a number of gentlemen who are well known, and who take a deep inter- est in the affairs of the District. In again offering my services. I can refer conscientiously to my conduct when a member of the Local Board up to a year ago. hly attendance at the meetings of various committees of which I was a member is an evidence of my devotion to the interests of the ratepayers; and my persistent advocacy of a policy of retrPi chment and economy, as far as was consistent with the efficient carrying out of the provisions of the Public Health Act, has I think,proved my ability to sit as a representative of my fellow-ratepayers. Therefore. In appealing for your votes and support in the pre- sent contest. I can with confidence pledge myself, if ieturned, to pace my time and experience at your service; and will en- deavour, as an independunt member, to do my very utmost to keen down the rates, and at the same time recure from the various departments under the control of the Board the most satisfactory and healthful results. There is no necessity for any further explanation on my part. All my life has been spent in Widnes and its neighbourhood, and the interest of every ratepayer whether cottager or property owner—is identical with my own, representing, as I do, more household property than any other individual in the Township. I am. your humble servant, JOSHUA MIDWOOD.
